Vsetnt , THE BATHER. list to the patter of waves, I list to her laugh of glee, And dream about beauteous coral caves And sirens beneath the sea. I imagine I see her put,

In a manner free and bold, In the ocean her dainty sandalled foot, To see if the water is cold. I dream of her shimmering hair, And her little snowy hand, And the half-forgotten' free-from-care Dear hours spent on the strand. • Once more I lead her about In the tossing, foamy main. But my vision is quickly put to rout, And my bosom filled with pain. As I wake to the merry cries, All coming with wondrous vim trom the bath-room, and I realise They're washing my brother Jim. B. B. MuNxrrnucx.

'ERE GREAT SOWER. Some fell to lowly hearts and:grew How, they knew not, they only knew Had opened in them a fuli flower Of trust and love and hope and power— Frost-nipped, before they met the Sower Trust unexplained, love satisfied To feel th' eternity of its tide, Simply because He at their side, Himself, seemed Love personified. And some fell where sun never shone, Where all dividing line was gone Of day and night, for all was night; . And not a star or other light Looked on this land, which once was fair—.

A vcoman's'heart. Love, sweetness, hope, had once been there— - Blooms upon tender branches, moved , By gentle winds, and loved, Which showed no signs that they might part' From joy and song of its spring-tide, Had died, and worse than died! And falling there it made strange sound,' Like Pity's speech to things tongue-bound By their own shame; For since this blight was in it sown voice more hopeful than its own Was heard in it, and all said, "Lost I" MALI He came And said that still in this dark land Were hidden sparks that might be fanned To a pure flame. And some fell from the Sower's hand To hearts—a kind of mountain land— Of men strong-breasted, used to sight Of billows of the stormy night, And signs from rising suns and wind And spellings of the sea-bird's mind How far a danger might be near, I • , Pr-where to cast a fishing gear; Rough-fibred souls from habit and birth— As clay is to fine garden earth— Yet honest, hating twists lie-made, And every sort of shape and shade , That shelled the downright truth from eyes,— Or wore a hypocrite's disguise. And though this seemed a foreign soil For what fell gently as the dew, Invisibly or half inv'isibly, , Tit )se hearts made by uncertain toil Wary of even that they knew, Sending one glance to Him who sowed Through a crust thawed by the Unknown,' Became 'all Mows like a rippled sea When promising their nets to load, And worshipped and embraced the sown. --Runday Illagazzne. E. G. CnAßLEswoirrn.

"A fellow feeling" in your pocket. for your purse does not make you feel "wondrous kind." A New:York woman has left her husband a large for- tune on condition that he shall remain single. Idappi. ness does come in double doses occasionally. Ggard, to old-lady who has been causing him a great deal of unnecessary trouble—" Well, I just wish you were an elephant; and then you'd always have your trunk right under your eyes." Was it an intentional joke when an Irish farmer de- inanded coMpensation from a neighbour for the death of his donkey, which, he averred, had been " ass-ass- inated " by the neighbour's mastiff? "I don't like these shoes," said a lady custtner, "be- cause the Soles are too thick." Is that the only ob- jection ? " blandly asked the shopkeeper. "Yes," was the reply. "Then, madam, if you take the shoes I can assure you that that objection will gradually wear away." An ingenious mother who has long been bothered by the fastidiousness of her children at table has at last dis- covered a way of circumventing them. She places what she wants each child to eat before its neighbour at table, and of course each cries for what the other has, and the ends of justice are promoted. - - Enter Bridget with a ten-by-twelve mirrror, from which part of the quicksilver has been scratched, in her hands, and the pallor of mortal fear on her countenance. "Oh, if ye plase, mum, the board fell off the back of this, and I see it was all covered with frost, but when I went to scrape it off, sure and it showed me hand in- stead of my face. This counthry is too cowld for me intoirely." An Englishman and a Scotchman had a dispute as to -which of their respective countries had produced the most eminent men. Every man of note was claimed by the Scotchman as that of a man born north of the Tweed, till finally the Englishman said—" Surely you won't claim Shakspere as a Scotchman ?" "No," replied the canny Scotchman, "but ye'll maybe admit that he was maist clever eneuch to be am?", A young man becoming engaged recently, was desirous of presenting his intended with a ring appropriately in- scribed, but being at a loss what to have engraved on it, called upon his father for advice. "Well," said the old man, "put on, When this you see, remember me.' " The young lady was much surprised & few days after at receiving a beautiful ring with this inscription—" When this you see, remember father !" "Mercy help us !" exclaimed a strawberry grower, " I'm a ruined man. "How can that be?" asked a friend; "your crop was magnificent, and it has all ar- rived safely in the northern market." "You know how careful I was to have the bottoms of my boxes close to the top ?" "Yes." "And that just as the crop was ready to gather, my old foreman got tight and I had to hire a new one ?" "Yes." "Well, that new man has gone and filled the boxes wrong end up." • A Scotch youth at school itt the Instittite, who lacked musical talent, and whose voice consequently jarred during:the singing lesson was always allowed a holiday on singing days. His mother, failing to divine the cause of her son's forced absence, paid a visit to inquire into the matter. In answer to her query as to why her .son was sent: home on such occasions, the teacher said, "Why, simply because he has no ear !" "What !" she exclaimed, " Nae ear? Did onybody ever hear the like o' that! Nae ear? Why he has a lug like a saucer, man!" FRESH AIR—TO be healthy and enjoy life, nothing is more important than fresh air.- The more fresh air we breathe, the less will be our doctors' bills. We must try to get fresh air without draught, and without feel- ing cold. The air should always be moving. This is cheapest done by having a hole cut, say ten inches square, over the door, and covered with perforated zinc, and by fastening a piece of perforated zinc to the top of the sash frame the whole width of the window and

about four inches deep; the top sash can then be lowered, and in this way the air is being constantly changed above our heads, and we do not feel draughts. Any working man can do this for a few pence. In bed- rooms this is even more important than in sitting- rooms. A costless plan is to open the top window and draw down the blind. AN INVINCIBLE ARMADA.—QIIe Of 'OUT wise men has been enlightening the world on the comparative value of railroads and bishops in Central Africa. One railway in his opinion is better than ten bishops. The question is not worth while arguing at length, but there are two points worth consideration. Firstly, that the value of a 't bishop" (a title which Our philosopher uses to include missionaries of all ranks, on the principle that the greater implies the less), is a variable quantity; that a man's efficiency, in fact, depends upon his power and character. Secondly, experience shows that the bishop invariably goes in advance of the lOcomotive, and not behind it. It almost looks as if this were the law—no 'bishop, no railway. What value would the same philo- sopher assign to the fleet, which is now an indispensable arm of the mission service? It is growing into a per- fect Armada now, invincible because its cause can never fail. The following list, not a complete one, has been published of the fleet :—The John Williams in the South Seas; the Enangowan and the Mayri at New Guinea; the Good News and the Morning star of the London Society on Lake Tanganyika; the Peace of the Baptist Society on the Congo; the Day 'Spring of the Free ' Church at New Hebrides; the Henry Wright on the South Coast of Africa; the illala on Lake Nyassa ; the John Brown of the Mendi Mission of .the Moravians; the Morning Star of the American Board in the Pacific Seas; and the David Williamson at Old Calabar. To these we must add the Venture of the London Missionary Society in New Guinea; the Blessing in New Zealand; a steamer ,belonging to Alfred . Saiter's mission; and by next autumn the Charles Janson of the Universities Mission in Central Africa.--Suntlay Magazine. There was once a consul at Bristol who indicated his office by a notice on his door, "In from ten to one." An old ship captain, who kept coming for about a week without finding the consul, at last furiously wrote, in the terms of a wager, under this notice, "Ten, to one you're out." Mother: "What did you mean by introducing me to Mr. Brown as your aunt ?" Daughter.: "Forgive me, mother, but Mr. Brown appears to be on the point of proposing, and it wouldn't do to run any risk just now, you know. Ile has a strong prejudice agaitast mothers- . _ ‘.

Have you ever observed (writes Sidney Smith) what a dislike servants have to anything cheap; they hate sav- ing their masters' money. I tried this expenment with great success the other day. Finding we consumed a great deal otsoap, I sat down in my thinking chair and took the soap question into consideration, and I found reason to suspect that we were using a very expensive article, when a much cheaper one would serve the pur- pose better. I ordered half a dozen pounds of both sorts, but took the precaution of changing the papers on which the prices were marked before giving them into the hands of Betty. "Well, Betty: which soap do you find washes best ?" "Oh, please sir, the dearest, in the blue paper; it makes a lather as well again as the other." "Well, Betty, you shall always have it then." And thus the unsuspecting Betty saved me some pounds a year. THE FASCINATION OF NATURE.-It is astonishing what power inanimate things obtain over the mind of man; once fall in love with the sea, and what can ever replace it in our hearts ? Nothing. It is for ever calling us; throug,h'the calm of a summer night we hear :it above every, other quiet sound; in the winter we picture it to ourselves in its thousand and one moods; and after being apart from it for any length of time, it is only the veriest shame that prevents, us casting ourselves on .the sand and touching tie waves as they come towards us, so glad are we to knatc_we can see its beautiful face again. It is the most perfect of companions, and never pails; but it is a subtle creature too, and so possesses itself of our inmost soul that we are never really happy unless we are within reach of the truest and most sym-

pathising friend we possess. This, too,•extends itself to some natures to the land. None can understand it per- haps who has not experienced it; but is entirely account for thetvay in which, year after year, farmers persis- tentlf4lose money, simply because fields and pastures that they have known from their youth are more to them, have more to give 'them of perfect happiness, than riches:and plenty have among houses and in citiek or in

I countries that they do not know.—Good Wards, Octobev.l I "Jou argers, sare dat .de world is flat and stands on I. big rock," sald 41211;10; "now I Want you tole me what &Crock stands On." a I'se s'prised at your. ignorance," returned Cato; "why it stands on annurer big rock." "But what does bofe of dem rocks stand on ?" said Sambo, confident that he had his opponent cornered. "Why, dar is rocks all de way down," replied Cato, after a moment's hesitation. "My coloured friend," said Sambo, with a pompous air, " I'se sorry to see such 'splays ob remitigated obscurity in a gemman of your egsalted pertensions ; allow me, who has experienced superior opportunities, yo correct de way deroneous repression you has, and inform you dat this. earf is round, and devolves on axles." "1 knows how to de- precate the feelings dat prompts you to distend to this gemman de information dat you furnish on de question dat we is at present debatin', returned Cato, "and wid all reference to s'perior opportunities to which you take occasion to prelude, I must disagree wid you on the freory dat you advances. Kase, if de world was round, dad turned ou axles, wouldn't de axle-trees broke down and spill all de people in the street? Answer me dat." It is quite unnecessary to add that Sarni:9 was utterly confounded by this overwhelming argument, and forced to "knock under" to the superior intellectual attain- ments of his opponent. DWARFS AS PETS.—DI the time of the Roman Empire it was the Custom for rich people to buy dwarfs and keep them as pets. Julia, the niece of Cmsar Augustus, I had a little favourite named ' Canopas, and a hand- maiden, Andromeda, each of whom was only two feet and a hand-breadth high. Augustus himself was very fond of dwarfs, and used to send to all parts of the world for them; but .he would not have anything ex- cepting those who were well-shaped, handsome, and lively. He and his little pets used to play, together in the palace; while listening to their pretty prattlings the great Emperor forgot his worldly cares. The Romans had a cruel practice of making dwarfs by keeping young babies in wooden boxes to prevent their growing; and by the time the poor little creatures were a few years old they were worth a great deal of money. In Egypt, and Peril, and Turkey pet dwarfs had been kept from the very earliest times, and from these countries the fashion spread to Europe. In the city of Mantua there is, in the Duke's palace, a suite of six very small rooms, with ceilings so low that it tall man cannot stand up under them. Two tiny staircases lead to these rooms, which are said to have been built for the Duke's dwarfs to live in. William, Duke of Normandy, had dwarf pages, and it, was the fashion among his 'nobles to have as many of these little creatures as they could get to wait on them and lead their horses in grand processions. CouLD SPEAK TO A Doe—Jesse Deems and Samuel Kemp, both about forty years old, had had many a quarrel and not a few combats. Finally Deems, who was the more pronounced and ardent character of the two, made a vow that he would never again speak to his adversary.. , "Gentlemen," he would say, "he is no- thing but a dog, and not worth a gentleman's speaking to. 1 would no more speak to him than I would to a dog." Kemp, good-natured, heard of the remark, but smiled, and ;said nothing in response. Not long after- wards Deems, having attended a camp-meeting where there was a great revival of religion, became powerfully exercised in his mind, and after some violent experience was thought to have obtained religion. Deems believed so himself, and having joined the church, after the meet- ing, Was over rode along home. Never had he been in so sweet a frame. On the way, in the midst of pious and happy meditations, he suddenly met his late adver- sary. He checked his horse, looked blandly upon Kemp, and then said: "Kemp, we've had many a quarrel and scuffle. I have said to myself often, Kemp, that I honestly did believe, that you were the triflin'est, low- flungest hound that I ever see, and that my intentions was never to speak to you again. But, Kemp, I've been to Big Spring Camp-meetin', where...they had a powerful rewiwal—powerful, Kemp—and I've got religion a thing I were afraid I never would git, bein' henderedby jes sich as you. And, Kemp, I now feels different. I feels like I could speak to anything. I feel, Kemp, like I could even speak to a dog. Good-bye, Kemp." Then I Mr. Deems rode calmly on, '

THE REIGN OF LAW IN SPIRITUAL LIFE.---EveTy drop of water is an example of certain chemical laws subor- dinating certain meclianical laws. Every plant and every animal maintain their being by the higher law of their life subordinating certain mechanical and chemical laws. Our civilisation advances only as we come to know the laws environing us, and become expert in ad- justing and subordinating them so as to produce new and useful results. The great triumph of civilisation, the steam-engine, be it in propelling the ship or speed- ing away with the train, is but a human combination of mechanical and dynamical laws, so as to subordinate and so far free the vessel or train from the first law of motion; or the vis inert is of matter. In like manner the spiritual life is maintained by the subordination of the lower law of sin by the higher law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus. But to be more explicit. The earth ,re- volving round the sun has, like all bodies revolving round a centre, a tendency to fly from its eentre,,which doing it would go crashing through tho heavens, destroy- ing and being destroyed. But from the destructive power of this centrifugal force the earth is made free by the operation of another force, the centripetal, Which draws the earth to its centre. The life of the earth is thus.maintained by the subordination of one law to an- other. The tendency of man is to fly off from the orbit of duty to which God has appointed' him, which to man as to the earth would be darkness and destruction to self and to others. But when man comes under the at- tracting power of Christ Jesus, the sun of righteousness, another force, the spirit of life, comes into regular opera- tion in his being, subordinating his natural tendency, and keeping him in the appointed orbit of his being "The law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made him free from the law of sin and death."--Good Words for October.

THE CoPTaiorr Coxottass.—The Congress of the Inter- national Association for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Copyright was opened at Brussels on Saturday by M Bernaert, the Minister of Agriculture. In this inaugural ad- dress he promised to bring forward during the next session of the Belgian Legislature a hill framed upon a very liberal basis for the protection of authors' rights and literary pro- perty. POACHING: KEEPER SUPPOSED TO BE •IWURDIIRED.—The Nottingbani magistrates on Saturday had before them three members at a gang of poachers who, when surprised in the act of netting rabbits on Colonel Seeley's estate, cammenced a murderous attack upon the keepers and nearly killed one of them. The men were sent to prison—two for three months and one for six months. On Saturday a head game- keeper on the Finlaystone estate, Renfrewshire, was found under conditions which support the theory of his having been murdered by poachers. THE HIGHLAND CROFTERS -- The Sheriff Courts of Poem and Locbnaddy baying clecided against the crofters in the cases selected by the land agents of the Highland Land-law Reform Association to test the legality of the sum- monses oi removal, affecting over 200 families in Skfre, South mat, &c., a document binding those who sign it to resist all ev,ctions, and to abstain from serving in the Militia, Naval Reserve, and all Government service till Parliament stops evictions and reforms the land laws, in re- ceiving the siguatures of nearly the whole male population f Skye, Uist, and other islande. An appeal to the higher courts will prevent the evictions being meantime carried nut, and Dr Fund, has issued an earnest appeal for contri- ! butions "to all who are interest-d in maintaining the rights! of the Highland people."

s THE WHEAT CROP OF 1884. The following appears in The Times:— Up to the end of June there was every prospect of a very abundant wheat crop. The seed time was all that could be desired, and the winter was unusually mild; the rainfall of every month from the end of January to the end of June was much below the average, and the I blooming of the wheat ha7d taken place during favour- able weather. Many farmers in walking round their fields at the time I mention must have felt that nothing now was wanting but a continuance of the favourable I weather through July to furnish an abundant harvest. The rainfall in July was not excessive, and if the whole amount of the rain that actually fell had eipended itself in the course of three or four days it would have done no harm. • At Rothamsted rain fell on 18 days during the month, accompanied in some cases with great storms of wind. I have rarely seen the wheat so completely prostrate, and in many of our fields it could not have been laid more flat on the ground, even by means of a heavy roller. During the two or three Weeks in which the wheat was lying upon the hot damp soil it suffered considerably from mildew, and many of the ears turned quite black. Fortunately the harvestnionth was bril- liantly fine, and the crops were secured in the best pos- sible condition. We have now arrived at the 41st season of our continuous wheat crop. The following ,table gives_ the produce of the same selected plots which, for the last 21 years, we have employed for the purpose of estimating the yield of the crop of the country : .---Averages--, 1884. 1874-83. 1852-73. 1852-83. The yield of the plot which receives farmyard dung, however, is nearly three bushels less than it Was-last year, being 324 bushels per acre, bistead Of 3.5 i bildlelffi,per acre, As this crop was not =inch laid, I fear it indicates that the 'damp w'ttlier in July affected even the standing corn, 814 that generally throughout the country the results of the thrashing machine will be disappointing. The mean re. sults of the figures give an average yield of ZBi, bushels per acre, weighing 62i1b. per bushel-equal to 201 bushels of 611 b. • This is six bushels in excess of the average of the same plots taken Over the last ten years, and rather less than two bushels in excess of the aver- age of 22 years. The present year's crop; therefore, may be considered to be more than an average, but yet , not a great crop: The area 'under wheat in the United Kingdom for the present year, as given in the Agricul- tural Returns, is 2,745,485 acres. Calculating the yield at 204 bushels per acre, and deducting bushels per , acre for seed, we have an available produce of 9,308,910 quarters. The estimated number of people to be fed during the year from September 1, 1884, to August 31, 1885, p slightly over 36k millions.' Upon. an average consumption of 5135 bushels per heed, our requirements will amount to 25,628,697 _quarters, of which our own crop will furnish 9 1-3 millions, leaving 16 1-3 millions to be imported from foreign countries. The imports of foreign wheat, less exports, into the United Kingdom for the harvest year of 1883-1884, amounted to 15,815,878 quarters, while the requirements, based on the yield of my own crop last year, amounted to 15,771,285: The actual imports, therefore, agree almost exactly with the calculated requirements; but this accuracy is apparent rather than real. The stock of foreign wheat in the warehouses on September 1, 1883, was known to be enormous, and this stock has probably been reduced. Theslow priice of wheat during the past year has also caused a larger proportion of home-grown wheat to be consumed by,stock, and the still lower prices which are likely to prevail during the coming year will tend to in- crease this consumption. The imports of foreign wheat during each year do not, therefore, at the present time supply so reliable a measure of the annual requirements as was the case formerly, when the stocks of foreign wheat had not assumed such gigantic proportions.—J. B. LAWES, ROthamsted, Sept. 22.

Thd last-named object, it may be stated at 'ace, cannot be ensured by the use of counter-irritants. On the contrary, it is quite as likely that the enlarge- ment will be increased as diminished by the use of blis- ters or firing. When severe lameness is present, repeated blistering is often very effectual, but both kinds of treatment necessitates a long rest, and it is often doubt- ful whether the rest or the treatment has most to do with the result. In many instances there is no doubt that great benefit would be derived from the constant use of the cold-water douche, with perfect rest in a loose box or stialm yard.

The appetite for Protection grows by that which it! feeds on. A deputation of French agriculturists has recently waited on M. Jules Perry to ask that the new' duties on foreign cattle may be more than doubled. The Dew= of Mysore, Madras, has sanctioned the expenditure of 1,500 rupees for the carrying on of ex- periments in preserving green forage in silos at Devam- budi, Rambanhanta, and Berur Kavals, and for growing green fodder on the Rambanhanta lands. LARGEST FARM IN THE WORLD.—TIie operations have been carried on Very extensively this season at the Bell Farm, in the Canadian North-West, which is said to be the largest farm in the world. Though this is but the second year of cultivation, there are already 8,000 acres under crop, 5,000 or 6,000 of which %re under wheat, and a portion of the remainder under flax. Last year 10,000 bushels were exported from the farm, and the excellence of the grain secured for it a good price in the market. The crop of this year is estimated to be 40 per cent. better.

SWINDLING A Faux:ED.—Mr. T. A. Sproat, of Heron- gate, has been victimised by an advertising swindler, calling,himself Percy Robinson, of West Ham. Mr. Sproat saw an advertisement in a daily paper for a manager of a poultry and dairy farm, and applied for the situation. He had an interview with Robinson, who got him to pay £5 on deposit, engaging him at £3 a week to manage a farm to lie' carried on by the Premier Dairy Produce and Cattle Breeding Company, Limited, at Wimbledon. After that Robinson was missing. SHEEP SceD.,—On Sattirday Supt. Farrah reported to the Bench,ht, Norton two serious outbreaks of scab in sheep in the Buckrose Division of the East Riding. The first was on the Heslerton Farm of Mr. Jackson, of Shar- dale, where 50 sheep out of a flock of 200 have been attacked; and the second at Mr. Cornelius Burton's, of Waverthorpe Pasture, where ten 'sheep out of a flock of 136 are down with the disease. The sheep had been recently purchased and taken to the respective farms, which were officially declared infected places. The divi- sion had been clear of this very infectious disease for many months, and strict precautions were ordered to prevent it spreading. A VALUABLE HEREFORD Cow—Mr. R. W.l Halls Lovely, by Preceptor (4030), which, with her twin calves Dorothea and Theodora' by Lord Wilton, formed such an interesting feature of the Royal Reading Show , of 1882, where the famous group took first prize in the family class, has during the-past week produced twins a second time. On September 16 she gave birth to two bull calves, beautifully marked, and of a nice rich colour, their sire being Godolphin (7664),4 son of Lord Wilton and Giantess, an eight-year-old cow, which at the Stocktonbury sale last month realised 92gs. Lovely won second prize at Maidstone, first prize at the Here- fordshire County at Ledbury, and was reserved in her class at the Royal. There are few cows that can get prizes and breed well at the same time, And Wily ?TN saw, her at Shrewsbury doubted her being in calf at all. THE HARVEST MooN.—Mr. B. G. ,TorarNs. F.R.A.S., writes to the Daily News :—There seems to be a general (impression that the present is the harvest mopn, because it comes upon the scene about the time the harvest is ending. Harvest moon, however, is not until the 4th of October. It is always the full nearest to the autumnal equinox, September 21, and was so called because for two or more nights the moon rises about the same time, and as this happens about sunset there would be con- tinuous light for he harvesters. • There are what may be called/good and bad harvest moons, which occur in al- ternate periods of about nine years. The present har- vest moon i a had one, not because it comes a month after the harvest is gathered, but because there is con- siderable difference between the times of rising, being about on an average thirty minutes taken over a period of seven days; -whereas in 1876, when the harvest moon was a good one, although happening as late as October 3rd. the average difference between the times of rising during a like period was only 12 minutes. We are now 'passing 'through a series of bad harvest moons, which will close about 1890. Even if we supposed the harvest moon happened as early as to-day-,-and it cduld not happen much earlier—the Bth of September must, as a rule, find the harvest over and the moon, for the purpose of helping; comparatively useless. If the evidence is worth anything, it seems to point to something of a change in the season—a quickening in ripening (which I think is partly due to improvement in the draining of land), and consequently an earlier gathering of the har- vest. A curious point about the harvest moon in Oc- tober next is that should any farmers in the north of Scotland be relying on the moon's kindly light for the night of the 4th they will have to "hurry up," as at a quarter past nine jlarkness begins to set in over the land, and lasts for about an hour and a half, the moon being totally Mired at ten o'clock. CO-OPERATION FOR VILLAGERS.—In a letter to 77ie Times, Mr. Arthurll. Dyke Acland has called attention to the great need of co-operative stores in country vil- lages. Mr: Ackland remarks that the agricultural labovers pay more for goods of a given quality than the members of any other class, except, perhaps, for meat and bread, and sometimes even for these. He quotes Professor Walker, who said :—" The curse of the poor is their poverty. Cheated in quantity, quality, and price in whatever they purchase, they are unable to get even as much proportionately for their little as the rich for their larger means." Mr. Acland knows a vil- lage in Warwickshire, with a population of 1,100, where the store which serves several hamlets in the neighbour- hood is entirely managed by labourers, and its receipts annually are £l7,ooo„its annual profits £1,250, its store capital £5,500, and the value of its freehold property, including a row of cottages, £3,300. He insists that the workmen must manage co-operative undertakings for themselves; but the rich or educated may give them the help of advice in starting. He 'insists on the need of security of tenure in the land on which the store stands, as the profits of co-operative undertakings in their early years are usually spent in the enlargement and improve- ment of the buildings. Information of. every kind necessary to enable villagers to start co-operative stores can be obtained of the Central Co-operative Board, City. Buildings, Corpotation-street, Manchester. FILLING A SILO WITH MAIZE.—In the presence of the Marquis of Cholmondeley and a large number of the tenantry on the Peckforton estate, Lord Tollemache last week filled a silo especially constructed with maize grown on an acre and a half of land. The rooks nearly destroyed the first crop grown in drills, and then his lordship sowed the land broadcast, with the restilt of producing a rich and luxuriant crop of maize, averaging quite 18 tons of green food to the acre. Lord Tolle- mache has long entertained the conviction that maize was not only better adapted for feeding purposes, but also capable of producing a much larger weight per acre than other green crops. The growth of this heavy' cropping food has already been adequately demon- strated, as the maize cut a magnificent crop, some of the stalks,growing to a height of eight feet. The maize was cut, tied into bundles of about 25 lbs. each, and cartedj to a shed adjacent to the silo, where it was put through, a chaff-cutter and transferred to the silo, a quarter of a pound of salt being mixed with each hundredweight of chopped maize, not for preserving purposes, but to make it sweeter for the stock. The silo completed is 12ft. by 15ft., and is built entirely above ground. Mr. Cawley, Lord Tollemache's agent, who superintended the filling, in the temporary absence of his lordship, expressed a strong conviction that this important experiment will turn out, like several others with ensilage at Peckferton Castle, thoroughly successful. NORTH LANCASHIRE.—The cereal harvest of 1884 in this district is now safe under thatch or slate. Our prospects for the year may now be briefly summarised. Hay crops about two-thirds of an average fcrop. Fruit j crops partial and poor on the whole. There has been a ' good crop of mushrooms, but the ffee rangers from the towns and villages claim the bulk of the growth, for they are on7the lands before daybreak. At one railway station in Westmoreland mushrooms have been sent to the large towns in waggon loads. Of the cereal crops wheat, of which little is grown here, is the best crop, but that is short in straw; barley is the next crop, also light in straw, and under average_ in ear; oats, which are the principal cereal grown, are the poorest crop of the three,7short in straw and light in ear. There are Some notable examples to the contrary, but the former is true of the bulk. Swedes, our principal feeding crop for the winter, may possibly make two-thirds of a crop at the outside; mangolds ditto, for the rains cleared off the maggot. Cabbages will not be of full weight, owing 'to a dry time after planting; carrots look like making I good crops; potatoes are on the whole a sound crop, but the tubers are smaller and fewer at root than last year. Taken altogether, our winter food supply must be a short one, and there is nothing in the present season which looks calculated to compensate farmers for the preceding bad years. The district agricul- tural shows this year, which are held at the end of August, and throughout September, have shown signs of the prevailing gloom that ' pervades all things agricultural. Through the summer farmers seemed hopeful that trade would revive, and that agri- cultural depression had reached its turning point; but the autumn has come, the iron trade, which is the staple of the district, shows no signs of recovery, nor does commerce generally. A dull, dealii winter lies beforeus, with wages at the lowest ebb, and this means low prices for all farm produce. Miners' wages at 255., and miners' wages at 555. make a wonderful difference in the prices of butter, eggs, milk, potatoes, and flesh meat. At most of the district agricultural shows the entries have been smaller, and the attendance less, so that we fancy some of them will have difficulty in making ends meet. At the parent show of the district, held at Ulverstone, on Tuesday, the cattle and sheep classes were smaller, but the horse classes were large and remarkably good. Evi- dently borse breeding is looking up again in the district, both in the heavy and light classes. The committee are evidently puzzled how to arrange the cattle and sheep classes. When they are" open' we are visited by some of the Royal winners and the tenant-farmers will not exhibit. When the classes are closed to the district, there are complaints from the public that the'' best ani- nals are not present, and that the show is shorn of its most attractive features. Both plans have been tried, but neither give satisfaction. :The cattle classes that filled best on Tuesday were tboso for animals not eli- gible for the Herd-book. Amongst them were some grand dairy Shorthorns, and one that is milking 30 to 32 quarts a day failed to receive notice from the

The Lancet has made up- its mind to the ghastl); con- clusion that conscious life persists in the human head after decapitation. The celebrated Jesuit Library of Cologne is at last to be united with the public library of the town, which 'ill gain 35,000 volumes thereby, and the town archives 6,000 documents.

A new cave dwelling has also been found at Lonathal, in the Swabian Alps, where others have been found be- fore. No remains of the inhabitants were found, only mammoth bones, fragments of horn, and bone scored as if with flint tbols, Some remains of prehistoric men have been found in grottoes, the entrance of which is below the lever of high tide at M'orbihan, in France. It is supposed that the rocks in which the grottoes are were once connected with the main land. • They were explored by torchlight. During the extensions of the port of Brindisi, remains of its ancient importance in Greek and Roman times are continually being turned up, the latest being a mosiac of the Labyrinth of Crete, and the Minotaur overcome by the blows of Theseus. It has been removed to the Municipal Museum..

• A method of military nocturnal signalling has been devised by a Russian, Captain Kostovich, and success- fully tested at Cronstadt To a small captive balloon is suspended an Edison electric lamp, which, by means of connecting wires, can be kindled and extinguished at will by an operator,stationed on board ship or in any other convenient position; a series of such extinctions and re-ignitions being employed according to a tele- graphic code.—Atheneunt. . . .

An American bibliographer has taken in hand the pre- paration of a sort of dictionary of the disguise names under which authors have issued their writings. Mr. W. Cushing, of Cambridge, Mass., announces a volume of "Initials and Pseudonyms." The first part will give an index of more than 8,000 pseudonyms, with the title of at least one work published under the pseudonym qr the occasion when it was used. The second will be an index of the real names, 6,000 in number, answering to the fictitious ones. • _

The Rev. G F. Browne has proposed to the Syndics of the Cambridge University Press that they should under- take the publication of a complete work on the early sculptured stones of England, in which each stone should be represented in its various parts by some pho- tographic method. The Atheneum says that the pro- posal is viewed with favour, but the Syndics desire to know what the probable extent of the work would be mad what astistance might be expected from local societies and from persons specially interested in these relics. '

A QUESVONABLE PRIEND.—The New Zealand Colonists, in their great war with rabbits, ought to remember that we may purchase liberty at too heavy i a price. The rab- bit is now the tyrant of the sunny isles, and the New Zealanders call in the mongoose, just as the Britons in- voked the Saxons to help them against the Picts and Scots.. The same policy prevailed in Jamaica against rats. There the mongoose has decimated the rats, but has also exterminated every creature that cannot beat it in fair fight, such as lizards, ground hatching birds, and many other members of the indigenous fauna. The lizard is reVered among the native New Zealanders, and they may rebel i,f the mong6ose destroys their favourite animal god.; • WHY NEGROES ARE BLACIL—The Lancet comments on an interesting communication made to Nature by Sur- geon Major Alcock on the reason why tropical man is black. The eyes of many of the lowest animals are generally to be descried by means of the patches of pig- ment which form their most conspicuous element. It is suggested that pigment placed behind a transparent sensory surface, such as the eye, increases the stimulat- ing effect of rays of light. The well-known absorbent power of dull black things for heat, and the increased activity of all living matter under the influence of warmth, are points bearing on this question. In the negro the pigment-cell are placed in front of the nerve terminations, and here the black pigment in the skin serves to lessen the intensity of the nerve-vibrations that would le caused in a naked human body by expo- sure to Otropical sun; so that the pigment plays the sameyart as a piece ,of hmoked glass held between the sun ankthe eye. The reasoning by which pigment, like the breath in the fable, is made to play the part of hot and cold,'does not seeth to be perfectly free from,objee- tion ; but the speculation must be admitted to be interesting.

THE STARS AND THE WEATHER.—A brochure just is- sued by M. Ch. Montigny at Brussels contains in con- venient torm the result of his studies on the state of the atmosphere as affecting stellar scintillation, with a view to forecasting the state of the weather. From the fact determined by W. Spring, that the colour of pure water in great bulk is blue, he explains the predominance of this colour in the scintillation of the stars just before and duritig wet weather. The luminous rays, he argues, traversing the air charged with large quantities of pure water are necessarily tinged with the blue colour of this medium. The excess of blue thus becomes an almost certain means of predicting rain. This theoretic con- clusion corresponds with the results of his obserdations continued for several years past on the appearance of' the stellar rays in connection with the state of the weather. 4.During the few months of fine weather in the present year blue has been much less conspicuous than in the corresponding Inoriths of previous years since 1876, when wet weathtli. prevailed. It also appears that green, which had always coincided with clear skies dur- ing the fine years befth'e 1876, has recently again become predominant,. Hence he thinks it probable that we have got over the cycle of bad seasons, and that dry weather and more normal summers may be anticipated at least for some time to come.

TELEGRAPHY.—Professor Edwin J. Houston, in the Journal of the Franklin Institute for September, gives an interesting account of " Delany's Synchronous-Multi- plex Telegraphy in Actual Practice," and describes "an extraordinary experiment in synchronous-multiplex telegraphy.' Professor Houston desires to state that he saw the experiment himself, and can vouch for the ac- curacy of the facts. "When," he wiltes, "we consider that a message made up of many wordlf, containing nu- merous letters, each letter consisting of numerous sepa- rate and distinct characters, and each character, under the synchronous-multiplex system, consisting of nu- merous impulses, was transmitted with certainty over a single wire, back and forth a great number of times, without the slightest interruption the he with the other, the fact almost challenges belief. Timing the in- tervals of the return of the original signal between the two cities over the sextuplex circles, it was observed that it travelled between Boston and Providence over these six circles 300 times, or covered the distance be- tween Boston and Providence 1,800 times in each minute, thus making an entire distance of 1,500 miles a second, or 90,000 miles a minute; or for five minutes that a dot was. kept going, the original signal in that short time travelled no less than 450,000 miles, or 18 times as far as the entire distance around the world at the equator."—Atheneion. •

THE UTILISATION OF THE NIAGARA FALLS.—At a recent meeting of the American Associalion of Civil Engineers, Mr. Benjamin Rhodes described what had_ been done, and what might be done, towards the utilisation. of Niagara for electrical purposes. He said: "The power of Niagara can be estimated very approximately. The average flow of the rider acoording to many careful measurements ,is 275,000 cubic feet per second. The fall in the river through the rapids immediately above the fall is 65 feet. The height of the falls is 165 feet, making a total of 230 feet; thus we have for the whole power 7,000,000 horse-power. To utilise' this amount of power by water-wheels, generate electrical currents, and transmit to various cities within 500 miles, would neces- sitate t plant representing at least 5,000,000,000 dols. Such figures as these give some idea of the enormous amount of power, here in reserve." He states that on the Canadian side the entire use of the falls is repre- sented by a small over-shot wheel, which propels a pump furnishing a meagre supply of water to the ad- joining village. On the American side there are five separate raceways, developing in all 800 to 1,000 horse- power. After describing the hydraulic canal, the greatest power now in use at Niagara, he says: "Further de- velopments of power at Niagara may be made at little expense. The hydraulic canal can be deepened and widened, and wheels may be set under greater heads, the total amount thus made available here being equal to the necessities of many years. It may safely be said that the use of Niagara has just begun. Low water is unknown; troubles from ice are slight; hours of use are not limited to eight or ten, but 24 hours in the day, and 365 days in the year, and unlimited power is ready, making this the rnost reliable, As it is the grandest, water-power in the world." The use of Niagara! It • sounds a little too utilitarian.—Harper'. Thiya:zne.

THE MANAGEMENT OF PONLTRY. SCOTCH GREYS. One of the least known breeds south of the Border is that which we select this week for our subject, and yet it Is undoubtedly one of the most useful of all the varie- ties of British domestic poultry. They have been de- scribed as "a large hardy cuckoo dorking, without the fifth toe," but they are rather longer on the leg than the dorking, and scarcely so square in body. Yet the de- scription given is not very far from:the truth, for the Scotch Grey partakes of the dorking type more than that of any other. How they have originated we as yet have been unable to discover, but they have been known and bred pure for a long period of time, and there is no suspicion that they_are a recently manufactured variety. At least, the manufacture must have been at such a re- mote date as not to be remembered, and probably that is quite as much as we can say for any of Our breeds. Some of the most popular kinds are of mushroom growth, and can claim no ancient line of ancestors. If such a thing is known in poultry lore, they have the "bar sinister" on their escutcheon. But, so far as we have been able to learn, this is not so with the Scotch Grey... ..

To describe the breed, we must be content to say that they are somewhat like the dorking type, but with the differences already noted. There is an upright carriage scarcely the same as that of the dorking, and the size to which they grow is not quite so great. ' The cocks weigh 81b. to Nib. when a year old, and the hens, as a rule, not more than a pound less. The groundwork of the plumage is a beautiful blue grey, with neat moons of a metallic .black on every feather. In both male and female the pencilling or marking should be equal all over, from the tiny feathers on the face to the sickles, though, of course, it is easier in this respectsto say what is wanted than to obtain it. The sickles themselves are often mottled with black or white, and not unfrequently are actually of the same colour. The comb of the cock is large and single, the wattles proportionately long, and, with the face and ear lobes, should be of a bright scarlet to look well. In the hen, the comb should fall slightly over to one side, but by no means so mubh as is the case with members of the Spanish tribe. If there is the slightest tinge of white on the face, or on the ear lobes, such a bird ought tO be rejected, as this is a fault that, once allowed to creep in, spreads very rapidly, and the leprous white streaks or spots on the face of any. fowl is most objectionable in our eyes. The legs should be white, but in Scotland spottled or sooty legs are not at all objected to, different altogether in this respect to dorkings, with whick a sooty leg is regarded as a fatal bldmisli. The foot is four-toed, in this again differing from the dorking, but here the advantage is all on the side of the Scotch Grey. The fifth toe both in the dork- lug and the houdan is a prolific source of bumblefoot, and that is a great annoyance to the poultry keeper, a 8 well as a serious loss. This nasty disease causes a great reduction of the strength of a fowl, and it would be I worth while abolishing the useless fifth toe altogether in I order to get rid of the tendency to bumblefoot which I appears to accompany it; and it is to us a great recora. mendatiOn of the' Scotch Grey not having more. than four toes. • There is just oild point More in .the out Ward appear- see ef the SCOtch Grey that needs to be specially noted, but it is most itaportant. The presence of straw coloured or red ftatlrrs in the hackle or saddle, and they sometimes need to be looked for, in order to be seen, will bring no end of trouble in breeding as well as be a great eyesore thethselves, breaking as they do the perfect uniformity of' the 'plumage. Birds with these objection- able feathers in them breed chickens red on the neck hackle, as red as a game cock in some instances. No judge can be forgiven who awards a prize to a bird in which the silver grey shade is broken by straw or brassy feathers, and the breeder VII find it a grave error to allow them to pass whenever they are found. A bird with them in had better find his destiny in the pot as speedily as possible, so as to remove all danger out of the way. 'Coming now to the qualities of this breed, it is' a first class all-round fowl, and for that reason very suitable indeed for farmers. It is a good layer of large white, well-flavoured eggs, not, of course, rivaling any of the non- sitting varieties, but laying an Average of over 100 eggs per annum, which is by no means a bad total for a hen that attends to maternal duties, and is also a. good table fowl. And 100 eggs of the size that ,Scotch Greys are accustomed to produce, are quite equal todso of some other breeds. They are eggs that need a bigger egg cup than the Staffordshire Potteries are accustomed to make. Scotch Greys are also capital mothers, not clumsy, are good sitters and very attentive to their chickens. As table fowls they are little if any inferior to dorkings in the quality et their meat. The frame is not quite so large, and perhaps the keel or breast bone not so deep as on the dorking, but there are very few who could tell the difference between one and the other when on the table. Then Scotch Greys have a very decided advantage over their cousins, if we may call the dorkings by this name, in that they are very, much harder, and can, there- • fore, stand cold soils where the others would die off. They cannot be said to bear confinement well, but farmers seldom expect this, and they need not regard it as a weakness, Scotch Greys are small eaters, but one thing they mukt have, and that is; green food, -if they do not get it they do, not thrive, and often contract the habit of feather eating. But where space and green food can be given we know of no better fowl than this jor farm purposek..,.

- SEASONABLE HINTS. Some readers of The Guardian may be glad if we again remind them of the. necessity for reducing the 'stock of birds, if the yard is at all full. The present offers a good opportunity for getting rid of surplus birds, for pullets i are always n demand at this season of the year in order to supply the needs of those who are looking forward to the winter. , Cockerels, if they cannot be sold for stook purpoes, had better be sent to the poulterers, or be killed and eaten at home. How the fowls are got rid of is not of so much importance as the actual getting rid of them, though the more that they will realise the better for the balance sheet at the year end.
Nearly ten tons of mushrooms were despatched last week f/om the railway station at Whitchurch, Salop, to several faro towns.

The Salvation Army bend at Heywood have struck against an nrder made by General Booth that they must cease play- ing quick steps in or out of the barracks. THE PREMIER —Mr Gladstone, who is staying at Hawar- den, appears to be enjoying excellent health. He takes walking exercise daily, and is guarded by a Scotland Yard detective and a few members of the Flintshire constabulary. Ileums DEFALCA.TIONS.—Experts who are examining the books of Messrs Arnold, Constable, and Co., New York, who recently discovered defalcation's among their confiden- tial clerks, have found losses amounting to nearly two mil- lion dollars.

A SELF•CONFESSED PERJORER.—Patriek Dale, of Delvin, county Westmeath, one of the principal witnesses in the Barbayille murder case, says he swore falsely against several of the prisoners. His wife encouraged him to concoct the story to save himself.

THE OFFICE OF HANGMAN.—The London Court of Alder- men on Saturday resolved that the retention of the services of Bartholomew Binns as public executioner for the City of London should no longer be continued. Binns was appointed to the post at Marwood's death. SIR WM. HARCOURT telegraphed to the Liberal agent at Derby, OH Monday, that in response to an urgent invitation he will address his constituen, s on Friday, October 10th. On the following day the Home Secretary speaks at the Chatsworth demonstration, with Lord Harlington and Mr Mandella.

SCALDING A COMRADE TO DEATH.—James Crnikshank, a fireman on board an Aberdeen steamer, has been remanded at the Thames Police Court on the charge of having caused the death .pf another fireman by pouring boiling coffee upon him. The affair occurred at Smyrtia. It was stated that though it was breakfaiWtime both the prisonef ard the de- ceased were drunk.

CATHOLICS AND Loma FIPON.—A movement is on foot to present a joint address of welcome to Lord Ripon, on his return to London, from the Roman Catholic elementary teachers of Great Britain, His lordship has not held the post of chairman of the Catholic Poor School Committee throughout the period of his Viceroyalty, the Duke of Nor- folk acting as his deputy. DEATH OF A BICH FARLIER.—The death has been an- noonced at Buenos Ayres of Senor Nicholas Anchclena, who was probably the richest farmer in the world. His property is said to have 'consisted of 1,770 square miles of land, 150,000 cows, and 500,000 sheep, together with a consider- able amount of house property in the city.- He was worth at the time of his death £2,400,000. MR. GLADSTONE AND His CRITICS —An anonymous pamphlet haying been sent to Mr Gladstone, in which the right bon gentleman is charged with supporting the Church of Rome and patronising despotism', the Premier has re- plied that no one blames the appointment of Lord Ripon to the 'Viceroyalty of India, The other statements in the pamphlet, he addoz are grossly notice'; and he asks why its author does not give his name, so that it may be seen who he is and what is his worth. THE FATAL ACCIDENT TO AN ENGLISH M.P.—Lord Legh on Monday received a cablegram from Mr Moreton Frewen, at Cheyenne, stating that the Hon Dudley Legh was ex- pected there. Cheyenne, the nearest railway station, is 250 miles from the scene of the accident. The telegram also states that the deceased left the camp on the morning of the 14th, and, having shot a wild sheep, fell whilst trying to descend into a canon after it. The body, was found on the 21st.

MANCE OF THE PEERAOE.—It is not generally known that the late agent of the Earl of Shewsbury, Mr. Thomas Hoggins, J P., Chester, whose death has just been recorded, was nephew to Sally Hoggins, who became the celebrated Countess of Exeter. Mr. Hoggins used to tell with much pleasure how a stranger giving himself the name of Jones came to Mr, Noggin's farm at Great Bolas, in Shropshire, how the simple manners and sweet face of Sally Hoggins won his heart, how their love-making was followed by a SIM. pie village wedding, and their intense surprise on the death of plain Mr. Jones's fartherto learn that he was an earl, and that simple Sally Hoggins was Countess of Exeter. div.head: LAMENESS IN HORSES.
div.p: LAMENESS IN HORSES.

The structures which form the basis of the foot, in- cluding the bones, cartilages, and ligaments, are liable to disease, and s6me of the disorders are of a character so serious as tokimstitute permanent unsoundness. Most common, and certainly not the least important among the diseases above referred to, are " sidebones" and " ringbones," which occur in all classes of horses, but particularly among heavy breeds, which are em- ployed for purposes of draught. "Sidebones"-fire in the first instance the result of the conversion of the cartilages which form elastic side wings at the,posthrior part of the foot, including between them a mass of fibro-fatty substance, which the late Professor Coleman used to describe as the "fatty frog." This elastic cushion naturally expands when the horse's weight is imposed on the foot, and causes a certain amount of outward movement of the lateral cartilages, which, how- ever, return to their ordinary position when the foot is lifted frpm the 'ground. 'file movement which takes place must be very limited as to its extent, but it may be allowed that it contributes in some degree to the freedom and elasticity ,of the animal's action. Conver- sion of cattilage into bone by the symmetrical arrange- ment of particles of calcareous matter among the cartilage cells is a physiological process which goes on congantly, during the early period of life especially, and to some extent as long as life continues; but while the change is gradually carried on, and is not attended with in- flammation, very little inconvenience arises—indeed, the only apparent result ' is a diminution of the elastic qualities of the structure in which the alteration has occurred. In this way a considerable portion of the lateral cartilages may assume the bony condition, as the horse advances in life, without any active disease being associated with the process. _ _

When ossificatiOn of the lateral cartilages is the con- sequence of inflammation brought on by overwork at an early age, the deposit of bony substance takes place rapidly, and commorly does not cease with the conver- sion of the whole of the cartilages into bone, but ex- tends beyond them to the bastern bones, leading to the formation of a nearly complete ring of ossific material, to which.the term" ringbone" is applied. " Ringbone " is a much more serious disease than sidebones, because it affects either the joint between the short pastern and the pedal bone (coffin joint), or that formed at the junction of the long and short pastern, and in some severe cases the bony deposit is sufficiently extensive to implicate both joints. " Ringbone" is necessarily attended with lameness more or less pro- nounced, and when the depOsit extends to the coffin joint, or the joint above it, it may be considered an in- curable form of the disease. Treatment may ',improve the animal's action to a considerable extent; but it is not possible to remove the ossific substance, nor to re- store the diseased articular surfaces to a healthy condi- tion. " Ringbone " and " sidebones " constitute un- soundness by the mere fact of their existence. Either of them will be sufficient to disqualify a horse, even when no lameness is present at the time of exhibition or purchase, because in the ordinary course of work lameness is likely to occur; and there is, besides, the fact now pretty clearly established, that the tendency to " sidebones" and "rmgbones " is one which can be transmitted from parent to offspring. These considera- tions alone would justify the application of the term unsoundness to either disease, even though no lameness were apparent at the time. . .

0 Admitting that all forms of sidebones and ringbone o constitute unsoundness, and that evidence of the exist- ence of either at the time of sale would suffice to prove a breach of warranty, it must nevertheless be borne in ' mind that there is a great difference in the nature and extent of the disqualification which the disease may occasion. Income instances, for example, the extent of o ossification of the lalat cartilageers is extremely slight, or in the case of ringbone there is but little osseous sub- stance round the coronet, and the animal's action is sound. Under these circumstances the animal may be very useful for certain purposes, chiefly for slow work, which he may perform for years without inconiTenience. The same extent of- i disease n a horse required for fast work, either in -Harness or saddle, would be absolutely fatal to the animal's usefulness,.as in all probability the strain to which tire diseased parts would be subjected on the road or in the hunting field would quickly lead to an extension of the disease, and necessitate a long period of rest, with no better result than the improve- ment of the animal's ;teflon for a time, restoration to soundness being impossible under any conditions: In both the cases above described, the horses would be unsound, but in ' one the unsoundness need-not dis- qualify the animal for particular kinds of work, while in the other it renders him quite useless for the purposes for which he is intended. Sidebones and ringbones are now admitted to be a disqualification in breeding ani- mals' and the care which has been taken of late years to reject stallions affected v4ith either disease at horse shows has had a very distinct effect in diminishing the number of cases in young horses:in:agricultural classes. Some years 'ago itowas quite common to find sidebone in heavy draught horses, even in the two-year-old classes; now the disease is comparatively rare in young animals; and by no mca is so common as it once was in older horses which have done a good deal of work. Treatment of sidebones and ringbone had not under- gone much oliangc since the primitive time of veterinary practice. The idea seems to be that in all severe cases of disease, especially when bones are affected, powerful counter-irritants are necessary, and the hot iron has, from time immemorial, bean in favour. At may be as- sumed that treatment of sidebones and ringbone will be directed principally to the removal of lameness, and, hi

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

FRUIT GATHERING.--SOMe of the earliest apples have been gathered, and as they are, as a rule, quicklY disposed of, it is not usual to bestow so much care oil them as on those varieties of fruit that will keep. It takes very little more time to gather fruit properly than it does to do it in a reckless manner, and the appearance , and general good condition of the fruit amply rewarda the careful gatherer for his trouble. A wicker basket should not be used at any, time either for gathering apples or pears, or for placing them in after they are gathered, unless it is well lined with hay or soft straw- The fruit at the bottom and nokt, to the sides of the hamper will be marked by the wicker, and every dent made hastens decay. Growers for sale would do well to improve on their present method er packing their fruit for conveyance to market. The Americans for several seasons have sent their apples to us in casks, which are fairly smooth inside and do not give under ordinary pressure. Boxes with handles are excellent for gathering. By the assistance of a wire hook one can be suspended on a branch, and moved from place to place. When full, we advise emptying them into boxes or barrelso to remain in them or to be conveyed to the store-room. We give preference to boxes not more than 18 inches deep, as- by using deeper boxes the fruit is liable to be dropped in, instead of being placed in as , gently as eggs. If we were confined to barrels, Ave - would lay them on their sides, and put as manyas pos- sible in them whilst in that position, for the work ut. easier and more expeditiously accomplished. Many' varieties of apples and pears this season are ripe -much earlier than usual, and they are above the usual size. Liveseys, or Tower of Glamrnes, are very fine, and have put on a deep sulphur tint. • They have been gathered a few days, as we found they parted freely from the branches, which is a sure indication that they are ready for gathering. A few Williams' Pears and Beurre d'Amaulis have also been secured.. Farty pears, like the above, are best gathered as soon as the pips or seeds are changing into a brown colour, and not wait till they part readily from the tree. We have proved frequently that they keep longer, and are much better flavoured. In fact, early pears are worthless after being gathered a few days, if left on the tree to ripen; many of them get dry and mealy. The best storing place for fruit is a dry room with equable temperature. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The growth of the Chrysanthe- mum is so brittle that it will not bear much strong wind, so they ought to be ,tied to strong stakes, or: if planted against a wall, which is an excellent position for them, they may have a string stretched in front of them and attached to nails at each end, and interme- diate nails and string every yard or so, to draw the main string closer to the wall and provide additional security from the wind's action. If. we are not visited by early frosts, we anticipate a fine show of these out of doors this season, as they are rather more forward than usual, and are in every way promising. Attention should be directed to all annuals maturing their seeds, which should be collected and laid on sheets of paper in a dry, airy position. Many of these, as well as some perennials, will perfect thir seeds this year better than they have done for some years.

TUE WORKING MAN'S GREENHouse.-Even to an onlooker, the action of the Corporation of Preston respecting these. is most vexatious; what, therefore, must it be to those who are most intimately concerned? What can be more irritating than to be called upon to destroy the labour of months, or years, and to part with objects we have loved and cherished so dearly? If the vigilance now displayed had been exercised at an earlier date, all this harass and worry might have been avoided. Seeing that the authorities have been the alders and abettors of the mischief, by allowing these greenhouses to crop up one after another, we think the least they could do would be to allow those already erected to remain. We can assure them that if every workman had a greenhouse at the back of his house, they need not be apprehensive of any evil results. For our own part, looking at the matter hi a sanitary point of view, we are more suspicious of the presence of dogs, cats, rabbits, and pigeons, which depo- sit their excrement at our threshhold, under our feet. in I our yards, and above our heads, than we are of the working man's greenhouse. It is evident most of them were put up in ignorance of any infringement of the by-law, and from the haste manifested by some in taking 'them down there is proof that there was no desire to maintain a defiant attitude. We hope that the authori- ties will not pursue an aggressive policy towards respectable class of workmen, .for such we take all to be who have a greenhouse and take an interest in Thrusting the the law on one side for a moment, and taking a common sense view of the affair, as well as calling science to our aid, we state without fear of contradic- tion that these structures, with their contents, are likely to do more good than harm. But the law demands air space. How much air space does a greenhouse ()muff, Just the thickness of the wood and glass. There is ag much air inside a'greenhouse as there is in a correspond- ing space outside, with this difference, that it is much purer and sweeter outside, and in consequence of the laps of glass and the crevices round the ventilators, it is constantly on the move, entering and escaping to bc purified and vitiated with undeviating regularity. It will thus be seen that a greenhouse, even where it is empty, is a different structure to that composed of brickg and slates or tiles. ' If the authorities had not been so obtuse as not to perceive this, they would not have ' contemptuously treated their owners as to serve them with a peremptory 48 hours' notice for their removal, aS, if the existence of the inhabitants was imperilled by the • presence of a e.iv square feet of glass here and there. VRGETARLE physiologists and chemical scientists are . most emphatic in their decision as to the part plants play in purifting this atmosphere of ours. They are, - necessary to our wellbeing and a country destitute 01 vegetation would be uninhabitable. These aerial scaven- gers have created a scare in Preston, and are conse- quently to be banished.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N. THE NILE EXPEDITION. CAIRO, SATORDAY.—Lord Wolseley and staff have left for the front. CAIRO, SIINDAY —Letters have been received from General Gordon by way of Massowah. They bear various dates from April to July, and are therefore anticipated by the later news received from Khartoum. Colonel Barnes died here to-day of dysentry. CAIRO MONDAY.—Major Cbermside telegraphs from Buakim that many Sheikhs have become friendly. The road frem Suakim to Barber is practically open, The Amaral' tribe are now supplied with English weapons and ammuni- tien.‘—Daily News. WADY HALYA, SIINDAY.—Two hundred and eighty mounted ,infantry have arrived here, and will go forward immediately. A detachment of mounted infantry arrived above Dal on the 24th inst. The heads of two Emirs killed in the battle of Korti hove arrived here, having been sent by the Mudir of Dongola. A steamer has been hauled with difficulty through the Semneh Gate. The body of Guards- man Cash, who WAS killed by a crocodile at the Sams Cat- aract, has been picked up here. ,WADY LEALFA, MONDAY.—A nugger, containing two officers and 36 men of the Royal Sussex Regiment, has been wrecked on the island of Nilwastiall. Two men were drowned, and all the kits, arms, and provisions were lost. The first steam pinnace arrived at Sarrar on Friday. She has been hauled down an improvised slip from the railway to the river. The task was a very difficult one, for thergronnd is hard, the drop steep, and the engineers had no appliances whatever for such work. After she is afloat the boiler and engines will be fitted to her. Col. Fraser went up to Sara, yesterday to inspect the progress of the work upon the extension of the railway to Ambigol. It is getting en rapidly.
HOME PREPARATIONS._

A large number of Nile boats arrived on Satu-day by rail and water at the Royal Arsenal, Woolwich, for shipment in the hired transport Horn Head. The steamship China, 2,000 horse-power, of 1,394 tons regireer, WAS surveyed on Satur- day at the Royal Albert Docks, Woolwich. She will take 30 Nile boats and 30 tons of telegraph wire, sufficient to ex- tend, when joined on tie the present terminus at Arnbukol, as far as the relief army marches—probably as far as Khar- toum, making a total length of 1,360 miles of telegraph wire laid down from Cairo within a few weeks. The tran- sport department of the Admiralty on Monday hired the steamer Cameo to convey to Alexandria, from the Thames, the extra stern paddle boat, besides which she will carry large consignments of victuals and stores for Egypt. The Admiralty have arranged to send from the Thames on October 18th the steamer Cameo, with a large quantity of stores for the army in Egypt, and another stern wheel paddle steamer for the Nile expedition to Khartoum. The document is couched in much milder terms than the Identical Note presented by the other Powers. INSPECTION OF TROOPS BY LORD WOLSELEY. His Lord- ship will be absent ten days, and on his return will remain here for a similar period in order to draw up his report to the British Provernment on the results of his mission. The French are now entirely masters , along the Tiver Day. The Paris, referring to the future operations of Admiral Courbet. announces that the plan is to io to Ke-Lung, and, after driving out the Chinese garri- son, to fortify the surrounding heights. A corps of occupa- tion will then be established there.
