CALCUTTA, Tnuesbes.—A. railway collision has occurred on the Eastern Railway at Arruaghatta, by which sixty per- sons were killed or injured. NEW Yana, WEDNESDAY:A collision has occurred be- tween two trains ore the Denver and Rio Grande Railway, near Denver. Thirty passengers were injured, but none fatally.

April 21st we have been almost daily engaged with the rebels, who now thoroughly surround Khartoum General Gordon is busily engaged laying out mines in front of the works in all directions. Yesterday and to-day the rebels came down to a village opposite and fired heavily on the palme. We returned the fire with artillery and musketry, and on both occasions the Arabs soon retreated. There was no loss on our side. The town is quiet. Over half the population before the siege began went over to the rebels, thus weeding out all bad characters. General Gordoa is issuing rations to the poor. Food is very dear. We have corn and biscuits for about four months. General Gordon

has issued paper money, as our treasure is still at Berber. The merchants accept it as money, and all the arrears to the soldiers can be thus paid off. General Gordon has sent emissaries to offer to all the slaves of the rebels their free- dom if they abandon their masters and come in. If they do this it will be a fearful blow to the rebels. The General has hired the large mission preiniies on the river, and has moved all the ammunition there; in case of attack with artillery on the fortifications it will be perfectly safe. A messenger from Seyid Mahomet Osman, of Kassala, who is an Emir of Mecca and chief among the Moreau'mans in the Soudan has coma in bringing a letter. The Seyid says he has beaten the rebels around Kassala, and he tells General Gordon to be of good heart and he and all his men will come to his relief. In such respect is this man held that the rebels did not dare to stop the bearer of the letter. One of General ' Hick's bandsmen came in last night from El Obeid. The Mandi has sent two guns, forty boxes of shells, and sixty Retningtons to be used against &deb Bey, who is still hold- ing out against the rebels at Mesalimieh. This soldier states that Slatten Bey, at Darfour, has not surrendered to the MAUL The Blue Nile is slowly rising, and we hope that in ten or fifteen days the steamers will be able to smite the rebels hip and thigh. The health of the town is excellent, and we three Eoglishmen here are well and hopeful. There are now around the lines, in addition to all other obstacles, such as crowsfeet, broken glass. wire entanglements, and chevaur de frisc, three lines of land torpedoes or percussion mines. They are enormously powerful, and are much feared by the Arabs. We have no news whatever of the in- tentions of Her Majesty's Government. We learned to-day that a mate with a post from Barber was taken by the rebels and killed.
FilaN-EMY DECIMATED BY MINES -COLONEL
STEWAR I' WOUNDED.

July 30.—We have' been now five months closely be- sieged and can at best hold rut bet two months longer. The soldiers and people liv in hopes olk English relief, as shoe last May there are daily reports of the English ad- vancing from Dongola and Kassala. The Arabs have strong forts with cannon along the riyar4 and they push the siege as vigorously as ever. General Gordon has protected all the steamers with bulletproof plates of soft wood and iron, and on the six armoured barges has put up castles twenty feet high, giving a double line of fire. We have no fears of a rising in the town, as before the siege 8,000 to 10,000 men left and joined the rebels. The troops to be loyal must be paid, and General Gordcm is badly off for money, none of that which left Cairo for his use over having reached Khartoum. He has issued £50,000 Worth of paper money. Food is daily distributed to the peer. Sinck March 23rd the following are the chief events of the siege :—March 23. Hassan and Seyid Pashas were pat to death for treachery in the battle of the 16th, in which we lost 350 killed and wounded. April 16, 17, 18, 19, and 20. Attacks by the rebels on the palace from the villages oppposite. Fearful loss of life to the Arabs from mines put down by General Gordon. April 27. We heard of the surrender of Saleh Bey at Mesalimieh to the rebels with 50 shiploads of food. 70 boxes of cartridges, 2,020 rifles, and a steamer. May 1. The officer commanding engineers havieg put down a mine of. 78Ibs of powder, trod on it, and with six soldiers was blown to pieces. May 3. A man reported an English army at Berber. May 6. Heavy attack from the Aral% at the Blue Nile end of the works; great loss of life from mines we had placed at Bari. May 7. Great attack from a vil- lage opposite; nise mines were exploded there, and we after- wards heard that they 'killed 115 rebels. The Arabs kept up a fire all day. Colonel Stewart, with two splendidly directed shots from a Krupp 20-pounder at the palace, drove them • out of their principal pssition. Daring the night the Arabs loopholed the walls but on the 9th we drove them out. They had held the Place for three days. May 25. Colonel Stewart, while working a mitrailense at .the palace, was wounded by the rebel fire, but he is now quite well. May 26. During an expedition up the White Nile Saati Bey put a shell into an Arab magazine. There was a great ex- plosion, sixty shells going off. Daring Ma Y and June steamer expeditious were made daily under Saati Bey. Our loss was slight, and much cattle were captured. June 25. Mr Cuzzi, English Consul at Berber' who is with the rebels, came to- our lines, and told us of the fall of Berber. Mr Cuzzi has been sent to Kordofan. June 30. Saati Bey captured forty ardebs of corn from the rebels and killed 200 of them. July 10. Saati Bey having burnt Kilakla and three villages, attacked Gatarueb, but with three of his officers was killed. Colonel Stewart had a narrow escape. Saati's loss is serious. July 29. We beat the rebels out of Burl, on the Blue Nile, killing numbers of them and capturing munitions and eighty rifles. The steamers advanced to El Efan, clearing 13 rebel forts and breaking two cannon. Since the siege began our loss has been under 700 killed.
COWARDLY g 0 LDIE RS -ARM ED FLOTILLA ON
THE NIL3.-CLEARINCI. AWAY THE REBELS.

Jinx 31.—This is the end of the fifth month of the siege. Yesterday,-I sent you, via Kassala, a despach giving the situation here and the chief incidents of the siege since March 23. I wrote you several times each week up to April 23, when all hopes of men getting through to Berber had cadged. For the last five months the siege has been very close, the Arab bullets from all sides being able to fall into the palace. Sines March 17th no day has passed without firing, yet our losses in all at the very outside are not 700 killed. We have bad a good many wounded, but as a rule the wounds are slight Since the siege General Gordon has caused biscuit and Corn to be distributed to the poor, and up to this time there has been no case of anyone serjensly wanting food. Everything has gone up about 3,000 per cent. in prices, and meat is, when you can get it, Be or 9s an 'ben The classes who cannot accept relief suffer most. Since the despatch which arrived the day before yesterday all hope of relief by our Government is at an end, so when our provisions, which we have at a stretch for two months, are eaten we must fall, nor is there any chance, with the sol- diers we have, and the great crowd of women, children, dm, of our being able to cut our way through the Arabs. We have not stiamers for all, and it is only from the steame-s we can meet the rebels. One Arab horseman is enough to put two hundred of the bulk of our men to flight. The day Saati Bey was killed eight men with spears charged two hundred of our men armed with Remingtons. The soldiers , 11. d at once, leaving Saati and 'his Vakeel to be killed. A black officer cut down three of the Arabs, and the other five chased our men. A horseman coming up rode through the flying mess, cutting down seven. Colonel Stewart, who was unarmed, got off by a fluke, the Arabs not having selsn him. With such men as these we can do nothing. The negroes art the only men we Can depend upon. The attack made by 'the Soudani troops under Mehemet All Pasha on the 28th of this Month was most successful; the Arab loss must have been very heavy. As General Gordon has forbidden the soldiers to bring in the heads of the rebels they kill, it is now hard to know the exact number. We captured that day sixteen shells and cartouchee for mountain guns, a quantity of rifle ammunition, seventy-eight Remingtons, a number of elephant and other rifles, nearly two hundred lances, sixty swords, and some horses. Our loss was four killed and some slightly wounded. This action has cleared away the rebels, who day at night have been firing int, our tines at Bari, on the Blue Nile. The following day (29th instant) a flotilla of five armoured steamers and four armoured barges with castles on them went up to Gareff, on the Blue Nile. I went with them. Ore the way no we cleared thirteen small forte' but at Gareff found two large strong forts—earth- works rivetted with trunks of palm trees. There were two cannons in one. For eight hours we engaged these forts, and with the Krupp 20-pounder disabled their two cannons. The Arab fire was terrific, but, owing to the bullet-proof armour on all the vessels, our lose was only three killed and twelve or thirteen wounded. Towards evening we drove the rebels, who were in great numbers, out of the forts. In three days General Gordon will send two steamers towards Sen- nar. It ishoped they will re-take the steamer Mehemet All, which the rebels took from Saleh Bey. General Gordon is quite well, and Colonel Stewart has quite recovered from his wound. lam quite well and happy.

BIRTH OF TWINS IN THE STREET.—Late on Wednesday night a woman named ,:iarah Carroll, aged 30, the wife of a labourer, was passim; along Hardman-street, Liverpool, when she was taken ill. and before medical assistance could be obtained she was delivered of twins. A doctor was at once called and the ambulance telephoned for. The mother and children, who had meantime been medically attended to, were at once removed to the Hospital, where, on Thurs- day morning, they were reported to be doing well.

SHOCKING MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT CLLP. TlAM.—Shortly before eight o'clock on Monday night a Shocking murder wee committed at the residence of a Mrs Weiner, 35, Larkhall-lane, Clapham. For some time past a men named Harry Thorpe, aged 30. bad resided in apart- ments at the above ad iress. lie has been employed during the evening as a billia,el marker at a local tavern. He was engaged to be married to a young woman. On Monday evening he returned home after spending a few days in the country. He was accompanied by Miss Florence Kemp, aged 2.0 years, who WAS living with her father at Battersea. They appeared to be on very affectionate terms, and the landlady made Thorpe a cup of tea, and left them together, while she went upsta:rs to prepare the room for her lodger. Shortly afterwards Thorpe went into his bedroom, and Mrs Weiner heard a scuffla, followed by cries for help. She ran upstairs, and found tho youg man cutting his sweetheart's throat with a razor. Mrs Weiner, with great presence of mind, struggled with tee murderer, and succeeded in get- ting possession of the razor, which was covered with blood. Miss Kemp had fallen on the floor, with a wound across her throat from which Woad was flowing. The landlady ran down stairs, and gave information to the police. In the meantime a doctor was sent for and on his arrival he ex- amined the wound and ordered the police to remove the wo- man to St Thomas's Hospitel, where she died on Tuesday morning. After Mrs Weiner ran downstairs, Thorpe real- ized thli position he had placed himself in, and, procuring another razor, he cut his own throat It was at once deemed expedient to remove him to one of the male wards at St Thomas's Hospital, where he now lies in a dying condition. On Wednesday morning the body of Miss Kemp was remo- ved to tbo mortuary at St Thomas's Hospital, London, to await an inquest. The alleged murderer, Harry Thorpe, lying in the Caine hospital, is watched by a police officer. Although the police have made every inquiry as to the motive for the murder, they have not yet succeeded.

THE FAMINE IN BENGAL.—INCREASING DISTRESS. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—The distress caused by the increas- ing famine in the district of Beerbhoom, in the province of Burdwan, is becoming very serious. The native bodies have begun to cqmniain that the Government system of relief works which have been started are quite inadequate to meet the demandsof the occaaion. The pay given to the People employel on tha works is wretchedly small, being in ordinary Cases as low as half an anna (three farthings) per day. DESTRUCTIVE WATERSPOUT. THE REFORM A.GITATiON.

Saturday afforded fresh evidence of the increasing sup- port given by the constituencies to the Government as the time draws nigh for the re-introduction of the Franchise Bill. The Cory minter demonstrations continue to show up very badly by comoarison with those organised by the Liberals. Last week there were 73 public meetings repor- ted at which the action of the House of Lords in throwing . . .

r-- out the Franchise Bill was condemned, together with the system of hereditary legislatorship. Meetings " for " the Lords in the same time numbered only nine Daring the past five weeks the public meetings condemnatory of the plers have outnumbered the counter meetings by 363, or in the propolion of fonr to one. Mr J CHAMBER&IN, addressing an out-door demonstra. tion of Liberals at Moor Green Hall, near Birminzham, said he did not conceal from himself the gravity of the issue, al- though he had not the remotest doubt as to what the end would be. When they remembered the work which their great chief had recently done, in a way that no man in or out of the Government could imitate, they knew that he had even enhanced the affection of the country. Mr Gladstone had addressed hiinself to the reason of the Lords; but that faculty of the Peers was like the Spanish fleet, which was invisible. (Laughter.) He did not think the Peers would yield to popular demands in the autumn. The Government were not fightin4 their own battle, but that of the people, with whom would rest the question whether they should re. tire from the contest or press on to a victory which should

advance the cause olliberty. (Cheers.) Mr W E Forster, it P., WAS the principal speaker at a re- form cl.monstration held at Otley. The great unanimity of °pintos as to county householders having votes was, he said, a very pleasant fact. In view of that weanimlty, why should sot the Lords pass the Franchise Bill, and leave the Redrstribution Bill—about which there•was some difference _
. _ of opinion—for subsequent discussion? He did not believe that the Tories either hoped or expected to preventsthe

_ ......._ , . tension of the franchise'bv the tactics they had adopted. The red reason why they insisted on the extension of the franchise and the scheme of redistribution being combin.d in one measure, was because they hoped thereby to get the redistribution of seats into their own hands. Although be
did not know that an appeal from a humble commone-r. like himself would have any effect, he ventured to appeal to the . . .

sense of duty and patriotism of the Peers—he believed they had as,inuch patriotism as any other class in the community —not to insist on continuing a conflict between the House of Lords and the House of Commons which, after all, could only end in one way. The duty of the Liberals in this matter was to support the Government with all th)e strength

that the whole Conservative party and many Liberals were against him, and seeing that the last election was turned about by two or three thuusaud votes, it might very well be , that tho Liberals bad not the real majority which they claimed. Toe House of Lords, taking the worst view, kaki only done in a less degree what the Government had been doing for four years, in postponing the Franchise Bill. Even yet he saw nothing to prevent the Prime Miuister bringing in his Franchise Bill three weeks hence, passing it on to the House of Lords. and then introducing bis measure of redistribution. Both could then be considered by the Lords, and probably the whole controrersy would be soived in a single session. If that session were not long enough, it could be extended till the work was done. He could not avoid tile suspicion that this agitation was not honest, and that Ministers, fearing to face the people whom they had deceived, had chosen to ob- scure their failures in the cloud arising from a general attack on the House of Lords. The question of abolishing the Second Chamber, he theught, had not yet come within the range of practical politics. The people still clung to that institution, but if the Upper House was to have no in- dependence and no power to contradict the First Chamber he thought it would be better to have no Second Chamber at all. There might arise an irremovable difference of opinion between the two houses, and in that case the simple Conservative suggestion was—let the people decide the matter. He protested against the dangerous tendency of the Prime Minister's usurpation of personal power, and predicted that the House of Lords would exercise their functions for the welfare of the country in which they lived, not in a spirit of timidity and terror, but only on the condition of absolute independence of every other power except that of the people. Lord Salisbury was heartily thanked for his address, and after he had briefly responded the pro- ceedings terminated. Lord Salisbury spent a quiet day on Thursday. After luncheon he went for a walk with his host, Sir Archibald Campbell, throagh the extensive grounds surrounding Blythswood House, and at half-past Mx be creased the ferry and proceeded to the residence of Mr Pearce, of Messrs John Elder and Co., shipbuilders, where he was to pass the Right.

CHESS BY TELEPHONE —The Bradford and Wakefield Chess Clubs played a match by telephone on Monday night, this being said to be the first time the invention has been thus used in England. The wire was 25 miles long, and ' the games were completed in four hours. SHOOTING A VIOLENT FATHER.—EarIy 011 Saturday, an engineer !limed Rose, who resided at Witney, Oxfordshire. was shot at and mortally wounded by his son, who tperns to have adopted this extreme method of preventing his father from ill-treating his mother. The deceased was a man of intemperate habits, and wee particularly violent towards his wife on Saturday. A coroner's jury has returned a verdict of" Wilful murder" against the son.

PHEASANT SHOOTlNG.—Pheasant. shooting c_ommenced on Wednesday, and reports are to hand from oorrespondents In various parts of the country stating the conditions of the sport. Tn Notth Wales pheasants are said to be very plentiful and in excellent condition. The seas n opening most auspiciously, birds are reported to be in abundance everywhere. In Cheshire, however, there were some heavy showers just after daybreak. Sport promises to be exceed- ingly good in the Canterbury district, where the weather was delightfully fine. THE DUKE AND DUCHESS OF EIHNEDDIGH, who are the guests of Mr C Sykes, M.P., at Brantinghamthorpe Hall, on Monday, inspected the Hull Docks. Their Royal Highnesses, who were cordially received by a large crowd, embarked on the steam yacht Mazeppa. The Mayor and Mayoress of Hull and the chief officials of the Dock Company accompanied their Royal Highnsses, who lunched on board the yacht. un the return of the Royal visitors, H.M.S. Repulse fired a salute cf twenty-one guns. The Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh visited Hull on Wednesday, and were received at the railway statiod by the Mayor and Corporation. Their Royal Highnesses subsequently laid the foundation stone of the extension of Hull Infirmary, and opened a hazier in aid of the Hull Seamen's and General Orphan Home.

Tits Loss OF THE WASP.—The six survivors of the Wasp's crew left Dublin on Saturday morning for Holyhead, whence they proceed to Portsmouth via London. Before the men left Dublin they were asked some questions about the disaster. One of the sailors, replying to the interrogatory "Who das to blame ? " expressed his opinion that it was the 'lieutenant of the watch, who, miscalculating the strength of the current, hugged the shore too closely in at- tempting to weather Tory Island. Admiral Hornby has been directed to assemble a court-martial at Portsmouth as soon as may be convenient. Mr Weir, coroner, has returned from Dunfanagby to Letterkenny, having basil unable, on ace,pant of the heavy sea, to reach Tory Island to hold an inquest on the body lying there. The coast guards who recovered the body are unable to leave the island, and there is no one there who can identify the bociy. Admiral Lethbridge, stationed at Queenstown, has ordered the gunboat Bantereir, to proceed from Westport to Tory Island to assist in recover- ing the bodies from the wreck of the Wasp. The Banterer will remain at Tory Island ten days. The b ?dy of the boy washed ashore has not yet been identified, and Admiral Lethbridge has despatched James Eva, able-seaman of the Wasp, to Dunfanaghy to identify it. The constabulary and the coastguard station adjacent td Tory Island have received lists and a description of the men lost.

THE TORIES AND THE MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.— ' The following letter has been issued by Lord Salisbury to his supporters :—" 20, Arlington-street, September 24,1884. —My Lord.—ln accordance with the intimation given at the close of last session, Parliament has been summoned to ' meet on the 23rd October. There is no reason to believe that any business ef importance will be brought before the Hone of Lords at the opening of the session, but it is pro- bable that at a later period—possibly before the middle of November—matters of the utmost importance will be sub- mitted to the consideration of the House. On that occasion, of which your lordship will be duly advised, the presence of every Conservative peer will be most urgently reqnired. —I am, &c,, SALISBURY." Sir Stafford Northcote has issued the followihg circular to the Conservative members of the House of Commons:—"Pynes, Exeter' Sept. 29th, 1884. Pear sir,—Parliament is summoned for Thursday, the 23rd October. As important business will be taken at once, I earnestly hope that it will be in your power to attend.—l remain, yours faithfully, STAFFORD ti Nottracorz." THE DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE IN DUBLIN.—The Duke of Cambridge arrived at Kingstown on Monday, and was re- ceived by General Sir Thomas Steele, K.C.B • commander of the forces in Ireland, and some members of the military staff, who conducted them to a state carriage attached to the mail train in which the illustrious visitor and his en- tourage travelled to Westland Row. From Westland Row his Roval,Highness drove to the Royal Hospital. Kilmain- ham,mthere he will be the guest of Sir Thomas Steele. The Duke's visit it purely an official one as commander-in-chief. His last visit to Ireland was in 1868, when he was present in St Patrick's Cathedral at the installation of the Prince of Wales as Knight of St Patrick. The Bake of Cam- bridge on Tuesday inspected, in the Phceoix Park, Dublin, the whole or the troops in garrison. The Lord Lieutenant and Lady Spencer were present, and although they were hissed by some of the large crowd who were on the ground, his Royal Highness was cheered, but not very en- thusiastically. In the gallop past, Colonel Chichester was leading his regiment, when his horse stumbled and fell. The rider was not seriously hurt. On Wednesday the Duke of Cambridge inspected the troops at the Curmgh and New- bridge, and on returning to Dublin was entertained at an official dinner by Sir Thomas Steele. commander of the forces in Ireland. _ _ _

The RAILWAY COLLISION AT WIGAN.— GrrauD's JOKY' —Colonel Rich, R.E. to the Board of Trade, has reported on the circumstancek attending the collision on July 26, at Wigan Station:on the Londen and North-Western Railway. An excursion train from Morecambe to Manchester broke in two while it was descending the incline to Wigan station, and the rear portion ran into the trent portion, which had been brought to a stand at Wigan upstation,platfor.n. Three persons were reported as having been injured. Colonel Rich exoresses an opinion that this slight collision appears to have been caused by the breaking of the drawbar hook and coup- lings between the fifteenth and sixteenth coaches of the special train. The breakage of these couplings must have keen caused by the extraordinary action of the guard in the leading van, who appears to have amused himself with put- firm on and taking off the patent break without any reason for doing so. The man's conduct seems to be quite unac- countable. He denies having applied the patent break, as the driver and fireman stated, but there can be no doubt that he did SO His behaviour in not lighting the lamps at More- cambe is also unaccountable. The rest of the company's servants appear to have done the best they could under the circumstances. Colonel Rich strongly recommends the London and North-Western Railway Company to adopt one of the automatic continuous air brakes. If the specia: train had been fitted with a good automatic continuous brake this collision would not have occurred.

CITURCEI CONGRESS.—Tha Church Congress opened on Tuesday, at Carlisle, with a meeting in the Congress Hall, when an addr.ss of welcome to the members was presented by the Mayor, and a pastoral staff, subscribed for by the clergy and laity in the diocese, was handed to the Bishop of Carlisle by Lord Muncaster. Afterwards the customary ser- vices were held in the Cathedral, and St Cuthbert's and St Mary's Churches, the preachers being the Archbishop of ork and the Bishops of Derry and St Andrews. In the afternoon the Bishop of Carlisle delivered his presidential address. Subsequently the Bishop of Bedford read a paper on overcrowded dwellings, insisting that the church must create and direct public epinion on the subject. Major Rankin, M.P., and others also read papers. Other questions discussed were the rights of parishioners, popular literature with reference to infidelity and public morality, and the teachings of England and Ireland in religions matters.—On Wednesday Sir Richard Cross introduced the report of the Ecclesiastical Courts Commission in a paper which gave a general approval to the scheme proposed by the Commis- sioners for the establishment of a new court. He condemned the present system of litigation which made the Bishop's Court a cipher, and hoped by the new court, as suggested, both the clergy and laity would be satisfied and litigation would cease. Other papers on the subject were read. In the discussion which followed, Canon Hoare protested , against the report of the Commission, declaring that instead of checking anarchy it would promote it, and the result would be a dissatisfied laity, a distrusted clergy, and a the- integrated church. The Bishop of Winchester and others took an entirely opposite view, warmly commending the terms of the report, and the President, in summing up the discussion, said he took that as the general feeling of the Congress, a remark which was much applauded. At Thurs- day's sitting the subjects debated in the morning were paro- chial missions and social purity. In the afternoon, in .the Drill Hall, there was a discussion on England's religious duties towards Egypt. At the Congress Hall the religious side of elementary education in Church and Board sohocds were discussed,

At Oxford, on Tuesday night, a largely-attended mewing unanimously passed a resolution in support of the Franchise Bill, and condemning the action of the Hou,e of Lords. Similar resolutions were also passed at a meeting of farmers at Dent, in Dentdale, Yorkshire, and at a meeting of West Norfolk Liberals at Swaffham. . A demonstration of the United Conservative Associations of Hastings was held on Tuesday. in the grounds of Fair. light Hell, the principal speakers being the Earl of Egmont and Mr Grantham, M.P. In • the evening there was a torchlight procession through Hastings and St. Leonards. LORD S ALISBURY IN SCOTLAND. Lord Salisbury arrived at Glasgow on Tuesday evening from London. At Preston and Carlisle on the way his ap- pearance excited much interest. On the station- platform at Glasgow he was greeted by an immense crowd, till- ing every part of the large Central Station. Mounting a raised dais he thanked the people very heartiy for this kind reception of one who came to Scotland to maintain the cause of Constitutional order and freedom ; and replying to an address by the Orangemen of Scotland, he complained that their opponents ignored their arguments, and accused them of insincerity. What the Conservatives wished was to pass the Franchise Bill; but, that before the new voters were made it should be determined in which constituencies they were to vote. If the Liberals gave the Conservatives no credit for sincerity, they might at least give them credit for common-sense. The Conservatives did not act as they were . . . -

Boast) OF GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of the Preaeot Board of Guardians wat held on Thursday at the Workhouse, Whiston. Mr Leatherbarrow presided, and there were also present Revs J Barnacle, T Finnegan. Messrs W Tyrer, J Fidler, W Newsome, W Birchall, T Sadler, J Matthews, W Ashton, J Fisher, James Buckley, E Syder. J Jackson, J Kenwright, W Swift, T F Hill, R 'Patton, Henry Halms, R A Leigh.—The Workhouse Master reported that the number of inmates this week is 418, against 427 last week, and 414 in the corresponding period of last year. Number of vagrants relieved 72, against 52 in the corresponding period of 1883. There were 173 boys abd girls at Kirkdale schools.—The Visiting Committee re- ..commended that a separate ward should be provided for women of bad character. In moving the confirmation of the minutes, Mr Newsome said the committee had some very painful cases before them, and cases of a very depraved character; in fact, some were of so revolting a nature that it was an unpleasant duty to inquire into them. The committee thought that allowing such characters to mix with other inmates would be injurious to their morals, particularly of the young and those who were respectable though poor. Mr Fisher seconded, and the minutes were confirmed.—Mr Hill, on the recommendation of the Finance Committee, gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the salary of Mr Parkinson, relieving officer,

On arriving at Paisley Lord Salis- bury received a 'dresses . from the Conservative Club and other political oaganisations. In reply his Lordship adver- ted to the obtervation of the Prime Minister that if Lord Beaconsfield had been alive the issue now before the coun- try never would have taken place, and that instead the Franchise Bill would have passed. Lord Beaconsfield, how- ever, always foresaid that the Liberals would try to play a trick of passing the Franchise Bill without re-distribution. The heartiness of his reception assured him that in their struggle reform should bs regular, equitable, and honest, and they would hays the sympathy of the working people of Scotland. Lord Salisbury subsequently proceeded to Ren- frew.

'I his, the Clerk said, was a considerable reduction, it being £26,499 in the corresponding half of last year. That sum of course included a large sum for arrears, but the overseers in most of the townships had pulled up most of their arrears. The ratepayers and overseers would now feel the benefit of the increased rateable value of the railways throughout the Union. Lord SALISBURY on Wednesday commenced the active work of his political campaign in Scotland by meeting in the Glasgow Mechanics' Hall the representatives of about 50 Conservative Associations in the West of Scotland, who ptesented his Lordship w th addresses recognising his ser- vices to the "Constitutional cause," and promising support in the eadeavour to secure se just and equitable measure of reform. The Matcpii-t, in reply, said there was a steady drift of opinion towards Conservatism, and he felt assured that the temporary anion of clashing Whig and Radical in- terests could not be long maintained, whereas the unity of sentiment in the Conservative psrty was a strength which must tell more and more as time went on. The great duty of Conservative A ssociations was to convince the working classes that industry and commerce were not safe in the hands of Liberal statesmen, who allowed the influence of this oountry abroad to become weakened and despised. _ _ - -

SANITARY CONGRESS.—On Tuesday the Sanitary Con- gress and Exhibition were opened in Dublin. The ceremony was performed by the Lord Mayor, who also presided at a public luncheon which preceded the opening. In the even- ing Sir Robert Rawlinaon, the president of the Congress, delivered his inaugural address. On Wednesday, Dr Grim- shaw, Registrar•Creneral for Ireland, delivering an address on "Statistical Measures of the Health of Communities." On 'Thursday Mr Cotton, engineering inspector to the Local Government Board for Ireland, read a paper, in which he gave an account of the progress the country was making in the way of improved drainage and water supplies. In the evening the members were entertained at a banquet at which Earl Spencer was one of the speakers.

LONGFORD EXCEISIORS V. HOWLEY WRITE STAR.—This match was plAyed on Saturday. Speakman, Scott, and Whitham played well for Loneford. Score: Excelsiors, one try, four minor points, two touches in goal; White star, one minor point. Bascom Iten v. Torrent —The Rancorn second fifteen opened this season on Saturday with a match versus Tox- tech, when a good game was played, Runcorn eventually winning by two goals, one try, and one touchdown, to Tox- teth one goal. RUNCORN' RECREATION V SUTTON RECREATION.— This match was played on the gronad of the fo-mer, and after a one-sided game, resulted in 'a victory for the home team by 1 goal, 2 touch in pals, and 7 touchdowns, to 1 touch- down, the try for the victors being obtained by I) Little- more.

/ WARRINGTON v. Sr. HELENS (2ND Taams).—Played At Warrington. The visitors could only muster ten men, but excellent substitutes were obtained. St Helens offered but a feeble resistance, the home players scoring two goals, three tries, and fifteen minor points to nil. T Barnes dropped one ef the goals, and the other was from a try by Tuner, Bashford, Lightfoot. and Littlewood also getting over their lines.

TOTTINGTON V. RONCORN.—PIaved at Tottington ou Saturday. A well contested match ended in a win for Tot- tington, viz.: 1 goal 4 minor points to Runcorn 3 minor points. Fogg winning the toss, elected to play with the high wind blowing in hug favour, and during the first half Fogg secured a try, (nal which Coop placed a goal. On change et ends the wind moderated, and a fast game was played, no points of value being scored on either side, although Runcorn bad hard luck in not scoring on several occasions. Teams—.-Runcorn: W Hughes, back; W H Broady, H Speakman, and T Johnson, three-quarter backs; H Hughes (captain) and H Andrews, half backs; W Wright. .1 Lewis, W Cox, J Clarke, J Hoffland, A. Lightburn, J Barns, J Dean, and W Mason, forwards. HAYCOCK TEMPERANCE V. OVER WANDERERS.—These teams met at Haydock for the first time on Saturday. The visitors won the toss, and elected to play with the wind in their favour, which was blowing very strong, but the home team were not long before they displayed some good points. and after about twenty minutes play a good skimming shot was put through by the teetotallers. Again the leather was set in motion, but the 'tome team kept pressing the viiitors, and had a very near "go " at notching another goal. At chenge of ends the Havdock men had the wind in their favour, and were continually storming the visitors' quarters.. It was not long before they registered another goal. The game was—Haydock Temperance two goals to Over Wan- derers nil.—The second teams of these two dabs met at Winsford, on Saturday, but owing to two of the Temperance second team being at home playing with the first team they were not able to place a good team in the field, and suffered a defeat of seven goals to two.

EARLESTOWN 2en V. EVERTON 2ND goodly number of spectators assembled at Wargrave Moss, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon, to witness the meeting of the second teams of the Earlestown and Everton Clubs; the first teams being engaged at Liverplol. During the first half the game was much in favour of Evertoa; and about twenty minutes from the call of time the score stood—Everton five goals; Earlestown, one. About that time the home players put en a spurt, and they very severely pressed their opponents. In quick succession second and third goals were registered, and the ball was sent through for the fourth time ; but Everton disputed the point. As an amicable decision could not be come to, the visitors left the field ten minutes before the finish, the score standing—Everton, five goals; Earlestown, four (one disputed.) The following were the teams : Everton : W Owens goal, II R Richards (captain), T New- ton, .1 Douglas, J Sinnott, T Mowbray, T Scott, W Brown, W Williams, W F Evans, and J Richards. Earlestown: J Gray (captain) goal, A Clayton, J Plant. T Fairclough, A Woolton, J Sims, W Blair, J Pennington, H Rich. j Apple- toneand W Thompson. _ _ -

NORTHIVICH VICTORIA 2ND V. WARRINGTON IST.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. The visitors winning the toss, elected to play with sun and wind slightly In their favour. The home team started the ball, when the Victories at once assumed the aggressive, and after some nice play amongst the forwards, Southern, with a good shot, scored goal number one. The visitors continued to press their opponents, and at half time had scored five goals. The leather being restarted, Harper got possession, and with a good shot registered a sixth goal. The War- ringtonians now pulled themselves toi,ether. . Warren with agood kick landed the ball in front of the visitors' goal, when out of a scrimmage they scored their only goal. North wich again Settled down to their work, and scored three more goals in quick time, continuing to press their oppo- nents to the call of time, when they had placed three more goals to their credit, winning the game by 12 goals to 1. The goals were obtained by Atherton, 2; Southern, 3; Pye, 1; Harper, 2; Goodwin, 3; Whitehead, 1. The North wich backs and half backs played a good game, while the forwards were all that could be desired.

BT. Hamm v. Wannutnrotz.—Played at St. Helens be- fore a good number of spectators. The first half of the game proved a very close contest, neither side beinr -ble to score a minor point, and the ininor points being r 1. in favour of Warrington. The game being resume t "et soon became observable that the Warrington men bad ovcplayed themselves, as they wer3 unable to keep the ball out of their own territory, St. Helens crossing their goal line twice within lifteen minutes. At the call of time St. Helens were left the victors by two goals and three minor points to War- rington three minor points. For ibe winners Bassnett, Hal- ton, Anders, Ross, and Haselden played a capital game, while Ashton, Speakman, Warburton, Walsh, Gilbert. and Calvert were most prominent for the visitors, Teams :—St. Helens: C Ross, full back; W Haselden, A Tickle, and E Foreman, three-quarter backs; T Finney (captain) and J Edwards, half-backs; A Borthwick. C Anders, J Bassnett. J Halton, W James, R Twist, E Chadwick, J Harwood, and T Rogers. forwards. Warrington: T Walsh, back; Jolley, Lishman. and Speakman, three-quarter backs; Gilbert and Warburton, half-backs; Ashton (captain), Povey, Humph- reys, Davies, Jones. Boyle, Boardman, Barnes, and Calvert, forwards.

WARRINGTON WHITE STAR V. WIDNES RECREATION.— These teams met on the ground of the former on Saturday, there being a fair number of spectators present. The home team wee not a representative one, several or the usual players being absent, whilst the recreation brought down their strongest team. The visitors decided to play against the wind. Howarth kicked off. Some quick play followed, both teams trying hard to score. Just before the call of half-time one of the visitor's forwards secured a try, which the home team disputed, on the ground that a proper scrim- mage had not been formed, only one of the home team being in the scrimmage, but the home team captain gave way, and the try was converted into a goal from a good kick. On the change of ends the game was again evenly contested, but the hems team, by some all round good play, at last forced the Widnes to avoid dropping out to touchdown. The visi- tors worked hard to again assume the offensive, compelling the home team to touchdown. The home team again worked hard, and at last secured a try. Howarth was entrusted at niece but failed. The visitors dropped out, but the home team getting warm, had all the best of the game and forced the ball over the line, but only a touchdown resulted. The visitors again dropped out, and following up well prevented a return, but the home team, not to be denied, rushed the ball down the field and again secured a try, which Howarth was again entrusted with, but he failed to add the major point. "No aide" was called, and the visitors were left vic- torious by one goal and two minor points, to White Star two trya, four minors. EARLESTOWN v. Evatcrote.—The winners (Everton) and runners-up (Earlestown) in the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup competition last season met on Saturday on the new ground of the Everton Club. at Walton Breck-road. It being known that a rivalry existed between the two clubs, the contest was looked forward to with great interest. The day being fine some thousands of spectators assembled to greet the two crack Association teams on their first appear- ance this season. Neither side was represented to their fullest strength, but Earlestown suffered greatly in this respect, and this, no doubt, accounts for the indifferent fight made by Earlestown. At 3-50 the rival teams faced each other, and Everton winning the toss, Ellison kicked off for the visitors. Far some time play was confined to neutral tocrwounntde,rtrhitoouryg,hdlarvinergaloni:coufrwsiohnicsh w Richards e m a dpea si snetdo tEhaerbl easl -1 to Preston, and the latter to Higgins, who sent in a flying tsheotb, ball and a fscored p play was he first goal c l foron confined Everton.tothe o ft he field, though eventually the Everton custodian was called upon to exert himself. Parry took the leather well up the field, and passed to Gibson, who brilliantly scored a second point for Everton. The visitors next relieved the pressure on their lines, Duxbury, Ellison, and Whalley doing capital service; but Wain and the Everton skipper again caused the visitors to resume the defensive, and a scrimmage in Earlestown territory resulted. bEuotriwn ahteshhnpreotrheivtniesytiiptiaomagriesa,aisngolmgureoeastrstfsoeaersretst:. play followed, and both sides caused the ball to travel resumedld' set- tied rapidlyied th the struggle gdloesy was a t e fie Parry, sPGill, and Higgins being the Appleton, however, for a time was equal to the call made upon him, and, assisted by Duxbury and Ferguson, the play was changed to the Everton lines. The relief afforded was only short stayed, and a grand kick by Parry, who, perhaps, was playing in his best form, enabled Higgins to get posses- sion of the leather, and be passed it to Whittle, the latter just managing to evade Appleton, and a third point was noted to Everton. Following the kick off, Duxbury made a grand dribble down the centre, and a capital shot by R G. ten was neatly handed out by Joliffe, which brought half-t-ue, the score being throe to nothing. On changing ends Whittle

gave motion to the hall, and the contest was again taken, • into Earlestown terrrtory, and several capital shots were sent in, though Appleton. in a coutin-iidable manner, stuck . . gamely to his post Ricti,rds, however, from a slight scrimmage in goal, inanaged to lc.: the ball past hint, and a fourth point was leci,cled to the home club. Everton now pressed their oppvnents, and thougo Earl estown gallantly defended their citadel, and several times brilliantly relieved the pressure, it Was evident they were out-worked. Follow- ing a throw in, Everton rushed the biaN to their quarters, add Whittle, being nicely fed by Gibson, scored the fifth and last goal for his s:iii%. Harrison and F,,:guson played up well, and were ably assisted by Whalley Daabnry, and R Green, but all they could du was to relieve the pressure, and when time was called the ball WAS in the quarters of Everton, who won by five goals to nothing. The want of good judgment on the part of the officials of the Earieatown Club in sending a weak and mixed eleven to Liverpool accounts for the thrashing which Everton, the winners of the Liverpool and Disirict Coal lenge Cup, ad- ministered to the silver medallists, or runners-up, on 6atur- day. It is obviously an unwise proceeding to change three or four players each week, and especially to try against such a strong club as Everton, one or two men entirely un- used to and unacqu.inted with the Association game. Ex- perience has now taught the Earleetoon Club the folly of Such an idea; and no doubt "the powers that be" will, in future, make an effort to keep a set of player, Or success will seldom attend the team. The Earlestown men were thoroughly overplayed by Everton in toe last quarter of au hour of the game, and the score of five goals to none in favour of the latter is about a true index to the state of the play. _ _
The Earlestown first team will to-day (Saturday) be engaged at Wargrave Moss playing their Lancashire Cap Tie with Rihcherttr.

The match betwmm the second elevens of the Earlestown and Everton cfM3s, at Ea,lestown, was a more eveu and ex- citing affair than the g4nris at Liverpool. Tiffs was es- pecially the Ca,(l towards the wften the Earlestown lads put the leather through the pots three Ulna{ in ten minutes. A dispute arose as to one of the goals with the remit that the visitors left the field before the expiration of time.

The E ulestown wanderers have been considerably strengthened by the accession to their tanks of Champion and Mather, late or the harlestown club. On Sat arday they met the Bolton Soutn End on their ground in Market-street, and a well contested match resulted in a win ler the Wan- derers by three gdals CO none. Champion kept goal excel- lently for the winners.

Another Bolton club, the St. Georze's, visited Earlestown on Saturday, aud they met the Earlestown Rovers on the ground of the latter. After a good game victory rested with the Eariestonians to the extent of four goals to <hies On Saturday, at Derby, Staeleyvwere beaten by Derby, Midland by one goal to none; at Perry Bar, Birminghatn . the Aston Villa, with a weak team, were beaton by Aston I, Unity by four goals to three; at Birmingham, Small Heath I Alliance beat Wednesbury by five goals to one; in the Wet- gall Cup competition the Swifts beat Stafford Ringers by ' two goals to none; at Halliwell, St George's. (Birmingham) beat Halliwell by three to two; at Bohan, tne Wanderers beat Sheffield Wednesday by two to one; Great Lever beat Wednesbury Old Athletics by five to none; at Sheffield, t Lockwood Brothers defeated Rotherham oy three to none; Sheffield Heeley beat Wesley C)tlege Athletic by 26 to none; in the Ayrshire Cup competition Lugar Boswell beat Kilmarnock Athletic by seven to two; at Edinburgh, Queen's Park (Glasgow) and Heart of Midlothian played a drawn gams, without scoring; at Glasgow, the Rangers beat Dumbarton by four to two; the Pollokshields Athletic, on their own ground, beat Vale of Leven by one goal to none; Cowlairs defeated Jamestown, at Glasgow, by 13 to one; at Paisley, Abercorn and Morton Played a drawn game—two I each; in the Scottish Cup competition, Harlford beat Kil- marnock (who defeated them a fortnight ago by six to one) by three goals to one; ard St Mirrens defeated Neilston by four to one.

Blackburn Olympic met Derby County on Saturday. when a eplenclld game was played. There were about 2,000 spectators prestmt, and just before call of time the Olym- pians won by four goals to three.—The Blackburn Rovers met the Burnley men at Turf Moor, being victorious by four goals to two.—Drrwen and Astley Bridge played a draw with one goal each, and Accrington beat Etgley, at Accring- ton, by four goals to nil.—At Darwen, in the Presence of about 1,000 spectators, Preston Zingari met Darweu Old Wanderers. Score :—Old Wanderers, three goals; Zingari, one goal.

div.head: WAR RINGT()N BOARD OF GUARDIANS, '
div.p: WAR RINGT()N BOARD OF GUARDIANS, '

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse lan Wednesday morning. There were present— Messrs Cdoper (in the chair), Derbyshire, Brown, Black- hurst, Caldwell, Jolley, Appletop:Greenall,Forster, Hunt, John Houghton, Owen, William Houghton, Rey G F Roberts, Jeans; J C Sutton (clerk), and S Sutton (assistant clerk).

A MISTAKE IN THE CONTRACTS. The CLERK mentioned, that a mistake seemed to have been made when deciding the contract for beef and mutton at the previous meeting.—Mr BLACKHURST said the mistake seemed to have been made in the reckoning at the Board table by which Mr Cress's contract for mutton seemed to amount to nd per lb. instead of 71d. In consequence of this error the contract had been given to McGill. He did not know whether the Board could do anything in the matter now.—Mr J3LLEY explained that toere was a good deal more beef than mutton used, and if they balanced the one against the other they would find that they were perfectly right after all.- Mr BROWN thought they must have something more tangible than they had before them before they could rescind their resolution of the previous meeting giving the convect to Mr Gill, as it would be a precedent whicn might be very dangerous. It was well known to these of experience that the expenditure between beef and mutton was very great indeed as to quantity, and therefore a farthing or halfpenny a pound on mut- ton would not affect them very much. They could not decide a contract merely according to the ' price of the , mutton; they must take it in the ag- gregate—Mr He/contort: Mr Cross's contract WM the lowest for both beef and mutton. He moved that the reso- lution passed at the previous meeting be rescinded.—Mr Four= said that as there seemed to have been a mistake made he would second this proposal.—Mr Jena= moved as an amendment that the contract remain as fixed. The meat supplied had been of the most satisfactory quality. Suppos- ing a mistake had been made, it had not Peen intentional- Altering a c mtract had not a nice look with it, and al- though there was nothing underhand about it, or nothing being kept back, it looked as though they would throw a man over for Coe seize of saving a farthing.—Mr BROWN seconded Mr Jolley's proposal.—The CHAIRMAN said that was a very important matter as regarded future contracts —Mr CALDWELL said ' that if there had been any mistake it must be blamed to the collective wisdom of the Board. He should support the amend- ment.—Mr BOUGHTON did not think they were act- ing fairly to Mr Cross.—Mr OWEN thought it was very unfair indeed.—Mr DARBYSHIRE complained of par- ticulars of what had transpired in the Board-room being told outside. They were there as a private body, and when members left that Board-room he considered it ungentle- manly if they went to those parties whom they had been discussing and told what individual members had said.—Mr CALDWELL could take it upon himself that he had never divulged what one parson or another person had said. He I would leave other members to sp‘ak for themselves.—Mr BLACKED:MST said that somebody very quickly carried out of that room that a mistake had been made.—The Cnarn- mew said he left the Board-room about half-past two and he was met by Mr Cross, who said the Board had not done fairly by him.—Mr Owner said that on the previous Board day he was passing Mr Cross's shop, when Mrs Cross asked if he would oblige her with the figures of the contract, which he did. They were ratepayers, and he thought they had a right to know—Mr DARRISHIRE : It is a breach of trust.—The amendment that the contract remain as fixed at the previous meeting was then put and carried by six to five —The Clerk was instructed to write to Mr Cross to let him know the decision of the Board, and to inform him that they were sorry a mistake had occurred. scatom COMMITEEE.

At a meeting of the auove committee, held on the 30th. Sept., the :-uperintendent nrceinced a specification in accor- dance with tto direction of the committee for the clock which is aporved, and be is directed to obtain tenders from a maker in this town; that John Warrington, a boy 11 years of age, who has frequently run away from the schools, be removed to the Workhouse where the boundary walls are more difficult to scale; that the thanks of this committee be given to Mr Wm Houghton for kindly giving a hamper of nears for the use of the children.

APPOINTMENT OP NURSE. Five candidates for the appointment of nurse to the hos— pital appeared before the Board, and after some consideration Miss RJ spittle, Manchester, was appointed. This was all the business of public interest.

An attendant at the Health Exhibition has died from in- lame caused by contact with an electric lighting apparatus in the Exhibition. PEW% p-ize fight took place near Epsom on Thursday. and was carried on with much vigour until the police appeared, just as the cornbatan.s were summoning their energies tor the final " round." Both the pugilists were clever& scoured by the police, together with ten of their adders and alWtore, and the whole gang were taken before the magistrives at Croydon and remanded on hail. SIIICIDX OP* BMIONET.—An inquest was held on Tuesday afternoon at Kensington on khe body of Sir James Lumsden Seton, Bart., who committed Inicide by cutting his throat. Lady Elizabeth Seton, wife of the deceased, said Sir James, who was forty-nine years of age, had latterly been in depress- ed spirits. lie went to his bathroom on Sunday morning. about eight o'elocK, and an hour later, the door being forced. he was found dead Other evidence showed that the de- ceased had an extensive gash in his throat. Lieutenant- Colonel Wm. Sam lel Seton, of Penally. near Denbigh, stated that some years ago the deceased had a fall from his horse. and in consiquence had suffered mentally at varying in- tervals. Verdict. "Suicide whilst in a state of unsound

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1884:

Sir B. SAMUELSON, M.P., on Monday even- ing, distributed the prizes and certificates gained by the 'students attending the Liver- pool Science and Art Classes, and delivered an interesting address on education. He quo- ted statistics to show the great progress that had been made in the elementary schools of Liverpool, and, referrinq to the subject of alleged over-pressure, he urged that, as it had a tendency to defeat itself, it could not be said in view of the results obtained that there ' was over-pressure in those schools. Dr. BROWNE, in a Parliamentary report recently issued, in dealing with this subject, pointed sl out that a good deal of worry and mental strain proceeded from giving children Home Lessons. There can be no doubt that a- mono.6st the poorest, where the number of the members of a family is often in inverse ratio to the accommodation, school ,children have a hard time of it in doing their home work; and we can well believe that in some cases their young lives are rendered miserable. They are in no frame of mind after school hours for mastering hard tasks, and it is quite certain that attempts to make progress under such conditions are hurtful rather than help- ful. Even where parents are disposed to smotth the 'way, it sometimes happens that a child from weakness, or the mental dullness that frequently accompanies rapid bodily growth, does itself an injury by puzzling over

tasks quite beyond it, except with aid from the teacher. In such a case the parent would do well to take the matter in his own hands, and arrange for the omission of Home Les- sons. There are few school-teachers who would press Home Lessons as against the judgment of the father or mother, and if they did they have no power to enforce their clic- turn. In a case'tried the other week, it Was decided that the schoolmaster was not justi- fied in punishing a child for failure to do home work when the parent had protested against home work being given It will thus be seen that this is a matter which parents may regulate for themselves, and it is a duty which they owe to their offspring to intervene when they think it desir- able. The first wealth, as Emerson says, is health, and a child which is in this way deprived of health has a robbery com- mitted upon it, the effects of which may last for a life-time. We grant that there will be few cases in which.interference will be neces- sary, for the majority of childten are fully equal to all that is required of them, as is de- monstrated by the success which has attended the. work of education during the past ten years. Speaking broadly, it is a question whether as a whole the scholars in our ele- mentary schools would not get on quite al well as they do without Home Lessons. There are teachers of wide experience witc'' believe that they cculd be dispensed with, the scholars who are free from thorn commencing work in the morning with a' freshness and vigour which enable them the more easily to get through their appointed tasks. It is an adage older than our national school- system that "All work and no Play makes Jack a dull boy." Mr. SAmo-ar..sox adopted the observation of Mr. OSCAR BROWNING at the Social Science Congress that over-pres Sure too frequent ' meant bad teaching, by which he explained that teachers were "expected to do impos- sibilities." They were expected to conduct schools with children as assistants, who ought themselves to be learners. He might have added that school managers, especiallY in voluntart, schoo's, were too prone to dis- regard applications for strengthening the staff," limiting themselves to what will just pass muster, and secure the full Govern- ment grant. With regard to Board Schools,. there is less ground of complaint on this head, for they are as la rule well staffed, the managers of them, having the rates to fait back on, being in a position to secure e ciency without troubling themselves over- much to maise ends meet. It is satisfactory to note that this power to dip in the public purse is not abused, for, 'when it is taken into account that less fees are received and higher salaries paid, it may be said that Board Schools are managed as economically as Voluntary Schools. Mr. SAMUELSON WS rather hard on Sir RICHARD CROSS for his remarks at Pemberton to the effect that if a child were taughta few simple things he could, teach himself anything, and nearly all bad been done for it that was necessary. They would only b.: too delighted, Mr. SAmuir.sol4 said, if they could find some patent ma- chinery in which all the children in the ele- mentary schools should be so far advanced as to be able to teach themselves anything. Havinz got the hint, perhaps Sir RICHARD CROSS will exercise his inventive powers with, . , a view to furnishing the requisite " patent.' There can be no question that if he should succeed i:i this direction it will be a great, success It will be much more valuable to artizans than the A•tizans Dwellings Act,. under which so few artizans have been fur- nished with dwellings. But we have no hope that Sir RICHARD will trouble himself in a matter of this kind. He. belongs ,to the • party—again to quote Mr SAMUELSON—wh°. believe in "giving the working-classes the, smallest amount cf education" Very few" and very simple" are the things that would be taught in our national schools if the Tories had all their own way. But whatever may be said as to "a lying spirit," there can be no question that the schoolmaster is abroad, and that, to do him justice, he is anxious to• do something more than teach his pupils "a few simple things." The tide of education is advancinc<, and it is not to be swept back by the Mrs PARTINGTONS of South-West Lancashire. (:-

iENERAL -.JORDON has at length suc- ceeded in raising the siege of Khartoum; but he has had a hard time of it. Mr. POWER, the Times correspondent, one of the three Englishmen at Khartoum—the GENERAL and Colonl STEWART being the 'other two—has managed after repeated efforts to send de- spatches home. They will be found •in another column, and. it will be seen that, brief as they are, they constitute an exciting story. There has been continual fighting, and it ta admitted that, on the side of the besieged,o there have been close upon 700 killed. The , loss on the part of the rebels is not stated,bot there is)reasian to believe it has been much greater. On one occasion some aoo of them were killed in an attack from Khartoum by SaA.Ti Bay, and on another we learn that.lls perished by the explosion of nine mines in a village which had been taken' possession of , by the rebels for the purpose of assault. , General GORDON has always shown won- derful 'resource in the most difficult circumstances. The mines he has lair's appear to havo been the means of saving Khartoum, for no dependencewhatever could be placed upon the Egyptian garrison be was seeking' to succour. In fact such a worthless body of soldiers it would be dif- ficult to find; they have no fight in them- " One Arab horseman," Mr. Lowait says, "is enough to put 200 of the bulk of our men to flight." It is a pity they were not from the first allowed to make use of their , legs, rather than make any sacrifice to rescue them. We warrant they would have got away, from Khartoum, and with whole skins —if General GORDON had not gone near them. SAATI BEY seems to have been the only officer among them worth naming; he shares honours of the sit ge with the three• Englishmen, and it is sad to reflect, 1 after the incalculable services he had ren- ' deiced, that he was a sacrifice to the COW ardice of the men who should have fought with him. The record of July loth may well say—" SAATI'S loss is serious." It is , swgestive of the confidence in General GOR" DON among a portion, at any rate, of the tra- ders of the community that his paper money should have been accepted to the tune of £50,000. They were not disposed to conclude that General, GORDON was " abandoned," or they would not have trusted him. They will now reap the reward of their faith; the" pa- per" which 'they hold will be found to be as good aS gold," It is stated that be- fore•the siw began, over half the popula- tion— some eight or ten thousand went over t the the, rebels. The ;" and it is pretty certain that, had the siege been protracted, the General with 20,000 instead of moot) mouths to fill, would have been beaten by famine if not by. the Soudanese. Since the Nile rose, General GORDON has been as good as his word in giving "a good account of the rebels," until, unaided, he has been able to raise the siege. He is now undoubtedly in a s position to leave Khartoum—indeed the latest news to hand is that he has re-captured Ber- ber—but it is a moot point whether he will return from the valley of the Nile until, to put It plainly, he is compelled. Whatever may have been his original intention, he has taken Lt as his latest mission to "smash up the Mandi." But this is outside the policy of the British Government—a policy which is summed up in—not the." abandon- ment of General GORDON "—but in the abandonment of the Soudan.

The Runcorn Sanitary Authority are in the , unpleasant position of having to do the best they can with abominations brought to their doors by means of what is known as the Old Quay Canal, or Old River, which commences at Manchester and terminatesat Runcorn. An outbreak pf diptheria at Walton Inferior has led to certain inquiries, and at the fort- nightly meeting held on Tuesday, an impor- tant report was presented by Mr. FARRING- TON, the nuisance inspector. He states that at the Manchester end of the Old River, the water at the time of the inspection was "of many colours, the prevailing one being black.'' Further, it was "almost stagnant" and "in a state of fermentation." It will thus be seen that there is some ground for the popular theory that the pollution of the Canal is in a large measure due to the filth and refuse turned into it by the employers of Manches- ter and Salford. But they are not the only sinners. Warrington has a share in the iniquity, for the sewage from the Workhouse School flows into the Canal near Dobbyss lock. A number of houses at Stockton Heath, Appleton, and Wal- ton Inferior also drain into the Canal; and there are contributions of liquid refuse from a tannery at Astmoor, in Hal- ton, and from the Highfield tannery in Run- corn. Indeed the Canal may be said to be the subject of pollution from beginning to end, and it is anything but agreeable to learn that, at some points, potatoes are " washed" in it— save the mark !—before they are sent to the various markets. Such a practice is highly reprehensible. Better send them with earth clinging to them—they would then get washed properly before use—rather than delude the buyer into the belief that he is getting something which has already undergone a process of purification. Speak- ing at the annual meeting of the Sanitary Institute, on Wedn-sday, Sir R. RAW- LINsorT said :--" In the world there is no value but in human life, and human life has most value when healthy and moral," The problem is how to make life " healthy and moral," and it must be admitted that it cannot be done under such conditions as are revealed by this report as to the State of the Old River. The remedy, such as it is, is in a resort to the law, and we are glad ,o see that the Runcorn Sanitary Authority have resolved to take steps with a view to bring- ing into operation the provisions of the Public Health Act of 1875, and of' the •Rivers Pollution Prevention Act. They have wisely resolved to forward, in the first instance, the Inspector's report to the Local Government Board. This, it is to be hoped,

will be followed by an official inquiry into the facts on the part of the Board ; and if the , Canal be found to be as black as it is painted we may be quite sure that something will be done with the object of rendering it more tolerable to humanity,
