WIDNES FIRE BRIGADE—Mr D Fetlierr and Mr J Carr have succeeded in forming a fire brigade of 15 men, which promises to become very efficient. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—At the weekly meeting at the National • Schools, on Thursday,_the Rev J Wright Williams delivered a lecture on "Our Juggernaut" to a fair aadience. WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.—These classes have commenced the Winter's work with every prospect of a suc- cessful season. The annual distribution of prizas will take place In the 141,h instant. MERSEY MISSIONS 10 SEAMEN, HllNCOnar.—The annual harvest thanksgiving service in connection with this inis• eion was held on Thursday evening, when the Rev T Patrick, MA, chaplain of the missions, preached to a crowded 'congregation. The choir rendered several hymns in a pleasing manner, Mr G Howard being at the harmo- nium. The room was tastefully decorated with fruits, flowers, and cereals. GOOD TEXPLARS kT WIDNES.—Ths weekly meeting of the Haste to the Rescue Lodge was held on Tuesday even- ing, when the members from the "Star of Wideem " and "Samaritan" Lodges attended. An entertainment was given by Bros T Taylor, Andrews. Wood, W Dickson, R Jenkins, and C H Smith. Supper was afterwards partaken of. During the evening one member was restored to fellow- shin, and two persons were proposed for membership. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT WESTON.--A thanksgiving service for the gathering in of the harvest was held at tne Church of St John the Evangelist, Weston, on Friday evening, the sacred edifice having been beautifully decorated with the various fruits of the earth. There was a largo congreoa- lion, and the Rev J W N Tanner, M.A., vicar of Antrobus, preached an able sermon. The anthem "Ye shall dwell in - the land" was creditably given by the choir, Mr W Arm- strong singing the bass solo in capital style. A collection was made in behalf of the Additional Curate Society. Sub- sequently the choir sat,down to an excellent repast at the . residence of Mr and Mrs T Ford. PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT WlDNES.—Special sermons were preached in the Hutchinson-street Primitive Metho- dist Chapel:Widnes, on Sunday, by Mr W 'Marine, of Liverpool, on the occasion of the annual harvest thanks- giving services. The edifice was tastefully decorated. On Monday evening a tea party, followed by a fruit banquet, was held. Mr T Marshall presided, and there %vas a good ' attendance. Addresses were delivered by the Rev .1 Calvert, and Messrs H Thornton. 8 Drought, S Pinches, T Rollason, and d Shuttleworth. During the evening the choir ren- dered several selections of music, under the leadership of Mr H G Seddon. Donations amounting to £4l were pro- I' mised towards the reduction of the chapel debt. SHOCKING SEICIDE AT HALENVOOD.—JarIIOS Grace, a' shunter, living near the station at Halewood, committed !suicide on Thursday afternoon, under distressing circum- stances. The deceased soon after coming home on Thursday morning after being at work all night went to bed and told his daughter, a little girl between six and seven years of age, to Wake him at four o'clock, as he hod to return to his employment. !It the time the girl went upstairs, and on onterimr, the room noticed blood on the be.l clothes, and told the next door neighbour, named Worrall, that her father had cut his finger. Upon Worrall entering the room he was horrified to find Grace on the bed with a dreadful gash in his throat, The bed clothes were saturated with blood, and an open razor covered with crimson ' stains lay on a chair • near. Grace was still alive, but only lived a few minutes, Dr Chislehtune, of Wooltom was telegraped for, but his ser- vices Were of no avail, and he stated that death niust have been almost instantaneous, the throat having been cut from ear to ear. Grace's wife was only buried on Tuesday last, and the'circumaranc, s of her illness and death, seemed to, have preyed noon the mind of deo,ssed, wrio for some time bad been in a desponding mood. ' Tile deceased was only 31 years of age, and belongs to a very respectable family in the neighbourhood.

/• Collar MINSTRELS AT Rl:remote/L-0n Saturday and Monday evenings these well-known minstrels performed before large audiences at Runcorn Public Hall, the entertainment being of a most laughable description. CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, Rineconw.—At theweekly meeting of this class, on Friday evening, Mr Simkin read a paper on" Scott and his poems" to a large audience. Mr altandie presided. 14HE SECOND COMING OP THE LORD.—On Monday next, and on Monday in the three successive weeks, a lecture on this subject will be delivered in Runcorn Public Hall, by an "Evangelist serving under the Lord's Restored Apostle- ship." THE ;CRY LISTS -At Runcorn Pattv Sessions, on Monday, the asaistant overseers of Runcorn. Halton, Weston, Su,ton, Aston-by-Sutton, Aston Grange, Norton, Clifton, and Stock- ham submitted lists of persons qualified to serve on juries, and as there were no objections they were duly signed. UNITED METHODIST FREE CEURCH, RUNCORN.—Good congregations assembled in this church on Sunday, morning and evening, when Mr R Hatton, of Winsford, preached the anniversary sermons. Musk specially selected was rendered by the choir, under the leadership of Mr J Elalford. Col- lections were made on behalf of the trust fund. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—At the Old Quay Copper Works, Runcorn, on Monday, a labourer named Thomas Jones, who lives at 2G, Nelson-street, was at work on a der- rick, when the rope by which he was suspended ova way and he was precipitated into a flue 25 feet deep. Both his arms were hroken, but he is progressing favourably under the care of Dr Mouritz. FORTECOI/lING MILITARY CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—From an advertisement in our columns it will be seen that a con- cert will take place at the Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday next, under the auspices of the brass band of the Runcorn companies of the tad C R.V. The concert has been organised with the object of defraying the cost of a new double bass instrument, of which the band has long seriously felt the need. MILTON-ROAD CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES.— Harvest thanksgiving and floral 90$ViCeS were held at this place of worship on Sunday. The interior of the building had been adorned with much taste and skill by several• members of the congregation. There was A large attendance at both morning and evening service, the preacher being the Rev R G Hughes, the pastor. At the conclusion of the evening discourse a service of sacred song was rendered by the choir, under the leadership of Mr Johnson., Miss F Travis preeided at the harmonium. ST. MARY'S CHURCH; GREAT SANKEY. —The Annual har- vest thanksgiving services were held in the above church on I Sunday. There were large congregations. he decorations were tastefully executed by the ladies of the congrogttion, who were greatly assisted in their work by the liberal con- tributions of fruit, hothouse plants, and cut flowers, sent by several kind friends in the parish and neighbourhood. Ap- propriate sermons were preached in the morning by the Rev E Li Vernon, and in the evening by the Rev E S Jackson. The collections for the day amounted to £2l is RELIGIOUS SERVICES AT RUNCoRN.— to-eight a fort- night's special religious services in connection with St Luke's Congregational Mission Chapel, Masoe-street, will ,be concluded. The services have been very well attended each evening, and the audiences have been moved with deep religious fervour. Several important conversions have taken place. The Rev Joseph Davies, i$ Buckley, h3s taken , a prominent part in the work, and good work has been per- I formed by the Rev J D Thomas, and Mr Joseph Slade and I Mr Coventry. Mr Welter Lacey ha e ably presided at the harmonium, MR/ Gfailieroleg AND A RONtnAN LIEEHAL.—LISt Week a Runcorn working-man, of staunch Liberal principles, wrote to Mr Gladstone, artking the right hon, gentleman to receive an addrees from the working-men of Runcorn on his return journey from Scotland. On Friday afternoon the following telegram was received from E W Hamilton, 1 Downing-street :—" Mr Gladstone desires me to thank you for your letter. He is much gratified by the proof supplied to him from many qumeers that the feeling of Scmlend and , of England is the same in relation to the present isis. He , regrets that his route will not take him pe-t Runcorn to- ' day, and that accordingly he will be prevented Lom person- ally receiving an address from yourself and your friends." ; CONCERT AT WIDNES.—In aid of Hartland Wesleyan Chapel a concert, under; influential patronage, was held ; in the Widnes Volunteer Hall on Monday evening, and the building was ceowded in every part. In the absence of Mr , W Outten, of Liverpool, Mr F H Gossage presided. The vocalists were Madame Laura Haworth, Miss Kate Meredith, and Mr Floe Morlais. and as they were all in good form those present ecio.yed a rich MuSical trelt. The Cambrian Vocal Union renlaed several concerted pieces with great harmony, and the Widnes Soap Werke Brass Bend (late Star of 'Temper- ance) perrormed Handel's "Hallelujah chorus" in a manner that left nothing to be desired. Mr 00 P t-ry performed the duties of conductor, and Miss alaggie E Evaca was an accomplished accompanist. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.— On Sunday evening a harvest thanksgiving service was held at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn. The cora- munion and pulpit had been most tastefully adorned for the occasion by Mrs Thom le, Mrs T Handley, Mrs Dobson, Miss Handley, Miss N Handley, Miss Littler, and Miss M Littler. The Rev J D Thomas preached an able sermon from the 26th. versa of the 2nd chapter of Joel. The choir, under the leadership rof Mr Fairbaret, rendered epeetally selected music in a creditable :nervier, In the atithem will Rive thanks " ;ba.seotod wors sung bS:, Mies N Handley and Slias Annie Ainsworth he unimpeachable style, the for- mer being in especially good voice. There was a large con- gregation, and a collection was made on behalf of tho chapel funds.

Br:Neoax Bowan OF GUABDIANS.—Mr John Ashton pre- sided at the fortnightly meeting on Tuesday. There were present the Rev J Lockwood, Messrs Norman, J Stocks, Aaron, W Fisher, E A Wallington, R Asbton, Warburton, W Handley, Jackson, C Rigby, Darbyshire, Mclntyre, Hatril- ton.—The only business of importance was the consideration of the various contracts, which were let as follows :—Flour, ' J Yapp, Halton; groceries, executors of the late Mr 8 Col- lier; drugs, dtc., J Speakman; drapery, Thomas Wright, Balton; clothing, A E Hawkins. Runcorn; coal, Wigan Iron and Coal Company; coffins, T Lightfoot, Dutton ; wines and spirits, R Rigby, London and North-Western Hotel, Run- corn; potatoes, Thomas Bate, Sutton; straw' Thomas,Ben- nett,Keokwick; milk and butter, W Grounds, Aston; beef, Dobson, Warrington. RoNCOSN Palace Cougm.—Befo-e Mr G L Davies at the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Bridget Brown who stated tbat she was the wife of the Frodsham billposter, was charged with being drunk and incapable in Greeuway- road on the previous night. The case having been proved, the Prisoner saiel she had come to Runcorn to bay groceries' and s e bad spent all the money in drink.—She was fined fie and costs or seven days.--Yesterday, before Mr W Bankes, Thomas Roberts, of Manchester, and George Raw.' linson, of Runcorn, boatmen, were charged with breaking into a but belonging to Messrs Win Guest and Sons, quarry owners, Runcorn, betweeo the Nth and 29th Septetnper, I and stealing therefrom a quantity of ropes. PS McMichael gave evidence sufficient for a remand and the prisoners were remanded until Monday--John Travenor, boatman, was sentenced to la days' hard labour for sleeping in the stables of Mr Samuel Crosby, High-street, Runcorn, on the previ• one evening. Natatuor ear FAMILY—John Broxton was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, charged with neglect- ing bid wife and child —Mr J W _Knowles defended. Mr Scannell said the prisoner was a furnace-man, and was in re- ceipt of high wages. He constantly neglected his wife and child, and on the 15th of this month witness called at the prisoner's house. He found the woman 'and child in the most. destitute condition, in fact, they were in a state of starvation. He sent them to the workhouse, and the pri- soner was communicated with in the matter, but be bad made no response in any way. He subjected his wife to great cruelty, and beat her in such a manner that she was not able to get her own living. Ho bad positively refused to do anything for her. On this evidence he asked for a remand. —The amount owing to the Guardians by the prisoner was 1.6 s 61—The prisoner was remanded until Wednesday next. He was liberated on bail, himself in £2O and two sureties of LIO each.

SHOOTING EXTRAORDINARY BY A WIDNES MAN. Mr Gil Fowler. proprietor of the Millfield Hotel and Pleasure Grounds, Appleton„ Widnes, made AO extraordinary perfor- mance at Sandbach, on Monday. in the presence of a con- course of about 3,000 people. His broke 48 out of 50 balls with a small-bore rifle, and then he fired at and smashed 100 glass balls out of 1084 n eight minutes, loading his rifle each time. 'lie had four mis,Ares, owing to one of his pins go- ing wrong. He cut a horae-hair in halves with a ballet, shooting from his head with his rifle reversed. He also, with one shot, broke six glass balls placed ill the neck of a bottle without damaging the bottle. His other feats were breaking a glass ball swinging at the end of two yards of 'string, shooting down the barrel of a pistol, and breaking a glass ball which it contained; breaking an ordinary whiskey bottle standing behind a log of wood a foot thick; he split a bullet on a knife blade, and with each half broke a glass standing on either side of the knife; he broke several balls holding the rifle in one handrand this performance he also accomplished with a shot gun, the balls being sprung from a trap. He then turned his back to the trap, and, without moving his feet, turned his body round, and broke the balls as they were successively sprung from the trap. The rifle used was a 360-bore exOress, made by Henry, of Edinburgh, Mr Fowler has undertaken to shoot and break 300 glass balls, and load his own gun each time, in 30 minutes. SHOCKING MEATH ,IN THE STREET AT WIDNES.—Mr Brighouse, the county coroner, on Monday held an inquest at the Widnes Police Court touching the death of John Henry, 35 years of age.—Evidence was given by J;dan Heniy, 28, Lngsdale-road, son; P.C. Cheers, Dr O'Keeffe, 'Alfred Williams, 38, Oakland-Street; and Sergeant Clarkson. It appeared that Henry was a man of very drunken habits, who loafed about the streets and slept in chemical works, and had frequently been before the magistrates on a variety of charges. About midnight on Friday Constable Cheers saw him staggering along Waterloo-road, apparently help- lessly drunk. After walking about 150 yards Henry fell, and the constable went and told him he would have to go tb the police station. At the railway crossing they had to wait, for a train tapas% and Henry saying he was "gassed" sat down on the doorstep of the Railway Hotel. The con- stable then saw that something was the matter with the de- ceased, and obtained a quantity of water off the signalman and sprinkled it en his face. At this time P.C. Holbrook, and Williams came up, and the deceased was placed on a wheelharow and conveyed to the police station, where it was discovered that the supposed inebriate was dead. The de- ceased smelt slightly of intoxicating liquor, and Cheers stated that he had heard be had been drinking in a house from nine in the morning to eleven at night—The jury. guided by the medictl testimony, returned a Verdict of "Natural causes."

LARGE MtsnaooM.—A n-mshroom, weighing 171 ounc,s was found on Sturdy last growing in a field belouging to Mr Glover, farmer, Lower Srretmo, Cheshire. DRUNKENNESS AT WIDNES.--At Widnes Police Court on

_ Monday, Bridget McMillan, Walter Hardley, Thomas Leop- ard, Patriek Smith, Thomas Kelly, Thomas McQuire, Sarah Spruce, William Marr, William Seymour, and William May were each fitted 5s and cosis for being drunk and disorderly on either Saturday or Sunday. ROBBERY BY A WORKMAN AT WIDNES. John Fury, a labourer, was brought up at Widres Police Couit on Mon- day charged with stealing a bricksetter's hod, value 4e, the property of Dominic Nyland, in April last. The circum- stances have been previously reported. The prisoner was fined 40s and costs, or in default 21 days' imprisonment A SUSPECTED THIEF AT Wins.—Yesterday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr F H. Gossage, a farm la- bourer, who gave the name of George Brookes; was charged on susp'clon with stealing a lady's silver grey macintosh. About five o'clock on Thursday afternoon P.C. Davies found the re isoner offering to sell the macintosh, which is a new one, to a second-hand clothes dealer at Simms Cross.—The prisoner alleged that he found the article and a ea' chel in Scotland-road, Liverpool, and he hid sold the satchel as he passed through Garston.—He was remanded for a week. NEW STEAMER FOR ISLE OF MAN TRAFFIC—The Isle of Man Steam Packet Company, with their usual enterprise, have ordered a large and powerful steamer from the Barrow Shipbuilding Company to be ready for next season. The builders guarantee her to run 19 knots, or about 22 miles, and she ought, therefore, to Cle the passage between Fleet- wood and Douglas (the station she is intended for) in anout 21 hours. She will be built and fitted in firSt class ; style, and will be about. the same size as the well-known clipper steamer " Mona's Isle," belonging to the same com- pany. . THEFT FROM A, SHOP AT WlDNES.—Befora Mr H S ILli and Mr F LI Gossige, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Michael Curren. middle-aged 'man, was charged with hav- ing on Saturday night stolen s±lbe of bacon from the shop of Mr 8 Sadler, Ann-street, West, Widnes. From the evi- dence of John Owen, the manager for Mrs Sadler, it appeared that .the prisoner about nine o'clock passed in front of the shop several times and thin suddenly rushed, inside, enatob- ed up the piece of b min produced, and ran away. He was pursued and caught in Ceroline-street. and was now reman- ded for a week.

THIS ASSAULT ON WIDNES MEN AT WOOLTON.—At Wool- ton Petty Sessions on Frid ty, berms Messrs Arthu,. Eerie, Holbrook Gasket', and W L Evans, three Irish labourers named Patrick and Michael Ginley, brothers, and Anthony Ginley, cousin, all of SpAre, wero chargeil on remand with having unlawfully assaulted and wounded Robert Moors, Alfred Moores, Gorge Stanley, John Jackson, and Philip Parkin, on the Soeke-road, Much Wootton. at 10 p.m. on the 13th ult. Mr Superintendent Barker prosecuted, and Mr W G. Swift appo tred for the defence. Tee prisoners were com- mitted for trial. _ _ _

, AN AGED INEBRIATE AT RrINCORN.—BefOre Mr G L ' Davies, at Runcorn Police Court, on Satuday, Elizabeth Kelly, 78 years of age, was charged with being drunk in Church-street—l'S. McMichael • said at eight o'clock on Friday night he found the prisoner in the Clarendoo Efitel in a state of helpless lotoxicition. He procured a hand- cart, and conveyed her to the police station.—The prisoner stated that she had been an inmate of Caester Workhouse for five years. She had come to Runcorn to look for her SOP, and a woman she had met made her drink two glasses of fool, PIA the liquor had been too much for her. She promised to at once return to the Worktoule if discharged, And his Worship ordered her to be liberated. THE LIVERPOOL, EOIIMPORT, AND PRESTON JUNICrION Itamwer.—We understand that the directors of the Liver- pool, Southport, and Preston JUnction Railway Company have arranged to let the contract for the construction of the company's line to Mr Charles Braddock, railway contractor, of Southport and Wigan. The line when made will form a connecting link between the Southport and Cheshire Lines Extensioa Railway and the West Lancashire Railway, and will be worked by the company owning the latter, civirk; them acccss to the Cheshire Lines system and the Liver- pool Docks, in addition to providing a through route between Blackburn, Preston, and Southport and intermediate stations and Liverpool and the South, and another through route by means'of the Blackpool Railway for Liverpool and the South to Lytha.n, St. Males on the-Sea, and Blackpool. ROYAL LIVER FRIENDLY FOCIETY.—A pamphlet by " Nemesis " on Friendly Societies makes the following in- teresting reference to this society :—" The Royal Liver Friendly Society has been in succlssful operation for over 34 years ; that this society has paid in claims nearly £3,000,000 for 282.089 claims; that the gross amount col- tented during 1883 as £355,028 7s id; that claims amounting to £187,183 41 14d have been n'id durino the Caine period; that the accumulated capital is £793,541 in- vested at the averatm interest of 41 per cent. in Corporation and Local Government Bonds, which are secured upon the rates, therefore being to all intents and purposes Govern- ment securities ; and that, since the establishment of the society, the sum of nearly £1,000,000 bras been return( d as bonuses or interest to the members, and further that the Royal Liver Friendly Society has an invested capital of more than £324,579 above all the other Liverpool societies put together." We may add that an advertisement of the society will be found in soother column,

zwzanctr Holm mutat Sdelefe, uccairrx.— The firet annual exhibition ot the above society was held on Saturday and ennday, in the infants' school-room, rs ew- church, which was kindly placed at the disposal of the committee by the Rector, the Rev Dr Black. The room was excellently fitted on for the occasion with tables and shelves for the deposit of the various articles exhibited. On the table in the centre of the room, were placed a brass pan, three copper kettles, and twenty metal teapots, being the prizes for the oniens exhibited, some of which were excellent specimens. The other exhibes were also very good, includ- ing cabbages, caulitlawers, potatoes, fruit and flowers. There was a very laree attendance, including the Rev Dr Black, Mrs and Miss Black, Mr C C Black, dm. The judges w:re —Meseta Davison, of Glazebury • ' Walton, of Calcheth Hall; and Webster, of Kenyon Hall, who awarded the prizes. Mr CC Black, previous to declaring the show open to the public, highly congratulated the committee and members of the society upon the pains they had taken to ensure the success of the exhibition, which was a credit to themselves and the village, and hoped they would continue 1 to improve in number of members and otherwise, untit they would require a much larger room than the one in which they were then assembled. A hearty vote of thanks was given to the judges for their services on the motion of Mr C C Black. seconded by Rev Dr Black. Great credit is due to the following members of the committee for the admirable ' arrangements which they had made for the exhibitiote namely, Messrs James Whittaker (chairman), James Parker, Richard Winstanley, James Pownall, Peter Gibbon, James Oultram, and Charles Gibbon (secretary) ; also to Mr Ralph Green, who kindly assisted the committee In arranging the various articles exhibited, ikc. SOLITE-WEST LANCASIIIRE REVISION.—Mr Butler, bar- I riater, held a court at the Warrington Police Court, on I ' Saturday, for the purpose of revising the list of Parliamentary ' voters in the South-West Lancashire division, (Warrington district.) The Liberals were represented by Mr G RC Powell (Liverpool), and Mr St Roberts (Warrington) ; and the Conservatives by Mr Woodnorth and Mr T Sutton. The only matter of interest which came before the court was the case of several farmers in Orford and elsewhere whose flume are situate within the borough ann who are upon the register of voters for the Parliamentary borough, and who were also published by the overseers on the £l2 list for the county. They were objected to by the Liberals on the ground that their being upon that list, and their being en- titled to be upon that list, disqualified them from being put upon the county register for the samb qualification.— vlr Roberts, in putting tbe case before the barrister, said that Mr Sutton and himself were agreed as to the facts, and it was consequently simply a question of law for His Honour to decide.—The Barrister said he had no doubt whatever that the persons in question had no right to be upon the county list, and he would therefore disallow the votes.

'RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The annual meeting was held lb the reading room, Town Hall, Waterlo-road, on Tbstred..y. Present—the Rev Canon Barclay, Messrs P BriscoeW Heedley, and F A Lake, and T I) Jones (librarian).—Eleetioa of Chairman : Mr Handley. • moved that the Rev Canon Barclay. be re-appointed chair- , man, remarking that no words of his were needed to recom mend the motion. Mr Barclay had fulfilled the duties of the position to the satisfaction of the Committee and the public.—Mr Briscoe seconded the motion wiih great plea- sure —The Rev Canon Barclay expressed bis obligations for the confideuce they were still, willing to repose in bim, but he would much rather they Would apPoint a gentleman who could take more interest in the Library and was prepared to spend more time in the work. It was also probable that he , might be leaving Runcorn before the expiration of the next twelve months, and he thought a permanent resident should be appointed.—Mr Handley thought they had better keep Mr Barclay in the chair, and Mr Lake bezged tb support the resolution, whieh made it the unanimous desire of the Committee. The Vicar then consented to take the position, and on the motion of Mr Lake, seconded by Mr Handley, Dr Steele was appointed vice-chairman.— librarian's Report.--The librarian reported that during the month of September there were 1199 volumes borrowed final the lending department, an increase of 59 on the co,- responding month last year. They were classified as fol- lows :—Theoiogy, 9; philosophy. political economy 15; history, travels, biography, 117; science and art, 21; pee- try and the drama, 18; prose fiction, 968; misceliakeons, 53 There were 38 reference books °omitted. classified as fol- lows :—Philosophy, 1; history, 4; science and art, 13; poe- try and the drama, 3: fictien, 2; and tniscellaneous, 15. There had been received for Snot, catalogues, .tc., the sum of £2 Ile 91. There had been presented by her Majesty the Queen, "Mote leaves from the journal of a life in be High- lands," with royal autograph; Or S'eele, 37 volumes, medi- cil and miacellane-us; Dr Bagman, 2 volumes gnonymons, 19 magagines —Accounts amounting to upwards of £2O were passed for payment.

Howei,er, in order that the question should be thoroughly thrashed out he would be willing to state his reasons for allowing the items, if Mr Leak would undertake to bring the matter before the Queen's Bench Division, or before the Local Government Board.—Mr Leak said that Would be the most satisfactory method of thoroughly investigating the matter, and he would give the required undertaking, and in the course of the day furnish the auditor with the names of one or more ratepayers who would become the appellants.—The subject, which had occupied about 50 minutes, then dropped. SWIMMING GALA AT LEIGH —Handicapper and starter, Mr R M Whitehead, Salford; judge, Mr It Tyldesley. The annual gala of the Leigh Amateur Club was held at the Public Baths on Tuesday evening, in the presence of a large ; and fashionable audience of ladies and gentlemen. It will , be seen that several local swimmers took part in the contests. The whole of the events were confined to amateurs, and the ' entries included a few of the best in the North of England., viz., Mr W It Button, Salford, champion of the Mersey., and 500 yards Lancashire champion; Joey Nuttall, of Staly- bridge ; and GA Barlow., of Warrington. The racing was first-class, several of the contests being very exciting,4 especially the fiaal heat of the 125 yards handicap. between Nuttall, Barlow, Bothwell, and Locker. Although the last- named, who has greatly improved, won, a ditermined set-to was witnessed for second place. Natal! beating Barlow by half a yard amidst great applause. Messrs Oldham and: Woletencroft gave an excellent exhibition of ornamental and scientific swimming. Subjoined we give the results of the - handicaps:—Amateur Handicap (five lengths; canfined to members of the club) :—Final heat: T Lonadale, 13sec start, 1; James Ratcliffe 4sec, 2; J Brown.l.4sec, 3. A capital race. Won by half a yard; same between second and third. Amateur •Handicap (open; seven. lengths. 125 yards):— Final heat J Locker. Warrington, 15sec. 1; Joey Nuttall. Stalybridge, scratch, 2; G A Barlow, Warrington, scratch, 3; W Bothwell, 4sec, 0. A most determined race between .the lot.- Locker won by two yards; a terrific struggle be- tween the. other three for second place ended in Nutted just outstaying Barlow by a foot, Barlow beating Bothwell by half a yard, although had Barlow not swain 'so often he would, have sedared second place. Nineteen competed. Amateur Handicap (nine lengths, 180 yards) :—Final heat: T Locker, Warrington, 17sed start, 1; W Bothwell, Tvides- ley, 6,2; A Barlow, scratch, 3. Another punfishing race. Locker kept in front, and won by a yard; a good race between &amen and Barlow for second place ended in the first- named just staying the longest, and winning by a foot. A very amusing duck hunt by members, and a well-contested game at water polo brought a Most successful and well- conducted entertaament to a close.

div.head: MRS. GENERAL 800 111 AT UNCO
div.p: MRS. GENERAL 800 111 AT UNCO

Yesterday Mrs Booth, wife of General Booth, the head of the Salvation Army, paid a visit to Itv.novo, and in the evening lectured in tb,e Public Hall on " The t'alvation Army; its past, present, and future." A large and respec-- able audience assembled a considerable time before the h.rur announced for the lecture, there being a good number of " soldiers " present from Widnes. 'Warrington, Wins- ford, and other places. Thas. platform was occup,ed by "daptains " of various " corps " in the district. Mrs.' Captain Parsons of Wi Ines sung a hymn from the "War Cry," entitled "Let him in," the audience joining heartily in the chorus. A perspective plan of the Salvation Barracks intended to bp erected in Runcorn was exhibited and received with an enthusiastic "volley." Shortly afterwards Mns Booth appeared, and Was received with a tremendous shout of " Hallelujah." Shemas accent. panful by Mr Edward Bolton, of Warrington, who took the chair, and Majcr Taylor. A hymm baying been sung, and prayer offered by Major Taylor, the Chairman said he praised God that he did not stand there as an ex-mayor or anything grand on man's side, but as a plain quaker lid, ifs believed the work of the Salvation Army was a very simple one. It was to distribute God's Bible and proclaim the spirit of that book to God's people, and to those who should be God's people, in His own appointed way. This was being done by their dear General of the , Army, in a way that had not been done in the early days of I the Reformation, or since. .

Male. Taylor referred to the woilc of the Army in the Lancashire division, which includes Cheshire. and remarked that while four years ago there were only 9 corps in the division, there were now 72, and the Army had a firmer hold upon the masses of the people, and had greater power of doing good thin ever they had during the foar years. The number of officers had increased from 20 to 150, and while four years ago there were only 500 soldiers, they had new increased to 7,000—k" Amen °)—most of them having been rescued from the gutter and not from the respectable circles of society. The circulation of the War Cry in the division had risen from 5 000 to 43,000, and the increaSe from £36 per week to £4OO per week. ("A volley.") Mrs Booth then commenced her lecture. She said she bad found there were the strangest notions about the Salva- tion Army. People seemed to think that the General had I an idea that he would like to be a great man, a sort of Pone —(laughter)—to say to one " come" and he cometh. and to another " go" and he goeth. They thought that he then sat down arid drew a programme in his brain of some or- ganisation, and that the Salvation army was the result. There never was a greater mistake. The Salvation /limy had been purely the outcome of what they believed most sincerely and drmly to have been the leading spirit of God, and of the providence of God. When the General com- menced what was then called a Christian Mission in the East end of London, he had no idea beyond local work. But he bad been prepared for the work of the Salvation Army for some years previous. Even when in the regular ministry the General was always planning new measures in order to reach the masses of the people. Mrs 'Booth described hew the General, under great irapqrtunity, commenced a mis- sion at Bethnal Green, and at length 'acquired the MEW. ham Theatre, where prize fighters, dog fighter), pigeon flyers were converted. The General began to see thatit was lawful and scriptural for these men, out of whom the devil of drink and blasphemy and uneleanness bad been cast out, to testify what had been done for them by Jews Christ. And he did that, and the salvation army had sprung up, but it had run ahead of them, and was running ah-ed of them. Mrs Booth concluded by giving some statistics of the army, after baying spoken nearly an hour and a half with good effect, " volleys " being frequently "fired." She denied that the General oe his family had received a penny from the Salvation Army. A collection was then taken, the chairman promising to give £3 3s. Afterwards several "tee- timonies " werregiven.

Tim BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINOTON.—For week ending Saturday, September 27th, 1884.—The mean ,emoerature was 521 Fahrenheit, and therefore 7.7 degrees colder than preceding week. The maximum temperature 69 Fahrenheit was recorded on the 21st inst., and the minimum temperature 38 Fahrenheit on the 27th inst The rainfall measured 13 inches. The general direction oi the winel was westerly. During the week, which was the 39th of the current year, 37 births and 16 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was e0u,41 10 186 per 14300, agiinst 245 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 21.2 the corresponding week of last year rne (1, aths included 4 from measles, 3 from ,diarrhoei, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from syphilis, and 1 from heart disease Two cases of typhoid fever were reported tinder the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JunN 11. Gunnierz, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

1 The fortnightly meeting was held at Da;ton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr John Aenton presided. arid there were pre- scut: Rev J Lockwood, Messrs J Stokes. -Derbyshire, ! Mclntyre, Aaron, R Ashton, EA Wallington, II Lioaker (clerk), W II Linalter (deputy clerk),. and Dr Adams (medical officer of health ) FRODSHAU WATER :t!UPPLY.—A letter was read from the Local aevernment Board &indicating 024 borrowing of £2OO for works of water supply at Frodsham. FEVER AND THE OLD QUAY CANAL —The Medical Officer of Health presented a special report in which he reported ari outbreak of diptheria at Walton Inferior in a cottage Oc- cupied by a min named Roberts. The too arming daughters of the occupier were the only persons attacked, and they were new convalscent. The sanitary arrangements were defective and the water supply was also open to suspicion. Toe doctor added that he had hid put into his bands that morning a notice to the effect that typhoid fever had broken out in those low damp cellars at Weston, where he reported that fever existed a fortnieht ago. He would inquire into the matter before the next Board day.—The Deputy Clerk I asked how far Robarts'e home . was from , the Old Quay 1 Canal.—The Doctor replied about forty or fifty yards. , The Deputy Clerk then referred to the report of Mr Farrington with respect4o, the Old Quay Canal. The report was to ti ollowing effect:— Mr Farrington, the nuisance inspects , presented an exhans- tive report of an examination he had made of the Old Qaay Canal, or, as it is oitea Wm-A, the " Old River," from Regent-road bridge, Manchester, to Runcorn. After point- ing. out the various sources from which the canal was pol- luted up to Warrington, showing that the canal was the recipient of sewage all along the route, the report stated there were five houses at Stockton Beath, Appleton, and 11 houses at Walton laferior that were drained into the canal, but nothing of an offensive nature flawed into the canal be- tween" Walton Inferior and Aatmoor. The main sewer for the drainage of Wilderspool and Stockton Heath discharged direct into the river at Wilderspool. The licinid refuse from a tannery at Astmoor in Halton, and also from Highfield` Tannery, Runcorn, flowed into the canal. The sewage from 63 houses in Hall,on-lene, Halton, flowed into a feeder complained of by the Bridgewater Navigation Com- I way. The liquid refuse from ' three tannerlei in Runcorn I was discharged into the same feeder. In accordance with 1 instructions the insprctor had procured four samples of i water and submitted them to the county anaiyet. The first sample was taken about 20 yards below the feeder come' pleined of, the second neer Tom Payne's Bridge, Wilders- pool, the third from the Jiver Irwell at Salford, and the fourth out of the same river just above where the Merely ! 'joined it in the township of Irlam, about mine 'miles from I Manchester. Mr T Ceder Bell, the county analyst, after ! giving details of the composition of the samples, remarks: l 1 —" It is rether a difficult question to say which is the worst I ! of theee four samples of water, when all are no bad, hut on a ' careful examination of the appearance and odour of the waters, any opinion is that No. 1 water carries off the palm I for impiarity, for ft has not only got the sewage odour ; which characterises all the samples, but it has a smell pa- caliaato itself of decomposing animal matter, such as may be not:ced from the drainings of tanyards, where skins are in 1 a partial state of decornpositton. I consider this No 1 water ! highly offensive, and in hot weather it must irritate the sur- !rounding inhabitants by the noxious vapours which must be evolved ; the great impurity which is in No. 1 must be I largely due to local contaminations.", The inspector eon- eluded his repoft by stating that when the rainy season set ! in some hundreds of thousands of tons Of objectionable and noxious matter would be washed down. It would be noticed that there were more contributors to such pollution than was generally understood, as Manchester as a rule got the blame. If the provisions of the Rivers Pollution Pre- vention Act were more strictly enforced much good would result therefrom.—The Deputy Clerk said he was of opinion I that if the statement of the inspector could be supported by! sufficient evidence that the parties by whose acts the nuis- ance arose or existed were liable to proceedings under the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, for the abatement' of the nuisances. As, however, the question was one which if takeo up by the Authority would involve the expenditure of a cnneiderable amount of money, he advised the Arr; thority to lay a copy of the report before the Local Go- vernment Board, and request them to direct an inspector of their Board to.hold a local inquiry into the facts,—On the motion of Mr Wallington, seconded by Mr Aaron, it was decided to follow the course suggested. A Cogan-nom—A letter was read from the medical officer correcting a statement made in his last report that Mrs eJotenson, of Dutton, had died from typhoid fever. It ought to have read that she was suffering from the dis- ease.
There was no other business of public interest.

THE BEASLEY COSTS.—INTERESTING ACTION BY RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. Mr John Dolby, the auditor, to the Local Government Board, commenced his half-yearly audit of the accounts of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday morning. Mr R Shaw (chair- man of the Board), Mr Fairhurst, Mr Pritchard, Mr Moss, and the officials were present. Mr 0 LeAk appeared on be- half of the Ratepayers' Association to apply that certain surcharges should be made by the auditor. The representa- tive of this journal presented himself in the room, but he was informed by the auditor that the proceedings would be conducted in private and asked to retire. Wee believe the following to be a correct summary of What occurrent—Mt Dolby asked Mr Leak which item* he objected to.—Mr Leak replied that his objections were in reswct of three items paid en the 4th July, 1883, namely, £l5O paid Mr W II Linker on aecount of costs; £440 103 6d paid to Mt 80-' hanua,sheriff'sofficer,amount of execution for debt and costs; and £2O paid Messrs Gregory and Co for additional agreed costs, all incurred in the action Beasley v. Runcorn Corn- inissioners and others.—Mr Leak said he should not be doe ing his duty to his clients unless he took the auditor with him through the whole facts of the case, which, would' occupy a considerable time.—Mr Dolby declined to go through the facts because he hadquade himself acquainted with them in the course of his audit last year.—Mr Leak ventured to say that there were facts in the case which Mr Dolby had not become acquainted with, or he would have come to a different decision.—After considerable argument, Mr• Dolby absolutely refused to listen to any statement of facts, and asked Mr Leak what grounds he had for making his application upon the facts which he (Mr Dolby) assumed himself to be already conversant with.—Mr Leak, in reply, contended that the individual defendants against whom , judgment, was signed were liable, and ought to be charged with the whole of the judgment debt and the costs incurred, they having by the judgment admitted that they had acted without reasonable and proper cause, and were guilty ' of such, negligence or misconduct as to bring them- selves within the 7tls sub-sectioa of 247th section of the Public Health Act. They were also, he argued, ' disqualified from claiming exemption under the pro- tecting clauses of either the Commissioners Clauses Act or the Public Health Act: At this point the Lew-Clerk (Mr W El Linakee) rose and said he had to make the preliminary objection that the items were not items which the public ' auditor had power to deal with, as they were accounts under ' the Commiesioners Clauses Ad, and not under the Public Health act, under which Act alone Mr Dolby held. his , authority. Mr Leak observed that this objection was frivo- lous, and stated that the Commihsioners purchased and held Waterloo House under powers given to them by the Public .Health Act,they having acquired that building for the per- poses of a public hospital. He therefore araued that any -recount arising in respect of the ownership of Waterloo House came within the jurisdiction of the pnblic auditor.— Mr Dolby overruled the Law-Clerk's objection.—Mr Leak then took various objections to the accounts being paid out a the public rates, and argued that the persons who were ream:ll4lde for the proceedings which led to the action of Mr Beasley against the Commissioners ought to be sur- charged with the amount which the ratepayers heti been compelled to pay. Although the Board were• joined with the individual defendants, as such, stil t bis was a case in which it was impossible 'hat the Board could have acted withott bona- tides, and if none of the other defendants had not, mala fide skipplied the negligence and wilful misconduct ekich was charged ia the pleadings, and on aceennt 01 which judgment was signed. After his depatches coolly announcing his intention of taking Berber, destroying the town, and then sending Col. Stewart to Dongola and thence to the Equator to rescue the southern garrisons, nothing particular has been heard of General Gordon. Colonel Stewart, if be • has been de- ep itched, has certainly not arrived at Berber ; and General Gordon seems to be quietly occupying h'inself at Khar- toum. Meanwhile Lord Wolseley is prersing 02 to the front, and British soldiers have already reached Dongola, which a couple of months ago was a town in the remote dis- tance whence comes despatches from the Mudir, the bona of which were much questioned. All the reports to hand indicate a general collapse of the Mandi's power, and it seems improbable that the relief column will have any fighting. There is an occasional drowning at the Cateracts, a boat catching fire, and at least one Guardsman killed by a crocodile. But no enemy has shown himself. The scare about the state of the Navy got up by an enter- prising journal, which has Already had its successes in the same line, has practically died away. Probably when Par- liament meets there will be some endeavour Made to obtain the appointment of a Committee or a Royal Commission to make inquiry. There would be no harm in that, and if it be pressed it will. doubtless be conceded. But" the truth about the Navy" is that at the present time it is as strong as ever it was and that the Navy of no other Power ap- proacbes it in was, qualities. This has been confessed, grudginglyebut honestly by all the Powers that were cun- ningly dressed up to make a buggaboo to frighten John Bull. Bath the French and German papers have seriously discussed the matter and from different points of view, and bet varied roads, have -reach d the one conclusion that the British Navy stend, as it al ways did, at the head of the Navies of the world. The truth about Englishmen is that they are always in a great hurry to depreciate their own prowess and resources, and are always ready to ha scared. A new industry has lately come into vogue, and is already so successfal that the inventor must expect competition. It consists of collecting all the references made in the public press to particular persons and forwarding them to the ia- dividcal most immediately concerned. I have before me a circular from the ingenious and industrious foreigner, who has undertaken this work in which he offers to send me at the rate of a guinea per hundred extracts containing any allusions made to myeelf or my work. He assures me, of whet I know to be the fact, that he is largely patronis.ed by members of Parliament, literary men, and all who in any form have acquired a public character and are likely to form matter for discussian or cemment in the commas of news- papers. Whether such organised attention adds to the daily happiness of a man is doubtful. Much more ill than good is on the average written about one, and according to the old proverb "what the eye does not see the heart does not grieve after." Lord Randolph Charchill mentioned to me once that he bad received a solieitation from the enterpris- ing picker-up et these trifles and agreed to snbecribe on con- dition that he sent him only. the evil things said about him. " At the end of a month," Lord Randolph said "I found I owed him about 30 guineas. A huodred a day was the fair average of abuse. It woold have been much cheaper if I had subscribed on his terms with the ,condition that he should send me only the good things said about me." Some of the people who went Out to the meeting of thel British Association in Canada are beginning to return, can 1 after having found time to pass through Boston and New 1 York. A lady who thus got her first peep at the Cnited I States Is chiefly trock by the proftvion of flowees. Upon the Blightelt provocation the Americans send flows, not in more or less simple bouquets as we h eve them, in England, but in enormous and often ugly bundles. Me own imprese eion is that, though the Americas spend large some on flowers, they do not really care for them. There is in their arrangement absence of that taete which can only coine of true lavingkindness. One of the few really beautiful florid i dicera.tioni I saw in the States was at a private dinner, at 1 the Union Chile in New York, where the table was lawishly covered with yellow roses.--only yellow roses—running at ' the time to sixpence apiece, as I found when a couple of days later I went to buy some. One occasion when Ameri- cans feel bound to come out with floral tributes is on the funeral of a friend. Those who attend the funeral and those notable to go 'end flowers, the tribute becoming in the end a sterile formality imposing considerable tax upon the parse, for people do not always die when flowers are abundant and cheap. It ha now coma to pass that in announcing funerals in the newspapers, or in sending out cards, there is nearly always a notice to the eff-ct " Plearie omit flowers" Another formula I have seen Is "Friends will kindly' omit , flowers." I hear the announcement of the new dynamite scare at Dover has already deflected a lot of traffic, from a once favourite route. People don't care to travel with a detec- tive watching ever theirlifety, or to run the risk of explo- sions, Italie detective ehould make a mistake. The British ratepayer little knows how much this scare is costing him Custom Howse officals have Le be well paid, ald, though this special branch of their duly lasts but half an hour twice a day, still it has to be kept up regularly. Folkes- tone ha more than double its ecouetorned number of re- venue inspectors, and Dover at present has more than treble. I see that in the care of the cross Channel passengers it has been proposed that a few revenue officers should travel over with the steamer and examine all the hand luggage before the voyage was eempleted One mutt has at least teen obtained by the scare. Every description of private smuggling is stopped. Contraband cigars are as rare as pro- hi the &id sports of the past season the ap- pearance of women as cricketers has to be specially noticed. I see that all over the country there have been mixed cricket matches, the methods of the pleY and the, instrumente of P being adapted to the powers of the' feebler sex. The men 1 , have hatted with broomsticks aCel the women with rackets, and the bowling ha been performed with a tennis ball.

fThis variation of the game bids fair to become popular. ft is extremely cotnical to look at, and gide have a great deal to learn in the way of fielding. There is no doubt but that tennis has taught them the use of their atms. Bat they have vet to orac.ice bow to make runs and how to take balls. Nearly every tennis tournament now euda with one of these hybrid games, which next season will probably. be quite established.

MANIIIAGE AND ITS SEQUItIi. —A singular case was heard at the Si Helens County Court, no Wednee,- day, before Mr TPE Thompson, judge. At a previous court William Brownhill, of Sutton, claimed from Stephen Ramsdale, his nephew by marriage. the sum of £5, de ney alleged to have been lent, but His Honour gave a vet dint for the defendant. A new trial was afterwards applied fcr, and beine granted it came on for hearing on Wednesday, when Mr J 0 Swift appeared for the plaintiff. He stated that the plaintiff was an old genteman who had retired from business, and lived at Sutton. He wile a friend of the defendant, and had lent him certain sums of money; which had been 'honestly repaid. In Fehtuary last defendant mar- ried his (plaintiff's) niece, and plaintiff lent him £5 in the, presence of several persons. Defendant promised. to pay it back at the rate of 10s per week, but he had only paid two sums of 58.• Ile had, however, offered to mettle the Matter by payieg £2 Sc; but he (plaint iffr declined to do ti),—The defendant denied having borrowed the money, and main- tained that it was lent to his wife (with whom he was not now living) for her separate uses. He considered that under, the Married • Women's Property • Act had nothing to do with him.—lra Ramseale (the defendanthi wife) was called and she said the defendant had received the money from the plaintiff and be (the de- fendaut) handed it to her. She gave defendant £1 hack again and with the other purchased a wedding ring, a wed- ding dress, and paid for the refreshments c 'mimed at toe wedding.-The defendant addressed the court at some lengeL. He said he and the plaintiff's niece were brought rather suddenly together, and he promised her marriage, anl ful- filled his promise like a gentleman. (Latighter.) His wife's circumstances, however, did not come to his knowledge until_ it was too late for him to honourably re'ract.( elan befoteee the wedding she foand she was short of clothes, and beit;e in "black "she said that she could not be married in thate • but suggested that her uncle would lend her the money and - she would pay him back out of her eoe's income and be (the defendant) gave her. Her son gave he: 20s a week and 'defendant gave her 225, 'and he., fully expected the money would be paid by his Who. Ire admitted that he had had a sovereign "if the borrewed money for the purpose of "standing treat" and to buy. a pair of trousers, but he had been a " to ilia wife.— • The Judge expressed the opinion that he wolikelesate much batter satisfied if Mr Brownbill bad' 'given the £5 to t his niece as a wedding present, hut as he insisted mains- rights he would 'order the defendant to repay the amount at £1 per month.

WARRINGTON BC/BOUGIE POLICE COURT. •SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. Darwamvsiass.—John Callen was fined 55 and costa for baying been drunk in Bridge-street on the previous even.

Mownar.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, Aldermen Davies, Holines, and Councillor Monks. Dransannsvan.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness. viz :—Timothy Mahar, fined 5s and costs or seven days; Kate Barker, dismissed on promising to leave the town; Patrick Mannion, fined 5s and costs or s4ven days; Martin Finley, fined lOs and costs; Jaines Welsh, fined 5s and costs; Peter Farrel, ditto ; Martha Atherton dismissed. SLEEPING Otrr.—Bernard Cony and James Coonv, last from Manchester, were charged with sleeping in a water closet in the goods yard of the Cheshire Lines Railway the same morning. They said that they had.come from Man- chester in search ot work.—Dismissed with a caution. A CA.RELE9s CARTEE.—John Flannigan, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in St James's-street, on the 15th ult., was fined 5s and costa. STRAY HORs3.--Thomis Snuffieton, for allowing a horse to stray in Hormemarket-street was fined 23 61, including costs. . .

A Miscurforons BOY.—A boy named Thomas Paton was summoced for letting off fizeworks in Eustace-street —He was discnarged with a caution. TtrusnAv.—Before Captain Litton. DRUNKENNESS —Patrick Mellor, for being drunk and die- tirderly in Dolman's-lane on the previous day, was fined 10s Rad costs. WEDNESDAY—Before Mr John Fairclough and Alderman Cbandley. A DEEM:RTES.—Francis Clarkson, who admitted being a deserter trom the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Orford Ba•racks, was ordered to be banded over to the military authorities to be dealt with. , FITCH AND Toss.—Edward Griffn was fined 2s 6d, includ- ing costs, for playinr. at pitch and toss. THURSDAY—Before Captain Litton and Alderman Webster. DRUNKENNESS.—Patrick Corfield and Emma Howard were fined 5s and costs each, or 7 daye, for being drunk and disorderly the previous evening in the Crown and Sceptre Yard.--WilliarnAbram, charged with being drunk in Upper Bank-street, was dismissed on payment of lock-up fees. Bazaar ore Tim PEACE Cowdell was ordered tet be bound over to keep the peace, or a month in default, for committing a breach of the peace in Mersey-street on the 22nd September. Funasm—Before Aldermen Bargees and Holmes, and Mr Marson. laamotrlovEss.—Sarah Carrington was fined 5s and 7s casts for being drank and disorderly in Dolman's-lane. SATIIRDAY.—Before Messrs R Houghton, T J Gillespie, C Pilkington, and A C IlleCorquodale. •Dsurncannasa—George Griffiths was stuumnned for be- ing drunk and disorderly at E irleatown on the 21st nit and was fined 53 and costs --Michael McDermott, Patrick Shaughnessy, and Jamee.- McDermott, young men, were summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 21st nit and thew were each fined 59 and costs.—Wm Bailey was summoned for being drunk at Newton on the 21at ult. As he did not appear a warrant for his apprehen- sion was granted.

Tamvoitaur Amrirotars.—Joseph Saunders was granted permission to sell at the Queen's Arms, Waterloo-road, under the license lately held by Thomas Vl'illimason. QUAIIRMSOIII4 WOMEEL—dlice Rowbottom. a respect- ably-dressed young woman, living in Norfolk-street, was summoned for having on the 24,h September used threats to Martha Orme, of Windmill-street, who was afraid that she would receive bodily -Minty. There was a cross summons issued. After hearing the witnesses the Bench bound both the parties over to keep the peace for six months in one surety of 01.

DARtSBURY PETTY SESSIONS. ThESDAY.—Before Messrs E Greenall, J Marson, W C Jones, and P Rylands, M.P. Jno.Oras' lAST9.—The assistant overseers of the various townships in the division presented the lists of persons qualified to serve on juries, which were sanctioned by the Bench after somealight 'emendations had been made in some •of them. DEUETICENNESS.--JaMeS; Povey was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Halton on the 30th August, but was discharged; and James Brindley was fined 5s and emits for having been drank and disorderly at Stretton on the 27th Angnst. A Tremors GAster EEPER.— Alfred Brody, landlord of the Halton Arms, Walton, was summoned by John Bayley, an underkeeper in the employ of Sir Gilbe-t Greene'', for having made use of malicious threats towards him.—Mr Browne appeared on behalf of the complainant, and Mr Jenkins represented the defendant.—The complainant, a strapping young fellow, stated that on the 18th ult be had been at the harvest festival at St John's Church and re- turned with two companions. On reaching the Walton Arms his two companions went in there, but he himself stayed outside because he was not on good terms with the landlord. After he had stood outside a short time Brody came out with a lantern in his hand, and corning up to him held it up to his face. Brody, according to the complainant's version, then threatened to "double him up," "knock him into splinters," and to do various other unpleasant things. In consequence of these threats he was afraid of defendant, and wished him to be bound over. This statement was in the main corroborated by complainant's mother and sister, but Brody' s version of the affair was materially different. According to him, he had been told on the night in question that a strange man had been hanging about, and, having been warned by the police to keep a look out, he went out- side to see if the man was about. Seeing someone leaning over the gate in the dark he went up and turned the light upon him, and found it was the complainant. Complain- ant then threatened to burst his mouth if he did not go into the house, and a few hot words were exchanged between them. Defendent threatened to report complainant to Sir Gilbert Greenall, upon which Bayley retorted that he "cared for neither him nor Sir Gilbert."—The Bench cln- sidered that it was a case which ought not to have been brought before them, and it would be dismissed, each party to pay their own costs. ALLEGED ASSAULT ST A GlRL.—Annie Fitzgerald, 13 years of age, was charged with having assaulted Francs Ellen Grieve, a girl eight years of age, at Stockton Heath on the 18th uit, but the evidence being defective the defen- dant was dismissed with a caution.

VAGRANTS.—For begging in Vine•stree—t, Wi"dneS, on the previous day, John Jones, an old offender, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.—Andrew I%latran, a tramp, pleaded guilty to sleeping in the works of meagre Goldin' g Davies. and Company, that morning, and he was sentenced to elven days' bard labour. —A similar sentence was impased upon James Gibson for steeping in a hut is Ditton-road. DRUNK AND RIOTOUS—John Forden and Bernard Doyle were each fined 5a and costs for being drunk and disorderly. —Dennis O'Brien, who did not appear, was convicted of be- ing drunk and disorderly in the Adelphi Hotel, Warrington- road, on the 20th September, and refusing to quit when requested to do so. He was fined lOs and costs.—Peter Riley, an old man, was charged with assaulting P.C. Cam- mings. It was proved that about a quarter to nine on Mon- day, the 22nd ult„ Constables Cummings and Cheers were walking along Pitt-street, each with a woman in custody, when the defendant rushed up to Cummings and attempti-d to rescue the woman. Finding he was unable to do so he struck the ~fficer a blow on the face with his fist. A fine of 10s and costs or 14 days' hard labour was imposed. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORE.—Mr Cr H Panbv, clerk

to the School Board, sommoned the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to sago' :—Mary Murphy, Mary Cullen, Jarnoa Hughes, James Cummins, Patrick Fitzsimmons, John Power, John Smith, Dennis

Malone, John Haßetio, John Martin, Joseph Shotie,Stephen I White, John Brannon, and John Kelly. The cases were I proved by Messrs Davies, Joynson, and Rowe, and the usuall penalty of 55 was imposed on each defendant. A VIOLENT FEMALE —Sarah Ann Jones, of West Bank, was charged with wilfully damaging the property of Ann Heys, who lives in the same neighbourhood. It was alleged that on Saturday evening the defendant entered the com• plainant's house and commenced a disturbance with the latter's son-in-law. She threw a lighted paraffin lamp at him, smashed all the pets on the table, and broke a chair. The son-in-law's hand was burnt. The defendant was drunk, and on Monday morning she was fined for that offence —She was now ordered to pay £l, including 9e damage, or go to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.—Defendant went to gaol. AN Onaraccrrox.—Michaet James Curley. was, on the evidence of Superintendent Barka., fined 2e ad, and costs 45 6,1, for obstructing the highway at Appleton by allow- ing his horse and trap to stand thereon: CRUELTY TO A Cow—Charles Jackson and Martin Col- lins, boye, were charged with cruelly illtreating a crow.— P C 1,175 said about a quarter to 12 o'clock on Sunday morning the 21st nit he saw the defendants ,runniog a cow about in a field at Halton View, Warrington-road, Jack- son took hold of the cow's tail and the animal dragged him from 15 to 20 yards, when it got away, leaving a quantity of hair in the defendant's band. Collins acted in a similar manner. The defendants' were each ordered to pay 8s 61 costs.

A HARDENED YOUNG THlEF.—Jimes McCormick, 16 years of age, was charged with stealing a rat trap worth 6d, from the works of Messrs Elutohinson, Waterloo-road. George Hackney. of 58, Cholmondeley-street, a farmer, iden- tified the trap, and P C Thompson proved finding it in the house where the prisoner lived. The prisoner stated he found the trap among a lot of dirt. As there was a very black list against the prisoner, this being his fifth offence this year, be was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

ASSAULTING A WlFE.—Heary Shepherd, a respectable. looking man, was brought up under a warrant charged with assaulting his wife Mary Ellen. He pleaded gullty.—The complainant said on the 29th of September she went for her husband to the place where he ought to be working, but net finding him there she called at a publichouse on her way home. She saw him coming out of the yard and she said "Well Henry it is a shame to atop here from seven o'clock this morning to a quarter past eleven." "lie made no more ado" but struck her across the eye. The previous week he bad only brought es home to keep seven of a family, and he had kept them short of food for some time—The Bench fined the defendant .21, and Costs 93 6J, or a month's hard labour.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR, GEORGE-1-1- ERBERT
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR, GEORGE-1-1- ERBERT
PILKINGTON, ST. HELENS.

On Wednesday forenoon Mr George Herbert Pilkiegton, second eorr of Mr William Pilkington, J.P., et Roby Hall, and of the firm of Messrs Pilkington Brothers, the exten- sive sheet glass manufacturers and colliery proprietors, St Helens, was married to Miss Nora Jessie Langton, daugh- ter of Mr Charles Langton, of Barkhill, Aightirth, Liver- pool. The interesting event was celebrated in the Moseley Hill Church, Liverpool. The sacred edifice bad been,very profusely decorated with greenhouse flowers, Arc, in honour of the occasion, this work having been neatly carried out by lady friends Of the bride. There was a very large and fashionable attendance and as the wedding party entered the building the organist played the "Wedding March" (Lohengrin) while appropriate hymns were sung daring the service. The bride, who was most tastefully attired, wag led to the communion rails by her father, Mr C Langton; the bridesmaids b ing Miss Bessie Langton, Miss Maggie ' Langton, Miss Pilkingtou, Miss Maud Neilson, Miss Maple Tod, Miss Joicey, and Miss Thorburn. Mr W Lee Pilkington officiated as best man. The bride's train was borne by two "pages," four years of age, the twin ens of the Rev Canon French, and nephews of the bride. The marriage service was conducted by the Rev W Berry, vicar of St Peter's Church, Ipswich, who was assisted by the Rev Thomas Chambers, vicar of Halewood. At the con- clusion of the service Mendelsohn's "Wedding March" was effectively rendered by the organist. The invited guests were conveyed from the ckurch to the residence of Mr Langton in eighteen carriages; and a sumptuous wed- ding breakfast was served in a large marquee, which bad been specially erected on the lawn. About 60 ladies and gentlemen sat down. The wedding cake was an extremely handsome one of three tiers, and had been supplied by Messrs Bollard, of Chester. During the breakfast it was crowned with the bride's bouquet of flowers, a splendid one, the gift of the bridegroom. The happy couple afterwards left for London, en toute to the Continent, where the honey- moon will be spent. Tho presents were of a cosarcharacter, and numbared about 1.00.

On Saturday evening a very pleasant gathering was held_ in Messrs Pilkington's schoolroom, St Helens, for the pur- pose of presenting to Mr G H Pilkington, in celebration of his forthcoming marriage, a splendid silver tea and coffee service, with a tray which had been subscribed for by the managers, clerks, and officials of the sheet glass norks. The articles had been supplied by Messrs Elkington and Com- pany, alai were of a chaste design ; on each being engraved the crest of the Pilkington family, and on the tray being' the following inscription : "Presented to G Herbert Pil- kington, EEq, on the occasion of his marriage, by the mana- gers,- clerks, and officials of Messrs Pilkington Brothers sheet glass works and collieries, as a token of their respect and esteem, arid with their sincere wishes for his future happiness. St Helens, let October, 1884."—Mr Mather made the presentation no behalf of the contributors; and Mr Pilkington acknowledged the gift in appropriate terms. On the Friday evening the foremen at Messrs Pilkington's Plate Glass Works, Cowley-hill, Marked their sense of the occasion by presenting to Mr Pilkington a silver inkstand. Mr Pilkington's kind and genial manner have made bim a favourite with all those to whom he was brought in contact. It should be added that on Wednesday the workpeople dis- played flags and bunting from various parts of the works.
THRILLING STORY. OF A MIDNIGHT
MURDER.

The Cornishman of Wednesday publishes a narrative of a murder alleged to have been committed in the locality, the narrator professing to have remained silent, under a fearful oath imposed on him at the time of the committal of the deed, some fifty years since. The writer, who igo s himself " G. 11. 0.," and from Penzance, declares himself willing to indicate the spot where the body of the murdered man was buried. Shortly, the story is as follows :—Thel writer, then a junior in a firm in London, of which he is I now the head, came to Penzance in September. 1834, to arrange terms among local tin smelters. He left Penzance one evening to visit a friend in St Just, which is some six miles from Penzance. On the way there, in a lonely part of the road, he met two men, when he heard one say, "That's him," while the other asserted "No, it is not." I They again faced each other, when the two men said they had taken him for another person. Almost immediately a man approached from the direction of St Just, and the writer called his attention to the suspicious character of the two men. The man, who said he was a mine agent, laughed, at his fears and went on his way. He had only proceeded about a couple of hundred yards when he was seized with ; nervous tremors. His legs refused to support him, and j he fell in the middle of the road, but thought it ! better not to stay there, and so proceeded on hand ; and knees across the dusty road, scrambled up a small bank, and found himself on a common which appeared t obe many acres in extent. He dragged himself to al heather-covered strip, between two clumps of furze, and threw himself at length and closed his eyes. After a little time be looked up and the moonlight revealed to him a newly-made mound. Hearing two shot fired he crouched and waited, and he saw the men just after coming with the body. To quote his letter, "Once more a thrill of horror ran through me." On they came towards the newly-made grave, almost touching my feet as they moved past. Then they turned to the right, and threw the body into the pit with a thud, which made every W)re in my body vibrate. The corpse in the grave the two men began to fill it up. Doing that disclosed me. They had not lowered the monad many inches when one of them discovered me. They pounced upon me and demanded what I was doing there. I explained, but all to no purpose. "The same pit will do for him." Yes, shoot him." "No, cut his throat." " I'll load my pistol again; don't leave any marks of blood about." "Push him in the pit first, and cat his throat after- -1 wards" These were the horrible threats, accompanied by frightful imprecations, whick greeted me. Said one of the ' men to meagain, "We have decided to bury you alive; slip oil your clothes, it's hardly worth while burying that good suit of yaurs. It will do for one of us." I pleaded my youth, my accidental and unpremeditated presence, my newly-made wife, and only child, and this at last seemed to I touch the hearts of the brute. "Well," said one, "we will spare your life on condition that you swear, as you hope for heaven and the salvation of your wife, child, and friends; you shall swear it, too, on the point of this knife and the muzzle of this pistol, that what yoa have seen this night you will never speak of or divulge to any human being fora space of fifty years from this day. when we shall all be as this," at the same time kicking into the grave a clod of light-coloured clayey soil. I did swear most solemnly. I bought my life on that lonely heath of West Penwith. I have kept my promise. It's a little over fifty years ago. I was then twenty•six years of age, so you ve I am an old man now. Those men were middle-aged, from forty-five to fifty, at that time. Of his re•visit to the spot he writes: "Asa ap- pro iched the fatal spot the road seemed entirely unaltered. I solemnly believe that I crept through the very gap in the low edge of earth which still imperfectly protects the croft; that I stood between the self-same clusters of furze which formed my bed—very nearly my bal of death—and peep- hole, as the murderers hid the result of their accursed crime, andth it I knelt on the undisturbed grave where their vic- tim's bones are now mere dust. After half a century I knelt again, not to implore mercy of man, as I did then, but of God. lest unwittingly I have sinned in keeping an extorted pledge, and to save myself from harm have reluctantly shielded heinous criminals.

Me AM Sullivan is seriously ill in Dublin, and Mrs Sul- livan, who is herself in delicate health, bas been sumo:lone.l to his bedside. TWO CHILDREN KILLED ON THE RAILWAY. Three children were playing at Middlesborough on Wednesday night, when A train OD the Guiaborough line knocked them down. Joseph SprOate, aged eight years, and Thomas Coulthard, children of railway employes, living in Frances. street, were killed: and John Charlton, aged seven, so se- verely injured that recovery is doubtful.

Foomu.n.—The Newton St. Pete-r.'e and Earleetown Albion Clubs met on the ground of the former on Saturday, the home team winning by six goals to one. THE Jun LINTS.—Ac the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, the overseers of the various townships in the Newton Petty Sessional division submitted the lists of per- sons qualified to serve on juries during the ensuing year, which w,re signed by the magistrates without objection or comment.

A SLEEPY Dervzn.—Ralph Unsworth, of Orford, was charged at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Messrs H Houghton, T J Gillespie, C Pilkington, and A C McCorgoodale, with being asleep in his cart at Bar- tonwood on the 20th September.—P.C. Grundy proved the case, and the defeneant was fined 2s GI and coats. PROPOSED UNITED KINGDOM ALLTANOR MIEEPING.— The frimids of the temperance movement will be glad to hear that a large meeting in support of the principles of the United Kingdom Alliance will be held in Earlestown in the course of a few weeks, when the anniversary of the Alliance will be celebrated. The committee of the Earlestown and Newton United Band of Hope and Temperance societies have the arrangements for the gathering in hand. Faiermfmowrt Fooraaa, Curn.—Tiac Committee and officials of the Earlestown Football Club, with several of the players, sat down to a capital supper at the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrave Moss, on Thesday evening. They had been kindly invited to the repast by Mr W W Owen, butcher; and Mr and Mr Morris (host a d hostess) and the party, numbering about 20, thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Mr P Beetle occupied the chair, and songs were given by several persons. During the evening a hearty vote of thanks' was accorded te Mr Owen and Mr and Mrs Morris for their kindness.

NEWTON Crronat SOCIETY. —Dr J W Watkins, Vice-president, occupied the chair at the 6-ls annual meet- ing of the members of the Newton Choral Society, which was recently held. From the treanurer's statement it ap- peared that there was a substantial balance in hand for the coming season, and altogether the Society was in a most flourianing condition. All the old officials were re-appointed. In addition to the usual glees, the cantata selected for this season's practice is 'St. Cecilia's Day," by Van Bree, and it Is to be hoped it will give as great satisfaction as the last I cantata, "On shore and sea." _ _ _

Tun GOOD Tnanmans.—" A night with our Juve- niles" headed the programme at the meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters, at the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. In accord- ance therewith a number of the members of the Juvenile Temple visited the lodge, and under the presidency of the W.S , Brother E Newman, gave a pleasing selection of songs, Ac. gUBERLL OF ME.r &HURL ABROWSHITH. The remains of Mr S Arrowsmith, of Legh-street, Earlestown, whose death we reported last week, were interred in War- grave Church-yard on Saturday afternoon. As a mark of respect a goodly number of members of the Sons of Temper- ance Friendly Society and the Order of Foresters walked in front of the hearse and mourning coaches; while several members of the choir and congregation of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, and a few teachers of the Sunday school, were also present. The funeral service was impressively conducted by the Rev Canon Whitley. IMPORTANT LICENSING QUESTION.—At Leigh, On Mon- day, two important questions in licensing were raised. In two cases publicans had refused to supply victuals because they were too busy, and this having been brought under the notice of the Bench, the holders of the licenses were war- ned that it was their duty to ,supply food. as' well as drink, and that if they refused it would be at their peril. In anotheg case a man named Wood, who held a license, had been twice convicted, and an application was made for a transfer from Wood to a new tenant named Churton. The Bench, however, decided not to renew the license to Wood, , and held that, as Wood's license would thus be terminated, there was nothing to transfer to Churton except the unex- pined portion of Wood's license up to October 10th. On Churton's behalf this was refused, and the case is to be car- ried to the Queen's Bench. THE ELELEBTOWN CONBEEVATIVE CLUB DISCUBS/ONS. —A large number of the members of the Eariestown Con- servative Club attended the first meeting in connection with the newly formed discussion class, held in the late billiard- room of the club on Thursday evening. Mr W Mandsley read a paper on "One plain reason for the House of Lords throwing out the Franchise Bill." The chair was occupied by Mr li Roberts. In a carefully prepared and excellent paper the essayist urged that the present Government had so disgraced the country in the eyes of the Irish and other nations, so discouraged loyalty and encouraged disloyalty, AO increased taxation, so involved the country in war, so sacrificed Lome to foreign industries, so harassed every in- terest with which it had interfered, that it was the duty of the House of Lords to take any legitimate means to hasten an appeal to the conntry. A discussion of an interesting character ensued. _ _ _
