ADJOURNED BREWSTER SESSIONS.

The adjourned Brewster Sessions for the Borough of Warrington were held at the Police Court on Monday morning, when the magistrates on the Bench were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alderman Holmes, Alderman Davies and Councillor Monks. The temperance party and the publicans were both represente& and considerable in- terest was taken in tbe proceedings.—The Clerk said that five licenses bad been adjourned for consideration, but in two cases the only intention was that it should serve as a caution to the holders—Kate Jenks and James Kennion.— The Mayor said that the case against Kate Jenks was for harbouring a police constable. He remembered the case very well ; she had no knowledge of the offence being com- mitted,—The Clerk stated that James Kennion, of the Black Horse Inn, had been fined ss, including costs.—The Chief Constable, made no objection to the renewal of these Been- sea, which were granted.--Jarnee Worrell, Bewsey Inn, Pitt-street, was objected to by the Chief Constable on the grounds that the license was not required, that the premises were not of sufficient annual value to entitle the licensing, and that the premises were not sultable.—Mr Woods, soli- citor. Warrington, appeared for the applicant. Mr Choriton. solicitor, Warrington, appeared on behalf of Mr Hichard Roberta to oppose the renewal.—After a short discussion between the advocates as to the precise objections made and to be met, Mr Charlton called the Chief Constable, who said that he had known the house in question for nearly 20 years. Many complaints had been made with regard to drunkenness and disturbances at and outside the house.—Mr R Roberts deposed that he had seen people come out of the house and immediately afterwards commence fighting in the street.—The Rev T Rippon, Wesleyan minister, late of Wavrington, and new of Preston, said that he lived opposite the house in question for three years, and had seen men go in sober and come out drunk. —ln support of his objection Mr Chorlton said that Mr Woods might contend that the house was licensed before 1889, but he should submit that the evidence that he had given camel within the grounds of objection. Having given such evi- dence he 'should submit that the discretion of the magis- trates was absolute, and that no argument Mr Woods might use with respect to what he might call their obligation to re- new the license on the ground that it existed before the Act of 1869, ought to have any effect against the evidence that had been given. He contended that the applicant had tailed to prove in the face of the evidence that he could pro. duce a satisfactory character, and that the house was not disorderly.—Mr Woods submitted that as he had not re- ceived notice of Mr Chorlton's objection he was not called upon to reply. With regard to the property he called Mr Pierpoint. architect, who said that the house contained twelve rooms and two cellars, of which he gave the dimen- sions, and Mr Owen, architect, who gave the rental value of the house at £22 103 per annum—The maeistrates retired, atid on their return the Mayor said that they had come to the conclusion that they had no alternative bet to renew the license. He thought it was only fair to state with reference to the applicant that it was not borne out that he was a man of bad character. They could not possibly put the construc- tion upon the matter, because a man of bad char- acter meant more than anything that had been alleged against Mr Worrell. There had been nothing specific urged and nothing specific proved, and they felt that hav- ing regard to the fact that the license existed before 1869 they had no alternative, whatever their private opinions might be, but to renew it. It might be a question for the owner or the occupier to consider whether it would not be advisable to increase the capacity of the house. If they were to refuse the license there was a power of appeal, arid they would look foolish indeed if they had refused it upon insufficient grounds.—Geo. Bradburn, shopkeeper, Folly. lane, holder of a license to sell beer off the premises, was objected to on the ground that the license was not required, and that the applicant had been convicted.—Mr Chorlton objected on behalf of a Mr Siddle, who, however, did not put in an appearance to give evidence.—Mr P Davies, solicitor, represented Bradburn.—lt transpired that the applicant had not been convicted, but that a case brought against him bad been dismissed on payment of the costs, and the renewal was granted.—The other adjourned case errs that of John Monks, who was objected to on the ground that the former tenant had been convicted of selling beer clueing prohibited hours.—Mr Browne appeared for the ap-- plicant, and Mr Chorlton supported the objection —The Mayor, in giving the decision of the magistrates, said that they had concluded not to renew the license, although at the same time they meant no reflection on the applicant,, whom they considered a proper person to hold a license.l They were, however, of opinion that the wants of the neigh- bourhood were not sufficient to guarantee the renewal of the license, and they desired, where possible, to reduce the num- ber of off-licenses.—This was all the business.

LIBERALISM AT EARLEBTOWN.—on Wednesday even- ing Mr Walter McEvoy, of Etrlestown, read a paper on "The political life of Mr Gladstone," at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, Fairclough-street. There was a fair attendance, and Mr Thomas Howard occupied the chair. The essayist briefly reviewel the career of Mr Gladstone, ob- serving that he had nobly worked his way to the front.— Messrs Birkhead, Ratcliffe, Gilmour, Holyocke, Joseph Davies, Tate, and Sturgess took part in the discussion which ensued; and during the evening the Chairman remarked that the abilities of the Tory great men such as Lord Salis- bury and Sir Stafford Northcote were small when compared with those of Mr Gladstone. As an orator and financier he thought Mr Gladstone was unequalled, and he believed the Tories would themselves admit when Mr Gladstone was dead that he had been the greatest statesman who ever lived. —The Essayist (Mr McEvoy) promised to resume the sub- ject on the 15th instant ; and a cordial invitation was given to all Liberals to attend.—Next Wednesday a public lecture on political questions is being given in the Co-operative Hall by Mr A Crilly, secretary of the Financial Reform Association.

THE WELSH PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL. In aid of the funds of the Welsh Presbyterian Chapel Tarnworth-street, a miscellaneous concert was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. The concert was a great success, the room being crowded with a truly appreciative audience, who manifested a keen interest in toe proceedings, and heartily applauded the efforts of the vocalists. Mr H J Durn3an, late organist of St John's Church, presided at the pianoforte with his accustomed skill and also officiated as conductor with tact and ability. One of the greatest successes of the evening was the appearance of Miss Katie Williams, of Sr Helens; a bright and charm- ing girl of about eleven summers. Miss Williams, who se- cured one of the chief prizes for pianoforte playing at the recent Welsh Eisteddfod celebrations at Liverpool, favoured the audience with a song "Birdie Mine" (Watson), a Welsh selection "Y gardotes fach "(Lewis), and a piano- forte solo consisting of Skeaf's fantasia" Jenny Jones." The young artiste possesses a sweet silvery voice, of wide com- pass; and though lacking cultivation she gives every pro- mise of making her mark in musical circles. Each of her selections was enthusiastic.all3. encored. Mr W M Hum- phreys, of Garston, was warmly welcomed, and his fine voice was heard to advantage in "Thou art so near" (Rich- ardt), and an expressive Welsh song, "Niagara" (Dr Parry). He, too, was deservedly enored. Among the local vocalists, Mr P Hastie, Mr Wright, and Miss Bothwell, secured the greatest share of applause. MR. SPURGEON'S SERMONS. Mr Spurgeon's life has been a busy one. He has published 1,800 of his Tabernacle sermons, and has issued about 500 in other forms and shapes. To the preparation of each sermon be has devoted a day, and to its revision after preaching another day. At this rate his Tabernacle sermons have taken about five years to re- vise for publication after they had been prepared and preached.

RANGEMEaTT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Messrs R Hoaghton, T .1 Gillespie, C Pilkington, and , A C McCorquodale, John Jolley, a labourer and winder, was ' summoned by his wife Margaret for assaulting her.—The defendant was represented by Mr J 0 Swift, of St Helens. The complainant stated that she had been married to the de- , fendant aoout five years and they bad had Emir children. , On day during the preceding week when be came home he brought some" lights" for the cat and toll one of their chil- dren to play with it. She (the complainant) said it was too ' dirty for the child and put it away whereupon the defendant picked np the "lights" and threw them at her, but they " wizzed ' past her head. He then ran her out the kitchen and began to assault her. He gave her black eyes, mode her ' nose bleed, cut her lip, and knocked out two front teeth.— In reply to Mr Swift the complainant admitted that on the night of the day upon which the Liberal demonstration was held at Etrlestown she had a row with her husband. Not- withstanding their recent rows she was willing to go back and live with her husband if he would make her a comfor- table beme.—The Magistrates remarked that they would like to hear the witnesses —Honore Wilson, nurse at the Haydock Cottage Hospital, stated that she saw the de- fendant assaulting his wife.—P C Hodgkinson deposed that the woman complained to him of his having assaulted her. Her month was bleeding, and her lips and one side of the face was swollen.—The Clerk (to the complainant) : Will you be satisfied if your husband is bound over to keep tee peace, and you try to live quietly together.—The Complain- ant: Yes if be will comfortably.—The hairman : You must both, try to live peaceably, together.=The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and the Bench afterwards cautioned him that he had violently as- saulted his wife and rendered himself liable to a severe pe- nalty. They hoped the parties would try aid live more hap- pilY.
LOCAL BOARD MEETING.

An ordinary meeting of this Board was held in the Board offices, Haydock, on Monday afternoon. There were 1:Ire• sent Messrs C Pilkington (in the chair), J Jackson, Bal- harry, Cook, Alker, and Turnbull (clerk). t HILYDOCK LOD3/11 WATl3ll.—With regard to the applica- tion of Dr Beaman fat a supply of Water to Haydock Lodge Asylum the Chairman reported that he and Mr Turnbull, as instructed by the Board, bad seen Dr Beaman and laid before him their proposition that he should pay a percent- age on the outlay. They told him that he had better look the matter well over before he entered into any arrangement with the Board. Dr Beaman .replied that he had already half arranged with the Ashton Local Board, and he (the chairman) thought as Dr Beaman was in another township it would be better for him to get the water from there.—Mr Jackson: He promised to write to the Board, I suppose?— The Clerk: He promised to let us know what he had de- cided to do.—Mr Jackson thought they conld do nothing further in the matter until Dr Beaman wrote again.—The Subject then dropped. THE GIBRALTER COTTAGES.—In answer to the Chairman, the Clerk replied, with regard to putting down water to the above cottages, that he had received a letter from the Liver- pool Corporation which put a stop to the proceedings at present. The letter stated that the agreement between the Board and the Corporation applied only to water required for the Local Board district. Under those circumstances the Liverpool Water Committee must be consulted before the pipes could be laid.—Mr Balharry thought this was a bad time for bringing these matters before the Liverpool people.—The Chairman considered that it ought to be men- tioned that it was only a very small number of cottages they wished to supply. He made a proposition that the clerk write to the Corporation and lay the matter before them.—This proposal was seconded by Mr Jackson and carried.

ESTIMATE.—The Clerk submitted the estimate for the general district rate required for the ensuing half-year, the total of which amounted to £545 is 3d, which was reduced by several deductions, to a nett amount of £177 16s 11d.— Mr Jackson proposed that the estimate be approved, and that a general district rate of Sd In the pound be levied, but that portion of this resolution referring to the rate was left over on the clerk stating that next meeting would be soon enough to sanction it.—The Chairman remarked that a seven- penny rate would cover all their requirements excepting .£l7. —The estimate was adopted. WASTE OF WATEII —The Clerk stated that, with regard to the summons against Peter Canliffe, Cunliffa had promised to pay for the water and for the cost of the summons if the latter was withdrawn. He had now paid the costs of the summons, but had not pild the water rate. He said he would wait till after that meeting to see whether the Board would really charge him the whole of it, as, he said, he had not used the water.—The Chairm in thought he ought to pay.—Mr Jackson moved that Mr Cunliffe be required to Alker seconded this proposal.—Mr Jackson rest:tacked that there was more water wasted by standpipe than by anything else, and he referred to one he had seen running at the school.—Mr Balharry: We should give the surveyor instructions to take notice of these eases.—Mr Jackson thought the best plan would be to put these pipes inside the schools. Being outside the children turned them on, and there was a shameful waste of water. He moved that the school taps be put inside.—Mr Balharry seconded this proposal—The proposals were carried. A CASUAL VACANCY.—Mr Jackson moved that Mr Joseph Evans (whose place had become vacant owing to absence
through illness) be re-elected a member of the Board.—Mr Baharry having seconded the motion, it was carried. This concluded the business.

HUY] ON. TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATIOIL—The usual meeting was held in the Huyton Park Schoolroom, on Tuesday evening, and was largely atttended. Mr E S Eccles occupied the chair, and gave a brief address; the Rev J W Walker also gave an address in favour of local option. The proceedings were varied by songs and readings by Messrs E Capper and W 0 Stoba. Miss Turner accompanied on the pianoforte. Several pledges were taken at the close. HARVEST FESTIVAL THANKSGIVING SERVICE.—At St. Michael's (Parish Church) the annual harvest thanksgiving service was held OR Monday evening. The church was elaborately decorated for the occasion by the ladies of the congregation. The west font was surrounded with delieate ferias and choice flowers, with a large bunch of grapes sus- pended from an ivy covered tripod over the basin, in which across of ferns and white geraniums floated. At its base were miniature sheaves and groups of fruit laid on a bed of moss and flowers. The ancient font was decorated with a garland of most brilliant cut flowers, lilliums, single and double dahlias, &c, and draped with festoons of oats. The screen on its lower panels was wreathed with flowers of every des- cription, ferns and fruit occupying its base the whole being surmounted by the text, a Thou crowned the year with Thy goodness," worked on a scarlet ground and fringed with oats and berries. The pulpit was bordered with apples and cle- matis, a cross of the same occupying the centre panel. The choir and stalls were richly adorned with the choicest plants and exotics and tasteful designs in cereals. Palms and plants of varied foliage were grouped on either side the communion table, on which were vases and a cross of deli- cate white flowers, whilst above the reredos a bank of ferns of every description was formed. The pillars were wreathed in different coloured dahlias with apples, berries, and chillis' alternate. The window sills were laid with scarlet cloth fringed with oats and ornamented with ferns. The ladies who took part in the work were : Communion table and reredos, Mrs Astley and Miss Jacques; choir and stalls, Mrs Mier and Fisbwick and Miss Newsy; screen, the Mitses Freldwick ; pulpit, the Misses Caw; west font, Misses Busby; ancient font, Miss B Penrhyn ; pillars, Misses Caw, Mrs and Miss Stone; window sills, Mrs Fishwick„ Ihler, Misses Fishwick,Leventon, and Blackley; west screen, Mrs W H Evans. The fruit, plants, and flowera were generously contributed by Messrs W H Crooks, T S Harding, C F Ben- nett, Mrs Ihier, Jowett, Turton, W Webster, Boyd, and Miss Busby; corn by Miss Rigby, Mrs Watkinson, Messrs Glover, Huntington, and Pinnington. The sermon was preached by the Rev W T Southward, M.A., of St Catherine College, Cambridge, from Psalm cxlv, 10th verse, "All Thy works shall praise Thee, 0 Lord; and Thy saints shall bless Thee." A cellection was made on behalf of the Additional Curates' Society, which realised £l2. The first lesson was read by the senior curate, the Rev J W Tyrer, M.A., and the second by the Rev H A SlacNaughten, Prescot. The prayers were beautifully intoned by the Rev H Cox, minor canon of Chester. The benediction was pronounced by the vicar, the Rev Canon Penrhyn, and the Rev H D' A Hubbard also assisted in the service. The musical portion of the service was, uttder the organist, Mr Hodgson, most excellently ten- dered. The edifice was Crowded.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

--• BRITISH WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—The [ members of this association on Monday met at "The Manse," where they had a tea kindly provided by Mrs. Evans, The Heyes, Haydock. About 50 persons were present, and after tea various matters connected with tem- perance work among women were discussed. Some of the members offered to become district visitors for the purpose of reclaiming women from intemperate habits. Seven more names were added to the regieter, and after spending a few pleasant hours at "The Manse." a public meeting was held in the Congregational schoolroom. The Rev H Wilson pre- sided, and there was a good attendance. Several short ad- dresses were given, and the temperance choir and others en- livened the meeting with Singing. KEEPING MALE SERVANTS WITHOUT A LICENCE.—Mr E F Crippin, Bryn, was summoned at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, for keeping a number of male servants without having a licence ter the same.—Mr Ellis appeared for the defendant, and Mr Hall prosecuted.— Patrick Flannagan, an officer of the Inland Revenue, stated that he visited the defendant's promises on the 27th of May, and saw several men employed by the defendant, who 'had only taken out a licence for the coachman, but not for the others —Mr Ellis admitted that Mr Crippin had net taken out the licence for the gamekeeper, but he was under the impression that one was not required. The Act of Par- liament stated that the term male servant did not include a I male servant who being bona fide employed in some other capacity was only partially as a servant. Mr Crippin had not taken out the licences, and Mr Ellis contended that none were required.—The defendant was fined 40s and costs. rHE ASHTON LOCAL BOARD AND THEIR RATES.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, an application was made by Mr Ellis on behalf of the Ashton Local Board for an order for the payment of certain sums, owing to them as general district rates by the Garswood Coal Company and the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Mr Dirlington appeared. for the Garawood Coal Company, and Mr Appleton for the Railway Company.—James Hill slid he was the cleric to the Ashton Local Board, and be pro- duced the rate book, which showed that the Garswood Coal Company were owing to the authority for general dis- trict rate the sum of £756 18a 43. It had been demanded and not paid.—Mr Darlingtors said he was not there to re- sist the order being made, but he wished to say that the Local Board asked for the money which would not accrue for the next six months—Mr Ellis said the Local Board exchequer was empty. They had many liabilities upon them, and no money to meet them with.—Mr Smethurst: We have no alternative but to make the ordee.—With regard to the Railway Company it was stated that they were owing £317 us 23 for general district rate, and an order for the immediate p iyment was made —Mr Gaskell, being a mem- ber of the Ashton Local Board, left the Bench during the hearing of the cases.

ASH TON LOCAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of mem- bers of this Board was held on Wednesday, when there were present Mr Moubert (in the chair), Rev 11 Siddall, Messrs Gaskell, Grimko, Lowe, C Latham, Boardman, Pimblett, Roberts, Britton, Barton, Crompton, Knowles, Laithwaite, W Latham, Painter, Wright, Goldsworth (surveyor), Hill (clerk), and Chambers (nuisance inspector).—Highway and Sanitary ,Committee: This committee gave instructions for further inquiries to be made as to the accident alleged to have been caused by the state of the road at Park lane. The medical offiEer reported that scarlatina still continued very prevalent, especially in the Stubshew Cross district. One case had been sent into hospital daring the week. He de- sired to call the attention of the inspector to the state of the ashpits at Rosehill, which required cleaning. It wasresolved that the attention of Mr Moubert be called to the state of the ' footpath from Long-lane to Garswood Hall collierlea—The minutes were confirmed.—Finance and General Purposes ' Committee: This committee met on Wednesday, September 24. On general district account the receipts during the month were £1,816 les 4d, and the expenses £1,802 23 Id. The receipts en gas account were £2,665 133 3d, and the balance due to bank was £379 53. Tlek sum of £BB9 16s 9d had been received on account of waterworks account, awl the balance due to bank was £2,588 13s sd. It was resolved that a joint meeting of this committee and the School At- tendance Committee be held for the purpose of considering what steps shall be taken to fill the vacancies caused by the death of Mr Livesley.—The minutes were passed.—Gas and Water Committee: A meeting of this committee took place on September 24th. The surveyor reported that fair pro- gress had been made since last meeting with the new engine house, dm., and the contractor had assured him that it would be completed by the end of next month. The minutes Were adopted.—The Death of Mr Livesley : The Clerk reported that a joint meeting of the Finance, General Purposes, and School Attendance Committees was held on Monday. It was resolved that the Board be recom- mended to advertise for a collector and school attend ince officer at a salary of £4O per annum for each office; the per- son appointed to devote the whole of his time to the service of the Board and to act generally under the directions of the clerk, and security to be given in the sum of £5OO. It was also resolved that the Board be recommended to call a special meeting for the purpose of making the appointment. —The minutes having been confirmed, Mr Gaskell moved a resolution of condolence with the late collector's family. He was sure they all sympathised very much with them in their sudden and very dreadful bereavement. So far as the Board was concerned he was sure they had lost a very good servant—a very good attendance officer, and in time he would have proved an excellent collector. So far as the township was concerned, as assistant overseer it was impos- sible for him to be improved upon.— Mr Crompton secon- ded the proposition. He was an excellent officer, and pro-- ved himself so in every department that he undertook.— The motion was carried, and the Board adjourned.

On Thursday morning the whole of the employes of the Albert New Mill Company, Heywood, numbering about 250, struck against a five per cent. reduction. The members of the trade societies and the Liberal Asso- ciations of Glasgow who took pert in the recent franchise demonstration have agreed to erect a monument to Mr Glad- stone in Glaqgow.

LIBRARIESISSOCIATION.--The Libraries Association, on Tuesday, commenced the annual Council, at Dublin, under the presidency of Dr. Ingram. On Wednes- day Lord Charles Bruce, M.P., read a Paper descriptive of Lord Spencer's library at Althorp. The Lord Lieutenant was preeent during the discussion which followed, and ex- pressed sympathy with the work of the Association. It was, indeed, a life full of agitations. anx:,ties, fears, and privations, but animated with what joy, us hopes! Every eveningwhen I came back from my work, I de- voted myself at home to making anatonimai drawings- from casts, while my wife did her inning iu the same- room ; and I drew until the hour of suppor came. It was- a pure, sweet pleasure to me to see that strong and lively creature coming and going with her flat irals from the fire-place to the table, and gaily ironing- and. bioging, "Schioppi, sciabola • fnoco—puhm ! ' (Muskets and brozidswords ; fire—fire—poum,) •• -

as she smoothed and beat with the flat-iron on the linens while her mother sat silently spinning in the corner. Truly, that blessed woman was right when she said, "We are so happy as we are," for one of the purest joys that cheers my present life is- the memory of those days. No joy is purer than that which conies from tlri memorY of that past time of work, of study, and of domestic peace. Those days of narrow means and acitations now shine upon me with a serene and lovely light; and I bless the Lord, who softens py His grace the hi Aerness of poverty and the harshness of fatigue, and ,o preserva this sweetness of remembrance in the heart, that neither time nor fortune has the power to extinguiA it, or even, to diminish it.—Thoughts on Art and Antobio'graPhi!". div.head: GAIIBLINCt AT TROTTVILLE.
div.p: GAIIBLINCt AT TROTTVILLE.

The Salle des Petits Jeux, where chances only ano sold, is the only sort of gaming pern.is-oble in France. But it is enough. The Course a Salon—the petits cheva.ux and the little courriers—hold a charm with which nothing else at Trouville can compete. The one verb which 15.' conjugated most often throughout all its moods and tenses is gagner. There is quiet about the tables of he couriers. Scarcely a sound is heard but the " Nolez ". of the starter, which is his own peculiar ,way of sarng roulez. It is curious to look down the row of hands setting the men in place. It is Trouville at a glance. Here are the brawny hands of the comfortable tradesman, the 194" slender fingers of the man of leisure, the glove stretcW on the hand of the fat bourgeoise, the tender fingers of child scarcely able to reach the little figure, the white bejewelled hand of the dandy, and the faultlessly gloved hand of the young woman who has come in alone and oblivious of everything but her game—she is lucky, for the silver and gold pile up in• front of her. Around the petits cheraux, at the other end of the room, the crowd surges, and the noise waxes louder and louder. The table is placed between two rows of raised seats intended for the players. But the game has extended out beyond, and ranks deep in the crowd. The table is divided into concentric circles. In each of these a horse with mounted jockey runs. The horses are set in motion by a lever and the speed is arranged by the distance of the circle from the centre. The chances are sold for one and two francs each on the horses, one horse always being reserved for the table. The horse stopping nearest the goal is the winner. As the speed slackens the excitement begins. The estimable mother of five children, whom we meet often at the tabled' h6te, rises in her seat with cries of delight or dis- appointment. Other doubtless estimable mothers, and fathers also, rise and express their various emotions. The last horse stops; the money is distributed. " Anghle has won 20 francs," our friend exclaims with joy; and Angele—a little lame fellow of nine—takes his money with a pleased blush, as if he had received a prize at Sunday-school. The game begins again. At 12 the room is closed, and as the hour approaches, the heat and noise wax fiercer. A second table is started. The eager crowd buy right and left from both tables. The chances are ex- hausted. Premiums are offered, bidding begins, and minx and women, buy, sell, and compete against one another with loud tones and excited gestures. The craze is at its height. We inount the highest rank of benches and look over the crowd. An English boy, with a female relative on each side of him, sits where we have seen him all the evening. A pile of money is heaped before him; but he leans back in a half dazed state as if unconscious of what is going on about him. All ranks and conditions are in the heated seething mass below us. There is but one level. This is, after all, the true democracy. —Harper's Monthly.

JOAQUIN MILLER'S INTERVIEW WITH A PUBLISHER. I came next day an hour before my time, but I did not enter. I watched the clock at the Piccadilly corner, and came in just as I had agreed. I think the clerk had for- gotten that I had ever been there. For my part, I had remembered nothing else. The great Murray came down —a tall, lean man, bald, with one bad eye, and a habit of taking sight at you behind his long, thin forefinger, which he holds up, as he talks excitedly, arid shakes all the time, either in his face or your own • and I was afraid of him from the first, and wanted to get away. He took me up-stairs, when I told him I had a book all about the great West of America; and there he shewed me many pictures of Byron—Byron's mother among the rest, a stout, red-faced woman, with awful fat arms and low, black curls about a low, narrow brow. I ventured to Bay she looked good natured. '"Aye, now, don't you know?, she could shie a poker at your head, don't you know? And the great Murray wagged his finger in her face, as he said this, quite ignoring me, my presence, or in opinion. Then he spun. about on his heel to where I stood in the back-ground, and taking sight at me behind his long, lean finger, jerked out the words: " Now young man, let us see what you have got." I drew fedi my first-born and laid it timidly in his hand. He held his head to one side, flipped the leaves, looked in, jerked his head back, looked in again,'twisted his head like a giraffe, and then lifted his long finger "Aye, now, don't you know poetry won't do? Poetry won't do, don't you know?" But will you not read it, please?" "No, no, no. No use, no use, don't you know?" I reached my hand, took the despised sheets' and in a moment was in the street, wild, shaking my fiat at that house now and then, as I stopped in my flight and turned to look back with a sort of nervous fear that he had followed me.— Memories and Rime. By Joaquin Miller.

div.head: DRUNKARD'S LUCK.
div.p: DRUNKARD'S LUCK.

Drunkards enjoy a remarkable immunihr from the con- sequences of injuries. One sometimes sees a drunken man pitched violently from a horse, and when the by- standers rush to the spot expecting to find him dead they are astonished to discover that be has been little injured. In his "Scrambles among the high Alps," Leslie Stephen tells the story of a guide who while drunk fell over a precipice so deeinhat a fall over it seemed certain death, and who yet sustained little injury. Stephen accordingly gives his readers the advice either not to fall over a precipice or to get thoroughly drunk before doing so. I myself once saw a man who had thrown himself, while drunk, over the Dean Bridge, in Edinburgh, a height of about 200 feet, on to the rocky bed of the stream below. A sober man would, probably, have been instantly killed, but this individual, though he had broken both of his thigh bones, quickly recovered. . . . The reason of' this immunity probably is that the nerve-centres which regulate the heart and vessels, are so much paralysed in the drunken man as not to be affected by the shock of the fall, which in a sober man would have acted on them so violently as to stop the heart, arrest the circulation, and cause instant death.—The Book of Health; edited by Malcolm Morris.

In that corrupt Florence of the corrupt eighteenth century, where every married woman was furnished, within two years of her marriage, with an officially ap- pointed lover, who sat in her dressing-room while she was finishing her toilet, who accompanied her on all her visits, , who attended her to balls and theatres, and, in fact, en- tirely replaced, by the strict social necessities of the system of cicisbeism, the husband, who was similarly employed about the wife of another; in this society, where conjugal infidelity was a social organisation supple- mented by every kind of individual caprice of gallantry ; where women were none the worse thought of if they added to the official eavaliere servante a whole string of other lovers, varying from the Cardinals of the Holy Church to the singers who played women's parts, in pow- der and hoops, at the opera; in th.s world of jog-trot immorality, where jealousy was tolerated in lovers, but ridiculous in husbands, such a couple as the 'Count and Countess of Albany was indeed a source of pity, wonder, and amazement.—The Countess of Albany. Eminent Women Series. By Vernon Lee.

div.head: WHERE SCULPTURE DIFFERS FROM PAINTDRI.
div.p: WHERE SCULPTURE DIFFERS FROM PAINTDRI.

Sculpture is an art ef much more simplicity and MA, formity than painting; it cannot with propriety,and the best effect, be applied to many subjects. The object of its pursuit may be comprised in two words—Form and Character; and those qualities are presented to us but in one manner, or in one style only, whereas the powers of painting as they are more various and extensive, so they are exhibited in as great a variety of manners. The Roman, Lombard, Florent:ne, Venetian, and Flemish schools all pursue the same end by different means. But sculpture having but one style, can only to one style of painting have any relation; and to this, which ig indeed the highest and most dignified that painting can boast, it has a relation so close that it may be said to be almost the same art operating upon different materiale. The. sculptors of the last age, from no attending sufficiently to this discrimination of the different styles of painting,. have been led into many errors. Though they well knew that they were allowed to imitate or take ideas for the improvement of their own . art from the grand style of, painting, they were not aware that it was not permitted to borrow in the same manner from the ornamental.. When they endeavour to copy the picturesque effects, contrasts, or petty excellencies of whatever kind, which not improperly find a place in the inferior branches of painting, they doubtless imagino themselves improving and extending the boundaries of their art by this imita- tion ; but they are in reality violating its essential character, by giving a different direction toffs operations, and proposing to themselves ieither what is unattainable, or at best a meatier object of , pursuit. The grave and austere dia. act er of sculpture requires the utmost degree of formality in composition; picturesque contrasts have here no place; everything is carefully weighed and measured, one side making almost an exact equipoise to the other; a child is not a proper balance to a full-grown figure, nor is a figure sitting or stooping a companion to an upright figure: If the business of sculpture were to administer pleasure to ignorance, ore mere entertainment to the senses, the Venus of Medicis might certainly re- ceive much improvement by colour; but the character of sculpture makes it her duty to afford delight of a different, and, perhaps, of a holier kind; the delight resulting from the contemplation of perfect beauty; and this, which is in truth an intetlectual pleasure, is in many re- spects incompatible with what is merely addressed to the ser,ses, such as that with which ignoramie and levity contemplate eleganoe of form.—The Discourse of Joshua Rey,4lds. Edited uNd A,nnoed by Edniusci Gouty

, WIT AND RUM( TR. What is the difference between a watchmaker and a gaoler? —One sells watches, and the other watches cells. Gibbons the bachelor asserts that a married ratan never has a cold dinner, for, when he happens to go home hate, his Wife always makes it hot for him. "I'm surprised. John!" said an old lady, when she found the butler helping himself to some of her finest old port. "So am I, ma'am," was the calm reply; "I thought you Yeas gone out." &nom' THE WISH OF THE DEAR BETTER HALF —"I Should like to see somebody abduct me!" said Mrs. Smith at the breakfast-table the other morning, looking up from 1 the newspaper. "Wm! So should I, my deer—so should I I, my dear—so should I! "said Mr. Smith, with exceeding I earnestness. I "What do you charge a quart for your milk here ?" asked a man, as he put his head in at the door of a milk-shop. " Fourpence,' was the reply. " Ain'tyou got any for three- Pence-halfpenny ? I rose on the stroke of six; half an hour later I sat down to breakfast; at seven I was at work, dined at twelve, ate sup,' Per at six, and in bed at nine-thirty; ate only hear:v food, , ' and hadn't a sick day in all that time:" "Dear me!" said ' the deacon, in sympathetic tones. He pointed oat that the domestic , Practice complained of was in itself reprehensible, tending I , only in very exceptional circumstances to restore family ' harmony, and open to objection on the score at least of un- manliness. But, in that he, the master, was himself engaged I and paid to assist in keeping the public peace, there were, in this particular case, additional reasons why the habit should be abandoned. People might justly think it rather a scan- dal that, whilst the magistrate was constantly interfering in other households to prevent violence, it should exist unre- preb ended in his own. IN AMERICA. I have often heard it said, and I think there is a good deal of sound sense in the observation, that if people would do at home what they are compelled to when abroad, they would have no occasion to emigrate; or, that they would succeed as well in their own country as in any other. It is not because America is an Eldorado, where gold may be had for the picking up, that men have got on there, or in more appropriate words, "made money." Hundreds have gone from England to the States, and Canada, with the idea of having an easy life of it, and returning home to spend the remainder of their days on the produce of an industry that would only have the name of being work. These have emigrated to find their dreams dispelled, and the result of the disappointment has not been in favour of the country of their adoption. It has been too often said by these people, "If I had only known I wouldn't have come out to such a place." Perhaps the emigrant has been a gentleman, accustomed to earning a living at the desk or the counter, and thinks that any meaner occupation, or one requiring extra manual labour, to be beneath him. He could not condescend to handle the spade, or carry the hod, and work side by side with the much despised and much misrepresented "nigger." No, shade of his grandfather Scrogginsl—who was butler to my Lord Bobbinhat, his dignity would not stand such a humiliation. A man of his character would be the first to have the "stuffing knocked out of him," and find in his dis- comfiture thee pedigree and position would not raise a vine, or a "cob" of Indian corn; nor would either be accepted for a week's "run" on the boarding-house. He would have to take off his coat, or go home, if he meant to live honestly. He must make up his mind to do aaything he eln get to do, and never admit that he cannot do it. He may do this with the pleasing assurance that there is no one looking down upon him. He may be a subject of her Majesty, and some- times be called a "greenhorn," or a Johnny," or a "sparrow ;" but these sneers do not reflect in the least degree upon the character of his occupation. He may be a rag-picker, or a junk dealer, but so long as he minds his business, and does not curse the land and the Republic, he need not plink into the shade when on the side-walk for fear of being observed. It is only when he descends to the level of a "bummer" that the eagle gets its claw into him. Many of the most successful men in America have begun the new life at the foot of the ladder. "Ay, lower than that—i'th' cellar," remarked a Lancashire friend of mine. In the better sense, nothing was too mean for them to do,—scavengieg, sewering, digging, sweeping, portering, hodding, —anything that had a dollar at the end of It, found a ready hand to do it And as the mind was made up to take what- would come, so early would the hand find something to do. Once on the ladderr with a de- termination to ascend, he may keep on in the upward course. The misfortunes, or malpract;ces of other people, may some- times interfere With his progress, and he may have to take a "back kick;" but if he laae the "stair.,' in him he will mount again. If he takes on airs it Will be so Watch the worse for him; and if he intends to succeed by "genteel" means, he must either become a politician, or get into the confidence of some banker. In either case he may have a chance of showing his "smartness," which is only another term for gilded roguery. But if he means his career to be an honourttble one the path lies before him. I have had millions dollars so much rung in my ears of late that, when I begin to talk about thousands, I feel small. "Oh, he:must be worth his millions," is a very comarm, observation, and applied to people, too, who, in a fere years, without gambling in stocks, or stealing from the public purse, have emerged from the gutter, and raiued themselves to a height of fortune as near to the sun as can be reached without the aid of wings. But it has not been done by taking thing' easily, or waiting, " Micawber " like, for "something to turn up.' It bee been done by sheer hard work, which admits of very little rest,--werk indulged in as it it was mere pastime, and returned to again and again until the object of so much labour has been accomplished. I have during my sojourn in the States been made familiar with the lives of some of these self-made men. Where I have not had their history from their own lips, I have had it from those of their immediate acquaintances. I have been spending a week ia Philadelphia, which I should take to be the finest " Manchester" in the world. I cannot Compare it to London, for the "Quaker city" is not the re- sort of hereditary nobility, or people who, as the phrase is meant to imply, have "had fathers before them." It is the home of the princes of industry, who succeed not to titles and fortunes but of their own creating. I passed the ware- house of a firm the other day, the principal of which hails from Lancashire, and commenced his transatlentic life by picking woollen rags at a remuneration of four dol- lars per week; "but," as my informant gave it, "he didno' efond at th' end o' Jack Lawton's every neet, makin' gam' o' folk as- they went pest. Ele're always workin', an saved out o' every little he made." This man took a step higher than rag-picking, and with the aid of a little of the simplest kind of machinery he commenced making tying- up thread for grocery stores. With this hung upon his arm, he would tremp a distance as fat as from Manchester to Oldham to dispose of his wares. By that dogged perse- verance which means winning, he acquired a "team," or had the temporary use of one He would attend market, and having sold up, he would return home with a load of vegetables, and "market" those before he finished his day's work. It might be tedious, but at the same time instructive, to trace this man's career from the time he shouldered his bundle on the banks of the Medlock, to becoming the greatest manufacturer on that nobler stream, the Schuylkill. But it will be sufficient for use to say that he and his partner, a brother, are at present the employers of 3,000 "helps," and that the former has been named for a seat in Congress. Bravo, "Owdham !" Other instances I could name of men who are known to me having risen from nothing to affluence by hard work— but in a fair field—and not shirking the labour offered to their hands. Generally speaking, the disappointed have not laid themselves out to make the best of their time and oppor- tunities. The revelations of a noble institution, the" Society of the Sons of St. George," which has its branches scattered all over the States, show how utterly helpless have been a class of immigrants who came to seek, not to make, their fortunes in America. They have not struck a "bonanza" at the first stroke of the pick, and. withbut farther effort des- pair of ever finding anything. Their hands have not been accustomed to wield other than a pen, or a pair of scissors, and to raise "Sops" on them, so that they could not wear seven-and-half gloves, would be a meanness that their pride could not submit to. If they had made up their minds to work at whatever offered itself, and adopted the advice of Horace Greeley when he said, "Young man, go West," they would not have been under the necessity of begging the means by which to return to Filgiand, as is too often the case, and without the cognizance of their friends at home. I wish it had been borne in the minds of those people who have been used to reading glowing accounts of America that they have to work hard here if only to make a bare living. —so hard that if they were put to the same task in England there would be a great cry about white slavery. Some might I say, "Well, I wouldn't do it." To these my advice would I be "stay at home." America will not support gentlemen ' who prefer " loafing "to working. The rosy representations ' of what the land will yield may all be true, but it will not do so yithout labour, and that of the most trying kind. I , was a fortnight ago shown over a plot in a neighbouring ' State that, to contemplate its barren appearance, and feel they would have to subsist upon it, or starve, would have broken some men's hearts, and it was not so very cheap, either, when compared with the prices of farming land in the old country. In a village near is a mill that has been " shut down " since May; and the whole of the inhabitants i were, or had been, dependant on working at this mill for a I living. , Going elsewhere to seek employment in the same trade would have been like "selling hip," as it was suffering from depression everywhere. They wisely determined to stay where they were, and make the best of the situation. Some lived on their savings; these were English people, and had not spent their "bottom dollar." Others, English people too, turned to farming in a small way. The hands that delved the land, and sowed the corn and potatoes on the plot I was shown over, three acres in extent, had been accustomed to work amongst silk, and were as soft as "my lady's." But these hands set to work at once upon the land, and broke a portion of it up. The whole was too much to cultivate the first season. It would have been an insult to a shop-boy in England to offer him a piece of such land for a football field. But now it is smiling with corn and po- tatoes. The uncultivated portion is devoted to the keeping of poultry, which are calculated to supply a family with ezgs and "spring chickens" all the year round. The excess of potatoes over what they would require for their own use, this amateur farmer told me, he could barter in the city for other necessaries ; and now he has no fears for the winter. It is not yet five years since this man, so he informed me, sat next to me at an entertainment in Leigh, Lancashire. He has done all this, and built himself a house, in the mean- time. But it has been a struggle to do it. He did not come to try his fortune, hut to make it. And now let me call the attention of your readers to the working of a society I have before mentioned, the "Sons of St. George." I had the privilege of being. present at the quarterly meeting of the Philadelphia branch in July; and I gathered from the secretary's report, as well as from the president's address, that which can only be a faint idea of the amount of good they are doing in the way of helping those who cannot help themselves. The society constitutes a self-elected, self-supporting, benevolent board of guardians, established for social intercourse in the first place, and in the second the relief of distressed English immigrants. But Irishmen have submitted themselves to be Saxonized for the time, in order that they might participate in the benefits of this useful institution. I gathered from the report that a considerable amount nf money—American money, bear in mind—is annually spent in carrying out the objects of the society. A very distressing case had just been brought before them. An English schoolmaster, the very last man who ought to Come out, had been driven from pillar Co post in his efforts to obtain a livelihood by " genteel " means. He had been relieved from time to time from the funds of the society, and as a lan item of assistance they offered to pay his passage back to England. The man was so overjoyed at the prospect of returning home that it turned his brain, and he committed suicide the week he should have sailed. The action of the president of the society cannot he too greatly commended. By his own efforts, incurring much loss of time, he on one occasion rescued from moral perdition three English girls _ _

About eleven o'clock a tremendous explosion was heard, and the locality was strewn with broken glass, the fine window on the east- ern siele of the building being wrecked, and the house op- posite having suffered similar injury. It was subsequently ascertained that the explosive had been deposited on a plat- form on which stands on old Crimean cannon, and on search being made a piece of tin, evidently belonging to a canister, and some sulphurous mixture were found. • On Monday. as. the police had no clue, the Watch Committee offered £2OO reward. THE REFORM AGITATION. Sie—Tn my wanderings to and fro, in my comings in and goings out, I have at various times met with individuals who hive not bean indisposed to discuss the present political situation, and, being an ardent politician, I have earnestly entered into the spirit ot the thing. I have occasionally met with persons of no very easily defin d shade of political opinion who have remarked that they could better under- stand the I eaders of the Franchise agitation if they advocated heart and soul for the abolition of the House of Lords, but that tee present position of the leaders of the Liberal party is calce tes:l not only to be of no avail in securing the sup- port of 'nespendent thinkers, but also to subtract from the camber of their present supporters. The House of Lords, they cisein, is only carrying out a prerogative exercised from tin a immemorial, and that the Peers, in carrying Oat what has by use become in their opinion a right are justified in their course of action. Therefore, they say, the crusade against the House of Lords as at present waged by the Government is simply en the lines of "abusing the other , sets in a had case." But if they reflect they will see that Mr Gladstone and the Government are wiser than they. Prebably Mr Gladstone, if it were expedient, would speak tnorrestrongly on the question of the abolition V. the House of Lorde than he has yet done, but I think that his speech at Reek Quay station. Warrington, last week, contains a covert but significant hint that the members of the heredi- tary chamber had better look carefully to their pceliion, else they may speedily find themselves hors de combat But ills not always wise to resort to severest means when there is vet 'eeesiiiiiity of mild ones being effective. Soft words first, and if they fail strong measures must follow. For weeks the Premier has warned the House of Lords of the conse- quences of persisting in their present suicidal policy.. If they heed not the warning voice so much the worse for them. But Liberals are anxious that matters should be amicably settled if such a thing be possible. Mr Gladstone has n t been in the political arena for nearly half a century without knowing what he is about, and the House of Lords will, if they do not mind, bring about their destruction more sneedly by their own obstruction than would be accom- puished by a cry of "Dawn with the House of Lords," from the Liberals.--Yours, NESTOR. Warrington, October, 1884. A REPLY TO "—CAPTAIN CUTTLE." • Sir,—l have been much amused at " Captain Cattl's " logic. As it is jellvtisli argument. we must make allow- ance for the want of the Icg:cal faculty. Fresh from the studies of Bentham, perhaps our friend would take a few lessons from Whateley on the Art ef Reasoning." The first thing to learn is that from a particular premise you cannot draw a universal conclusion. There is very little argument in his letter. It is declamation and abuse of a system from beginning to end. Take, however, his main proposition: Christianity has been disgraced by some of its professors, therefore Christianity is a worthless system. To show the flaw in the conclusion we pat it in this form: this apple is rotten, therefore all apples are rotten. The "professing Christian is a Ithnbag,"—ergo Christianity is a " humbug." Because the Liberator argues for the separa- tion of Church and State, consequently—mark the logic— " Chrietians persecute one another." I might as well say, that because dune Atheists have been swindlers, there- fore all Atheists are swindlers, "backed up as they are by the Atheistic iditiee, are the chief CUM of our trade depression," If "Captain Cattle " desires to overthrow Christianity, be must proceed upon other lines, and show that it is not adapted to man's moral nature, nor the faculties of his moral being. iiis is the reductioad ab- surdam argument, illustrated by "drunken clergymen, swindling hypocrites, toadying the patron, Cr fawning on the rich employer." "The tree " is bad, becauSe "the fruit is. bad." Query, some fruit, not all, as examples plan opposite character can be brought forward. The vision wh ch apparently fascinates "Captain Cottle" is the dream of the French Atheists of a past age, and which proved to be a dream, "Liberty, fraternity, equality," "The uneducated dissenting minister," dre. What authority has "Captain Cattle " for such a sweeping assertion ? But, a word in your ear, my friend; flay as little as you can ehout educa- tion, or you may be called upon to show cause, or qualifi- cation, to pronounce upon this question. Be advised, keep well under cover of the shellfish. John Wesley lived in a very superstitious age—no wonder it he was touched with the prevailing belief. Bur, mark the sequel." supersti- tious" because "uneducated." Shades of Wesley! What next? To charge Christianity with evil, has no foundation in its teachings, ner in its precepts.—l am, faithfully your? A VILLAGIIR.

I may add that, although it is quite pos- sible for both midis to Asia, from their own point of view, on the revision of the overseers' lists. such has not been the case on this occasion, and if von or one of your reporters have an hoar or two to spare to go over the lists with me roe can easily verify whet I now say. TaE WARRINGTON GUARDIANS AND THE VACCINATION ACTS. Sir,—My name being conspicuous in your report of our -last Guardians' nferting, your Liberalism and lore of fair- play will doubtless (even to an Anti-Vaccinator) affard the freedom of a reply. With the family likeness of the War- rington Guardians, and officials, the Suttons, and Coopers I am not concerned; and whether such Guardians, deo, are trying to appear hereditary lords at present I care not. The Vaccination Acts, as administered at Newton during the last few years, have become a bye-word and reproach. For this even the magistrates, some time ago, were humiliated by having to return certaio fines illeeally inflicted. Again, the Home Office, naturally very tardy, is moving to secure justice and fairplay to others more recently prosecuted. Once more, several of the late cases under exactly similar notices, conditions, &c, were dismissed; while others were let off with the full possible penalty of 20s and costs. This occurred under both the 29th and 31st sections of the Vacci- nation Acts, some summonses being jointly issued under both sections, a proceeding totally at variance with all law and rractice' and from the very nature of the two sections can never be made to unite. The usual monthly meeting of tile Lymni Local Board was held in the Board-room, Lyme', on Thursday. THE SCARLET FEVER AT LYMNL—Mr Mort also pre- sented a report on the prevalence of scarlet fever in teeinm and the surrounding district, and spoiee of the probability of the disease spreading from the schools in the place.—Dr Fox, medical officer of health, said the deaths during the last quarter had been small in number compared with the average ratio of mortality. Only 16 had been reported to him, giving a death rate of 136 per 1,000. It was true that within the last few days there teed been an outbreak of scarlet fever. The cises that kad been reported to him he had visited, and the impression produced on his mind was that the disease had been im- ported in the first instance. lie did not think it could be made out with certainty that the schools had been the means ' of spreading the disease. He had desired the inspector to call at the schools to ascertain the number of absentee, in order to find the number of cases of illness not notified, and these were about 12. But than there wrre ' many who did not go to the schools. He knew some infected houses where the children did not go to the schools. 11,s object in wishing the inspector to call at the schools was to prevent the schools becoming a medium for the spread of the disease. At the present time the fever was bad throughout i the county, and he was harreesed to death with the nisei' In . his district, some of the cases being singularly fatal Mr Dewhurst suggested that it would lis well in the event of case 3 occurring in a row of cottages to disinfect eack house, as people had greater facilities for visiting each other where the houses were so close together.—Dr Fox said he would rather go in for disinfecting the ashpits and gul- lies. In most of the houses he had visited he had seen in- sanitary conditions that might be connected with an out- break of any emetic disease. His experience proved more and more every day that these complaints would exist in I Proportion to the prevalence of insanitary conditions, in fact if unhealthy matter, such as refuse, were removed care- fully there would be an immunity from these complaints. There were many new buildiugs in the district requiring the attention of the Board which the Board really knew nothing about. In many places there was no provision for carrying off storm water. The channe'e and gullies were in a bad state, and the ashpits unc3vPred. He thought there was great room for the application of the Fowler closet system. There were many houses coming into eccu• pation which had been closed for a very long time, and some of these were hardly under the notice of the officials of the Board. It would be necessary for the Board to have a report on the matter in order to see what was neces-ary to be done.—Mr Dewhurst said he supposed it would mere. ly be a question of laying oat a few pounds —Dr Fox said that was so. The means of improvement were not wan, inv. but an outlay would be required.—The diseassiun was tete mately adjourned. SWISS BAZAAR AT WARWTiITON• On Wednesday afternoon the Mayor of Warrington (Al- derman Harrison) opened a Swiss Bazaar held at the Drill Hall in aid of the building fund of r mmanuel Church, Warrington. Amongst those present at the opening cere- mony were the Mayoress (Mrs Harrison), the Rev W Mules and Mrs Mules, the Rev J Yonge. the Rev E Moore, Mr Ziba Armitage, Mr Woods, Councillor Mackie, Om. After , singing and prayer, I'the Rev W Mueesrose to effer the Mayor the thanks of the Bazaar Committee for his kindness, not only is being a Ipatron of the bazaar, but in coosenting to perform the open- ing ceremony. He had also to thank thole gentlemen whose names appeared on the bazaar placards and on the pro- grammes as patrons for their influence. The MAYOR said that be should like to take that very earliest opportunity of expressing himself with reference to the very kind manner in which the Rev Mr Mulee and the . congregation of Emmanuel Church had been pleased to • recognise him by asking him to perform that opening ser- vice. He responded with feelings of very great pleasure to their request, because he was of opinion that anyone hold- ing the office of Mayor should, irrespective of all sectarian considerations, endeavour to identify himself with any movement which he conceived to be for the benefit of the community, and he would be a very bold maa indeed who would venture to say that the erection of a ceurch or chaps, was not something to benefit the community. Theretore on that ground he thought that it was the duty of the Mayor to identify himself with such a movement, and it had been a source of great pleasure to him to do so. If that were the Jest bazaar ever held in Warrington he might possibly have something new to tell them, but as it waa not the first—and he was sure it would not be the last—he was deprived of the opportunity of sayiag something new with reference to bazaars. Titers were many people who entertained a great antipathy to baz tars and made no secret at all of showing their dislike to them, but he was of opinion that, those whe had to encounter and incur the anxiety and toil in getting up a bazaar had far more Tenon to fight shy of them than they who simply went to them and spent their money, generally getting a quil pro quo for what they spent. lie thought that there was great credit to them for carrying out a limier to a successful issue, and he must confess that he had not seen many bazaars that were not ultimately successful. If the objec- tors to bazaars could advise other means ef getting meetly for religious and educational purposes, the clergy and others who had so frequently to appeal to the public would be glad of the information. BAY lus, or sales of work, to use a term which appeared to be more popular, were by far the best and most effectual means of raising money. As they knew. the clergy were constartly coming to them for contributions of one kind or another, and he was sure that it was a matter as unpleasaist to the clergy as it might be to those who were asked to subscribe. Money must be Ruler:Woad if they were to carry out these excellent purposes, and therefore they did not think that they should be tee stringent in the way which they opened their pockets for the purpose of con- tributing to these good objects. He did not suppose thet there was a church, school, or chapel in Warrington that was not deeply indebted to biz-Lars for considerable sums of money, and he had no doubt that hut for that melhed of i raising money they would frequently find theMeelecit placed lin great difilcultiee, Nes one teti!?, look round thet Tien). land tee the betutilui thines there exposed for sale without , eoming to the conclusion that much exertion had been I necessary to produce the effects they saw. He hoped that they would show their appreciation by the purchases that they made. They were, of course, aware what was the ob. ject of the hazier. It was one of the instincts of their natures that when they sant a brother or sister in affliction they should at once endeavour to render them assistance, and the same ales applied to a community of persons. The little community of Emmanuel Church, in Bold-street, WAS at that time inflicted with an incubus, which could not be thrown off without assistance, and it was in their power to give aid. in the building of their pretty little church le Bold-street they got into debt, and were at erseant Indebted in the sum of £550, and the bazaar had ben got up to try to &per off the liability. Debt under any cireumslances was difficult to contend with, and it was only natural that 1 the pastor and worshippers of Em mantle Church should be ' anxious to shake all that "Old nun of the sea." Be trusted that excellent purpose would be aecompliehed as the result of the bezear. All Christian communities onotild help in a woe& of the,: hind, for they were all working together for one go ,d elleCf-e=the epreed of Christianity and the glorifi- cation of the Creator', that God who Wei not only the God of the Jaws, but the God of the Gentiles: He thought that the various religious denominations slionld be as one grand brotherhood of men, sinking distinctions, and hembling themselves towards men and man, 134 s and class, Church- men and Nonconformists. There was plenty of good work to be accomplished, and they might rely upoe it that the mil- lenient was vat far distant. The scepticism of the age and the growth of atheism proved it. It appeared to him thet if professing Christians, instead of querrelling about trifl-s such as the Eastward position, or disputing about the nature of the Trinity, as Christians did in oldies tiine, or the efficacy of the Sacrament, as they did at peesent, and would unite iir counteracting the per- nicious teachings of atheism and make a dead set against it—of course he did not mean by a violent and dangerous system of toad-throwing, begot of ignorance and carried out ' in rancour, but in a peaceful, tolerant spirit of charity and , forbearance—they would do far more good than by i creating dissensions amongst themselves. Even iris matter of policy—and that was looeine at the question from a low point indeed--the discountenancing of atheism was of im- mense advantage to tha community at large. In his opinion , it behovsd every lover of his country to give what help he could to every religious ore.anieation that recognised the existence of a Supreme and Sentient Being. There were only too many who audaciously presumed to deny such an existence, and who did their very best to destroy the belief in a Divine power, and who, if they ceuld have their way, would set at naught the controlling power of the Deity. If that could be withheld, if it could be wiped out, as it were, then the main distinction which separated our human nature from the brute creation would be destroyed. the moral law would cease to exist, and nothing but fear of detec ion would stand between men and the indulgence of their grossest passions. Robbery, licentiousnees, and even murder would become questions of expediency, the human race would sink into heedless depravity, and the law of the strongest alone would be recognised. Tbat was what had happened in the French Republic (luring the eiorrible scenes of the great revolution, and that was what would in all probability occur in England if it were nor for the in- fluences used in a contrery direction. All the churches, chapels, and schools that they could build were needed to counteract it, and in supporting that bazaar they were raining another obstacle to the progress of Atheism, and stimulating the growth of those Christian principles which were mixed up with their very being, and SO influenced their national life. Therefore let Churchmen and Noncon- foemists unite on one common platform to promote the great canes of religious and social progress. He had great plea- sure in declaring the bazaar open. The following is a list of the stall-holders and the names of the -stalls, viz : Excelsior Lodge : Mrs Mules, Miss A Brown, Mrs Page, Miss E Brown, miss. nootoisay. Mountain Home: Miss Sutton, Miss Mottram. Mrs Lowe, Miss Hindley. Geneva Cot- tage : Mrs Howard, Miss Lake. Miss Shepherd, Miss Bowcock. Mont Blanc Villa: Mrs J C Spinks, Mrs H. Gandy, Miss Jawkes, Miss M Pant, Miss Gandy, Miss Heald. The Castle (refreshments) : Mrs Parsons, Ms O'Brien, Mrs London, Mrs Dickens. The Arbor (Flowers, tiro:. Miss, Dickens, Miss H Nixon. Bon-bon Cottage (Confectionery) : Mrs Birchen. lMr Garland, of Bridge-street, had a stall stocked with lamps of various descriptions, which was attended to by Mr Revenscroft and Miss Nixon. The amusements were many and varied, and were well patronised. They included a panorama of Egypt and the Soudan, magical illusions, an automaton sailor, the Alpine well, an Egyptian mystery, and a living mummy. Behind the refreshment stall was a beaetifally palmed representation of the Lake of Lucerne, and the Swiss cottages were as realistic in appearance as could well be expected. 'On Thursday and Friday the bazaar was fairly well at- tended by visitors, and the sales were satisfactory. It is Intended to keep it open to-day from two to nin o'clock. when the reduced charge of sixpence admission will be made and the prices of the articles will be reduced as the ladies are determined to dispose of the whole of the goods.

BAND OF HOPE Mitirrimo.—On Thursday evening pleasing and instructive magic lantern entertainment WAS given in connection with the Working-men's Mission, Bank , Quay. entitled "The trial of Sir Jasper." The connective readings were given by the Rev W R Parry, the newly appointed minister of Cockhedge Mission, and Mr T Ashley had charge of the lantern. A few remarks were made by Mr H. A. T. Pickersgill, the president, after which votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close. I THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—A deputation from the Provisional Corn. mittee of the Manchester Ship Canal, consisting of Mr Daniel Adamson, Mr H BOddington, junr, Mr W Fletcher, Mr Richard James, Mr SAROD, awl Mr Lawrence, on Sem.- ' day met a number of the members of the Warringthn Town Council, at the Town Hall, where a conference took 1 place in reference to the revised plans of the canal, and operations fcr the ensuing session. The membera of the Corporation present were—The Mayor (Alderman Harri- son) ; Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, and Davies ; Councillors Monks' Marsh, Mackie, Pierpoint, Wallington, w Burgess, Litton, Dakin, Taylor, Dixon, Caldwell, Bolton, Ashton, and Hutchinson; and Messrs Brook (town clerk), Longdio (borouo surveyor), Chorley (borough treasurer.) The plans were explained at length by Mr Adamson and Mr Leader Williams. After a discussion on the details, Alder- man Burgess proposed, Councillor Marsh seconded, and Councillor Dixon supported a resolution to the effect that 'The Town Council of Warrington be recommended to join ' in the promotion of the 1311 in the ensiling session, and to contribute a sum equal to 21 in the £ out of the borough rates towards the expenses." The resolution was adopted. Subsequently, when the business of the meeting had been concluded, the Mayor invited the deputation to luncheon at the Warrington Club.
