There were present Messrs itylands (in the chair), Blackburst, Appleton, Darbyshire, Cooper, Long, Owen, S Sutton (deputy clerk), and W Owen (valuer.) THE RATING OP TELEPHOSEI.—The following letter was read :--Manchester, let October, 1884. Telephone Com- pany. Dear sir,—We have your notice informing us that the appeal would be heard at half-past eleven on Friday next. We do not know whether you are aware that the same question has arisen between the Company and the Manchester Overseers. The court has decided against our clients, who have given notice of appeal. The appeal will be heard in the early port of next month. We should be glad if you would kindly let our appeal against your rates stand over until after the decision of the appeal court in the Manchester case, which will govern most of the Cases in which the Telephone Company are concerned.—Youre faithfullz, GRUNDY, KERSHAW, aft Co. James C Sutton, Esq , Warrington.n—The CHAIRMAN dild the Company charged very high and they ought to be charged in propor- tion —Mr APPLETON asked what was the nature of the Company's plant.—The CHAIRMAN said it was posts, &c, but the qaestion was what they could be let for.—The mat- ter was left over as rquested. Yearn's 13nroaT.—The VALUER (Mr Owen) reported th,t he had made the following valuations and had entered them in the Union books :—London and North-Western Railway at Collins Green station, gross £lO7 10s, rateable £BB 10s; station master's house and land adjoining, gross £B, rateable £7; Mr Naylor, the rev Pear Tree Inn (now reduc_d from 25 ours to 20 acres by land taken for building plots by the London and North-Western Railway station purposes. and by the Collins Green Colliery Co), gross £32, rateable £29 10s. He (the chairman) had looked into the ass ssment of the florae and Jockey Inn, )Vinwick-toad, and htd ex- amined the lease. He was of opinion the assessment ehould be reduced to' gross £125, rateable £l.OO, ac the cottage in- cluded in the lease is sop irately asaes,ei. lie had inapectod the premises of the Bull's Head Inn, Bridge-street, War- rin;ton, and examined the book, and he WAS or opinion the assessment should be reduced to £4B gram, £4l rateable. With regard to the high level assessment of the London and Nortri-tVeetern Railway he had not b-en able to meet Mr Edmonds on the question as he was detained in Scot- land last week beyond the day in which he had endeavoured to get an appointment with him.—With fegard to the assessment of the Bull's Head, Mr Owner said he had seen some books which showed that the business of the plaee hal dropped a third since 1879.—Tee CHAIRMAN thought they must be very careful in lowering assessments on that account —Mr DARBY. BYSIIIRE said he would be beeter pleaaed if the reduction of the assessment could he made on other grounds than tho,e put forward. He thon:eht it wonld be a bad precedent to go upon.—Mr BtackHnnsT said tradesmen might take advan- tage of a precedent of that kind.—Mr DARBYSIIIRE : And plenty of farmers, too.—Mr OWEN explained that the case we quite different from those of a farmer or tradesman.— The CHAIRMAN said booke and balance sheets were not to be relied on too much, and he hoped Mr Owen would remem- ber Mr Darbystoire's remark that it WO a very dangerous precedent—The report of the valuer was then confirmed, and the business concluded.

THE RECENT RETlSlON.—Yesterday, Mr Millis Coventry. Revising Barrister, sat at the Lion Hotel to " read over " after the recent revision of burgess lists for Warrington. Mr 11l Roberts appeared for the Liberals, and Mr Nicholson. solicitor. and Mr Hampson for the Conservative.. On the conclurion of the business, which was of a formal nature, the Registrar thanked the parties concerned for the way in which the business had been conducted, and they in turn thanked the Registrar for his patience during the revision. WArERINGTON TOWN COUNCEL —A monthly meeting of this body will b 3 held at the Council Clsamher, on Ttasday next —The Inspector to the Scheel Attendance Committee reports that 51 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 49 cases for 94 children; that 31 cases tiad been taken before the magi!, [rates, when fines were inflicted in 26 wee, two adjourned, two warrants ordered, and one boy ordered to be whipp4d. 45 criV9 were brought before the committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the different pehlic elementary schoole during the month of Aurrost was 0 5(31, and for the c4rresoonding period last year 6 620 ; decrease 89, owing to sickness in the town.—The Museum, Library and Arts Committee report for the month of August : Visitors to the Museum, 2080; volumes issued to subscribers, 2,116 ; ditto to readers, 1.044. The report of the registrar states that for the pis, four weeks the interments were: Adults, 28; minors, 62 ; stillbern and premature, 7; and for the corresponding period of last year: Adults, 29; minors, 57; stillborn and premature. 9.—The Bathkeeper reports to the Town Hall. 'Park and Bathe Committee that the income from the baths for the pant four weeks wan £56 Hs 101,i and for the corn's- pending period of last year £42 103 41 an increase of £l4 Os GL—Various estimates will be submitted to the Council of expenditure for the half-year commencing the 29th Sep- tember. 1884. The Council estimate that the amount of £3,456 3e 41 will, in addition to the borough fund, be re- quired and sufficient for the purposes to which the borough fend Is applicable, and it will h moved that the Council order a borough rate to lie made in order to raise the said amount.—An improvement rate of Is 6:1 in the £, and a sewers rate of 2d in the £, an recommended by the Finance Committee, will be submitted for approval.—Mr Councillor Burgess will move "That the Council is of opinion that the nightsoil pails should be collected during the night, and re- commends the Sanitary Committee to make arrangemeuts accordingly." A FUSTIAN CUTTER HEAVILY FINED —Edmond, Mills, a master fustian cutter, carrying on business at Warrington, was yesterday summoned to the Borough Police Court for, on the sth September, unlawfully employing Selena Woods in his cutting shop after the hour of seven o'clock in the evening. There was a second charge of a similar character against him in respect to a girl named Margaret Welsby.— Mr A Browne defended..--Mr Mead-King, inspector, said that the case was a natural sequence of one heard before the • Bench a short time ago. What he was prepared to prove was to the effect that the girls were employed by the de- fendant from six o'clock on a Friday morning until seven o'clock on the following Saturday morniog. It was one of the worst cases, if not the worst, that he had ever had to bring before the mitt ; and it would be his duty to ask the Bench, if satisfied with the evidence, to inflict as severe a penalty as they could.—Selina Woods was then called, and deposed to working daring the hours named. She was cross-examined by Mr Browne, to show that she had not been working the whole of the time stated, and that she was at work late because she bad neglected a piece that had to be finished within a given time.—Mr Browne admitted the offence, but pleaded in extenuation that the girl had neg- lected to finish her work in time, and if it had not been corn- pleted her master would have had to be the sufferer.—The facts of the second, which was not gone into, were similar. —The Bench fined the defendant 50s in each case and the costs; Alderman Holmes, who presided, remarking that if there was a recurrence of such an event, either by the de- fondant or anyone else, the full penalty would be indicted. --At the same Court, Mills summoned Ada Gorst, a girl, to show clues why she should not be committed for disobey- ing a magistrates' order requiring h-r to fulfil her contract with the complainant—Mr Browne appeared for complain- ant, and Mr Davies for defendant.—Mr Davies said that the indenturea had been entered into without the knowledge of the girl's father, and since what had transpired at the court on a recent emersion the father refused to let his daughter work for the complainant. He should ask them to dismiss the summons, and he would bring an action to have the in- dentures cancalled.—The father having confirmed the state- ment of hie wilcitor, the Bench dismissed the summons.-- A case brought against Margaret Troy by Mills was ad- journed for a month to give her an opportunity to pay 10s due to the latter.

BOWLING MATCH EETWEEN JAMES SHAW AND JOSEPH GLEAVE.—On Monday afternoon the above well-known local players met on the Bank Quay Bowling Green to de- cide an engagement to play a game at bowls, 61 up, in I which Gleave agreed to give Shaw five points start, the stake at issue being .£lO. There was a good attendance of spectators, and the greatest interest was taken in the match, as Gleave is considered to have few superiors on the green, which was in excellent condition. Shaw was the first to score, and, playing in good form, only allowed his opponent to get once within the points conceded, when his score stood at 34 to Gleara 30. Shaw afterwards rapidly left his oppo- nent in the rear, and at the conclueion of the game the scores were: Shaw, 61; Gleave, 45. SOUTHWORTH-WITH-CROFT SCHOOL TIGARD —A special meeting of the above Board was held at the Board Semol on Tuesday evening; present: the Rev T P Kirkman (chair- man and clerk), and Messrs James Hatton, Lewle Birchall, Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon (attendance officer.)—This probably being the last meeting of the Beard as at present constituted, and several accounts having been passed, Mr Birchall moved, and Mr Hatton seconded, a hearty vote of thanks be given to the Chairman and Clerk for his services to the Board for the past nine years, which bad been given without remuneration.—The motion having been supported by Mr Turner was carried unanimously.—A vote of thanks was also given to Mr Hatton (who has left the township), for his services as treasurer to the Board for the lest nine years, on the motion of Mr Turner, seconded by Mr Birc- hall, and supported by the Chairman. DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT FIDLER'S FERRY —The body of an Irishman named William Quinn, a labourer employed at Penketh Hall Farm, 45 years of age, was on Tuesday taken out of the canal at Fidler's Ferry. The de- ceased was last seen alive on the 26,h September by a fellow workman named William Coppinger, with whom be on that day attended a sale in the neighbourhood. They went to Fidler's Ferry to purchase some drink, and Coppinger left the &ceased on the canal bank for a few minute% On his return his companion had disappeared. In consequence the canal was dragged, and the body recovered on Tuesday It was removed to an inn to await an inguest.—Yesterday morning Mr Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest respecting the occurrence at the Ferry Inn, Fidler' Ferry, when Coppinger gave evidence to the effect that he left the deceased on the canal side to go to the Ferry Inn, and when he returned nothing was to he seen f his companion— Henry Draper deposed to dragging the canal and finding the body,—The jury returned a verdict of "sound drowned."

Mr Swinburne brie joined the League for the abolition of the House of Lords. • The ex-Empress Eugenie arrived at Dover from Paris on Friday evening, and proceeded for Faruborough per Sonde Eastern Railway. Lieut-General Robert Leith is gazetted Colonel of the Worcestershire Regiment, and General Edward eorrierset Colonel Commandant of the King's Royal Rifle Corps. A Conservative meeting, held at Derekam, Norfolk, on Friday, was the scene of considerable disorder, the speakers Sir J Buxton,• M.P., and Mr C S Read, M.P., being re- peatedly interrupted by a number of unenfrarichised artizans and labourers who were present. PiNSDNED BY EATING .`IIRIMPS: SIXTY-NINE VICTIMS. —The Press Association's Margate correspondent telegraphs —Sixty-nine inhabitants of East and West Northdown Hamlets, situated near Margate, have been poisoned by eat- ing seriinps. The Hamlets comprise 22 houses, at 18 of which shrimps were delivered, and 14 out of the 18 fatni• ' lies have been attacked. The four families which escaped , boiled their shrimps, and from this it has been conjectured, though without proof, that eaeing them unboiled caused the mischief. One of the victims has died. CIREAT STORM—NINETEEN SHIPS AND MANY LIVES Loar.—Messrs elimou'e steamer Craigforth, which arrived at Leith from Iceland, brings intelligence of a fearful hur- ricane which swept over the island on the 11th September. The storm is said to have been of the nature of a cyclone, and has caused great destruction to property and shipping. It is said that nineteen ships, chiefly Norwegian traders, have been lost and thirty two disabled, while sixty small fishing boats were totally wrecked with great loss of life. Among the vessels wrecked was a Hartlepool fish jog smack named the Escurial, the crew of which have been brought home by the Seafortb. The inhabitants of the island ele- ' Scribe the gale as having been of unprecedented severity. SERIOCS CARRIAGE ACCIDENT TO LORD CRICHTON'S FAMILY.—On Tlaureday night a shocking carriage accident , occurred at Beefiten Castle, Cheshire. The children, go- I verness, and Maid servant of Lord Crichton, who had been chiting at Little Haworth. were driving to the station en route to Crum Castle, Newtown Butler, Ireland. 'While coming down the hill approaching the railway station, the spring of the caeriage broke, the horse ran away, and in a few yards the carriage tient, and Lord Crichton's children and govercess were plebe out with great violence. Tbe horse galloped home with the shafts only attached to the harness. The carriage turned completely over, burying the children beneath it. They were rescue& but it was found that they had suffered severe bruises. The maid servant, who wee riding on the bex, fell on her head, and on. Fri- day morning lies at Ramon Ceette Hotel unconscious. having been in that condition all night, Slight hopes only are entertained of her recovery.
FRENCH REGARD FOR ENGLISH INTERESTS IN

div.head: CHINA.
div.p: CHINA.

The Central News save :—We have received from the Foreign Office a copy of a note addressed to the British Em- bassy in Paris, by M Ferry, in reply to a suggestion by Earl Granville tbat the Freoch Goverment should cause to be made known in Engtied the steps svh;ch had been taken to secure the safety of foreign residents in China. M Ferry states that the Commander-in-ChM of the French fleet in the China seas, was from the commencement of operations specially directed to take every rOssible measure for secur- ing the safety of foreigners resident at the ports, and the protection of their interests with the 'kW of securing the Treaty ports and the foreign concessions against a Chinese rising. The French plan of operations was so arranged as to keep such places as far as possible outside the sphere of the direct action of the French forces. For instance M Ferry points out that the bombardment of Foochow by Ad- miral Courbet was exclusively dirscted against the Chinese fleet, the arsenal], and the fortifications of the river Ching, and that no attempt was made against the town itself as distinct from the fortified positions, at the same time the Chinese Governor of Shanghai, in accordance with an un- derstanding arrived at with the French Consul, published a proclamation intended to reassure the inhabitants, and threatening severe penalties against those who should at- tempt to cause disturbances. This arrangement, however. the Court of Pekin subsequently refused to sanction. M Ferry is glad to learn that these assurances are considered to be of a nature calculated to produce a good impression, with the English public, an showins the eolicitude of the French Government for the interests of British commerce.

BOMBARDMENT AND RECAPTURE OF BERBER BY GENERAL uoßnmv. FLIGHT OF THE REBELS. CAIRO, FRIDAY.—The Khedive has received a telegram stating that Berber has be.n recaptured from the rebels, who, however, succeeded in removing their treasure. Sixty more rowing boats have arrived from England. The block on the railway to Assiout has been cleared away, and 40 rowing boats can now be sent up daily. CAIRO, FRIDAY AFrERNOON —A messeozer from Atobi• kol has arrived at the front, and reports that General Gor. don, with a force in armed steamers, has descended the Nile sod bombarded Berber

The Prss Association is enabled to state that the Govern- ment received a telegram from Sir Evelyn Baring this morn- ing which places Veyond all doubt the truth of the report in Renter's telegram from Cairo of the recapture of Berber from tke rebels. Sir Evelyn reports that General Gordon, after bombarding Berber for some time, entered the town and recaptured the place, the rebels and the hostile inhabi- tants having fled after the bombardment had taken place. THE REPORTED RECALL OF LORD WOLSELF.Y. CAIRO, FRIDAY.—The statement of a London morning paper that Lord Wolseley has been recalled and that General Stephenson will assume the command of the expedition is denied en official atithority. A Central News Cairo tele- gram confirms the statement that Lard Woieeley's recall is there officially denied.

The Pe kall Gazette, referring to the telegram in Fri- day morning's Tenses. stating that Lord Virolseley bad been recalled, says: "The ,whole story is a canard. How it originated we do not knotr, nor can we even gne.s. Lord Wolselev tuts not been recalled. He is within telegraph range of Downing-street, but at Downing-atreot they know nothing of any such summons home an that which the un- impeachable correspondent at Alexandria announce."

The pnlice offered a stout resistince. but the mob overpowered them, .eized the Court- house, and killed the alcalde. In the confilct the chief of police and twenty other persons were also killed. THE A MEER IIF AFGHANISTAN AND THE BOUNDARY COMMISSION.

Sinics, Fan)Ay.—The Ameer of Afghanistan has issued a proclamation informing the people of the passage of the Afghan Boundary Commission through Afghan territory, and urging them to assist the Cortmaission in every way. The proclamation has been read at a parade of troops, and in the chief mosques or Cabal.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON MAN AT NTIGAN.--- About noon on Wednesday a man named Henry Wright, 44 years of age, who resided at Fennell-street, Warrington. and was in the employment of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, of Daliam Forgo, died at Wigan, from injuries accidentally received whilst following his business as a fitter's labourer. The firm by whom he was employed having purchaerst a forge at Spring Branch, Wigan, the deceased was sent there temporarily to aesist in pulling down a quantity of shafting'. While at work on Wednesday he Was struck on the bead by' the and of one of the shafts, sustaining such injuries that he died alums'. instantaneously. The deceased /eaves a wife and family.

THE SHOCKING GUN ACCIDENT TO A CHESHIRE FARMER. —MrJohn Ward, farmer, of &fathoms, near Middiewich, died on Tuesday morning from the effect, of an accident which betel him last week whilst out shooting on his farm. Accompanied by a neighbour (Irfr Hrett), he was walking into his fields for the,purpose of shooting rabbits. He car- ried a double-barrelled gun, and it Ia supposed that the pin which held the barrel and stock together fell out, and, the turret dropping to the ground, the charge exploded, entering one of Mr Ward's legs. Drs Moore and Moreton placed the sufferer ander chloroform, and amputated a portion of the right leg, but death took place after a few days. The de- ceased was much respected in the town and neighbourhocd. PANGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT :SOCIETY.— The seventh session of this society commenced on Thurs- day, when a very enjoyable soiree was held in the Wesleyan School-room, presided over by Mr Edwin Richardson. The programme opened with a pianoforte solo, "Silvery Waves," by Mr Walter Bennett, after which Mr Richardson, in an interesting and appropriate address, alluded to the impor- tance of societies of this kind nowadays, when every ques- tion has to be discussed thoroughly in all its bearings and to stand upon its own merits. The programme was then pro- ceeded with as follows :—Song, "love that Slumbers," by Mr W H J Jenkins; recitation, "England's Dead." Mr Leslie Wrightson; pone, "The Watchman and the Child,' Miss Yates: reading, " Mrs Candle's Curtain Lecture on Shirt Buttons," Mr Andrew Rathbone ; song, "The Roll- call," Mr Percy Grange ; reading. "The Lifeboat," Mr Frederick Wright;. song, "Tit for Tat," Miser E J. Bennett ; reading," The Prince of Wales," Mr J E Richardson;. song. "Golden Love," Miss Yates ; some, Anchor's Weighed," Mx Jenkins; reading. "The Kelpie of Cor- rievreckan," Mr Arthur Bennett; and pianoforte solo, "Home Sweet Home," Miss Nellie Bennett. Miss E J Ben- nett was encored for her rendering of " Tit for Tat," as were also Mies Yates for her song "Golden Love," and Mr Jenkins for "The Anchor's Weighed." The usual votes of thanks brought a very pleasant evening to a close. On Thursday evening neat a public lecture will be given in the wealeyan school-room by the Rev J MoTurk, in connection with the society.
